choices.label: Offer half your turnip

outcome.text: You split your turnip and gained a friend for life. The finest trade you will ever make.

choices.label: Challenge them to a pebble contest

success.text: You lost the contest on purpose (mostly) and won a friend. Cunning diplomacy.

failure.text: You won too hard and gloated too long. They stomped off. The pebble remains your only trophy.

choices.label: Hide behind the goose

outcome.text: Sir Quackbeard hissed. The smith’s child fled. Your social circle remains: one goose.

events.title: A KINDRED SPIRIT
events.text: A traveller laughs at your worst joke and stays for the explanation. By the time you share a bench, you know the kindness was deliberate.

choices.label: Stand them a round (3g)

outcome.text: Ale flowed, tales grew taller, and by closing time you had sworn eternal friendship twice. Once even sober.

choices.label: Swap stories but guard your purse

outcome.text: A fine evening of talk. You part warmly, but strangers stay strangers when the purse stays shut.

events.title: A DEBT OF STEEL
events.text: In the training yard a falling practice beam nearly brains another squire, and you shove them clear at the last instant.

choices.label: Help them up and make light of it

outcome.text: "I owe you my skull," they grin, clasping your arm. You have gained a shield-brother, the kind who stands beside you when it costs him something.

choices.label: Demand a favour in return

outcome.text: They pay you a grudging coin and remember the price of your help more than the help itself.

events.title: ENVY IN THE LANE
events.text: A neighbour has begun comparing your fortunes in public. The list contains every piece of your luck and none of the work that preceded it.

choices.label: Try to win him over

success.text: You disarmed his envy with honest flattery about barrels. Not a friend, perhaps, but no longer an enemy.

failure.text: He took your kindness for gloating. The feud is now official; he has already composed insulting verses.

choices.label: Let him stew

outcome.text: You ignore him. The grudge ferments nicely in its barrel. Aldwin is now, formally, your rival.

choices.label: Mock him first, publicly

outcome.text: Your jibe about his wobbliest barrel drew roars of laughter. Aldwin will never, ever forgive it.

events.title: THE GREYING COURTIER
events.text: An experienced courtier offers to teach you which doors to knock on and which invitations mean you are being sent out of the room. The second lesson was expensive to learn.

choices.label: Become their protégé

outcome.text: You gain a mentor who knows where every body at court is buried, and can point to three of them from the window.

choices.label: Suspect a trap and decline

outcome.text: At court, kindness is usually bait. You bow out gracefully, and wonder for years what they knew.

events.title: A LORD TAKES NOTICE
events.text: A lord offers a place in the retinue, with protection and obligations to be spoken before witnesses. The promise is useful precisely because it will be remembered.

choices.label: Kneel and swear the oath

outcome.text: You swear fealty before the hall. A liege’s favour opens doors, and his wars are now your wars.

choices.label: Keep your independence

outcome.text: You decline with careful courtesy. Bramwell nods slowly. Freedom kept, favour lost.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE COMES
events.text: A traveller is taken ill in the square. By evening the news has reached every door, growing more certain as the evidence becomes harder to find.

choices.label: Flee to the hills at once

success.text: You fled to the high pastures and waited it out. Lonely and hungry and breathing.

failure.text: You fled, but carried the sickness with you. The fever finds you on the road.

effects.death: Taken by the Pestilence on a lonely hill road.

choices.label: Stay and tend the sick

success.text: You nursed the dying with rags and prayers and somehow did not fall ill. The village calls you blessed.

failure.text: You tended the sick, and the sickness took you in turn. A merciful death, the priest says. He is lying.

effects.death: Died of the Pestilence, tending those who could not be saved.

choices.label: Barricade yourself indoors

success.text: You sealed the door and rationed turnips for a grim season. The Pestilence passed you by.

failure.text: It came through the rats, through the very walls. There was no barricade against it.

effects.death: Died of the Pestilence, alone behind a barred door.

events.title: A WORLD MADE EMPTY
events.text: The sickness has eased, leaving exhausted households and urgent work. People are counting who is available before agreeing what labour is worth.

choices.label: Ask for wages that reflect the actual shortage

outcome.text: You earn more for urgent work and gain standing among labouring households. No particular neighbour is declared dead merely to explain the wage.

choices.label: Pay to restore a neglected dwelling

outcome.text: You improve your own household’s shelter and standing. You do not acquire somebody else’s cottage simply by noticing its empty door.

choices.label: Help with the ordinary work of recovery

outcome.text: You improve household food and public health conditions through practical aid. The quiet work does not require a triumphant explanation.

events.title: THE LEVY IS CALLED
events.text: The levy is called. A spear and a place in the line are offered with considerably more certainty than any account of when you will return.

choices.label: March with the levy

outcome.text: You march off to war, one frightened spearman among hundreds. The mud is the only certainty.

choices.label: Hide in the turnip cellar

success.text: You hid among the turnips until the sergeants gave up looking. Coward? Survivor? Both.

failure.text: They found you cowering and dragged you out by the ankle. Now you march AND everyone knows.

choices.label: Pay the fine to stay (8g)

outcome.text: A few coins to the sergeant and you keep your skin and your turnips. Money well spent.

events.title: THE GOOSE IS SUMMONED
events.text: The reeve summons Sir Quackbeard in a disputed theft. The clerk leaves space for a mark; the goose inspects whether it can be eaten.

choices.label: Interpret the honks

outcome.text: You translate three honks as "the baker did it." The baker confesses to avoid further poultry law.

choices.label: Let the goose speak

outcome.text: Sir Quackbeard bites the reeve. The court accepts this as strong testimony.

choices.label: Blame the pie

outcome.text: You accuse the pie of tempting honest men. The court pauses, then fines you for nonsense.

events.title: A PIG ON TRIAL
events.text: A pig is accused of eating chapel flowers. The court debates intent while the defendant attempts to consume the evidence basket.

choices.label: Defend the pig

success.text: Your speech on floral temptation moves the court. The pig is spared and immediately eats the verdict.

failure.text: Your defense collapses when the accused eats your sleeve.

choices.label: Demand harsh justice

outcome.text: The pig is sentenced to public shame. It appears immune.

events.title: HOLY BATHWATER
events.text: A friar sells holy bathwater that smells of yesterday’s broth. He calls the floating onion a sign that the blessing has taken.

choices.label: Buy a bottle (5g)

outcome.text: You drink it and feel warmth in the soul, or possibly leek. The friar calls both miracles.

choices.label: Expose the soup

success.text: You find a turnip floating in the relic jar. The crowd turns on him with ladles.

failure.text: The friar declares the turnip a sign. You are booed by people holding soup.

choices.label: Ask for bread too

outcome.text: The friar, impressed by your theology of lunch, gives you a heel of bread.

events.title: THE DOCTOR'S CURE
events.text: A leech seller offers to treat unpaid rent. His argument is that the landlord cannot demand blood if somebody else has already taken it.

choices.label: Pay for the dubious treatment (4g)

outcome.text: The treatment costs blood and coin without touching the rent. You leave with a clearer sense of what the leeches actually consume.

choices.label: Ask whether the landlord has agreed

outcome.text: The seller has not consulted the landlord. You gain judgement while the leeches continue to make a much simpler living.

choices.label: Sell a false specimen to the seller

outcome.text: You earn six gold and create a fraud charge. A worm in a cup has proved more difficult to defend than to sell.

events.title: SAINT SOMEBODY'S TOE
events.text: A seller displays a waxy toe attributed to a saint whose name becomes less certain when you ask for the history of the other nine.

choices.label: Buy the toe (7g)

outcome.text: The toe is wax. Your faith wobbles, but your candle supply improves.

choices.label: Ask it to bless you

outcome.text: Nothing happens. The seller says the toe is shy before crowds.

choices.label: Report him to the priest

outcome.text: The priest confiscates the toe, then quietly asks if there were any fingers.

events.title: THE ALEHOUSE OATH
events.text: The tavern agrees to dig defensive works before dawn. Nobody has agreed which side of the ditch Swineford ought to occupy.

choices.label: Dig bravely

outcome.text: By dawn you have made a ditch, lost a shoe, and invented a new smell.

choices.label: Sell shovels

outcome.text: You sell shovels at heroic prices. The moat is poor; your purse is excellent.

choices.label: Sleep under the table

outcome.text: You wake to find the moat is actually around you.

events.title: THE MILLER'S TOLL
events.text: The miller calls his enlarged scoop an improvement in accuracy. It is certainly more accurate at transferring flour into his own store.

choices.label: Challenge the measure

success.text: You find a stone hidden in his scoop. The village laughs until flour comes out of their noses.

failure.text: The miller talks faster than his wheel. You leave poorer and dusted white.

choices.label: Pay and remember

outcome.text: You pay quietly. Your revenge ripens like damp grain.

events.title: THE BELL RINGER'S BET
events.text: The bell ringer bets that you cannot sleep through matins. He holds the rope like a man whose confidence has a very direct source.

choices.label: Take the bet

success.text: You sleep like a blessed log. The bell ringer fears you may be part stone.

failure.text: The first bell launches you out of bed and into a bucket.

choices.label: Ring it first

outcome.text: You ring early. Half the village arrives angry, dressed, and spiritually confused.

events.title: THE TURNIP ORACLE
events.text: A root split by frost is being read as a weather omen. The keeper promises an answer before supper, when the evidence will be eaten.

choices.label: Study the crack rather than buy the prophecy

outcome.text: You learn how frost split the root and improve household food planning. The forecast is useful precisely because nobody claims it speaks.

choices.label: Buy it as food and end the performance

outcome.text: You make a meal of the disputed evidence. The household gains food; no prediction is proved merely because you are fed.

events.title: THE WRONG SPOON
events.text: The steward gives you a spoon whose use depends on the guest seated above you. You have been placed directly beneath a person who will not eat.

choices.label: Use the spoon and accept the risk of a joke

success.text: You choose correctly and gain a little courtly standing. The spoon performs the undistinguished task it was made for.

failure.text: You choose badly and lose standing. The steward now has a story in which the most important object is cutlery.

choices.label: Use bread and leave the rule untested

outcome.text: You eat neatly with bread and gain a little judgement. The idle guest remains the only person waiting on the spoon.

events.title: THE JESTER'S BITE
events.text: The jester has prepared a joke about your boots. The room is waiting to discover whether your power is large enough to survive a small laugh.

choices.label: Laugh loudest

outcome.text: You laugh first and steal the sting. The court likes a target who can bow.

choices.label: Insult him back

success.text: Your reply lands so neatly the jester bows to you. Terrible for him, excellent for your legend.

failure.text: Your comeback limps out and dies near the salt cellar.

events.title: A VERY OLD FAMILY TREE
events.text: A clerk offers a royal pedigree with space left for your preferred ancestor. The oldest branch of the family tree is still drying.

choices.label: Buy the ancestors (18g)

outcome.text: You gain three dukes, a saint, and one suspiciously handsome oak tree.

choices.label: Expose the ink

outcome.text: You point out the wet seal. The clerk says your eyesight is lowborn.

choices.label: Add the goose

outcome.text: Sir Quackbeard is inserted as a Norman baron. Somehow the chart improves.

events.title: THE GOLDEN FLATTERER
events.text: A courtier praises your judgement so extensively that the favour he wants has begun to sound overdue.

choices.label: Reward the praise (8g)

outcome.text: The praise doubles at once. Your nose is now compared to a noble ship.

choices.label: Ask what he wants

outcome.text: He wanted a post, a purse, and your cousin's hand. You give him none and keep your spoon.

events.title: THE BISHOP'S FISH
events.text: The bishop claims the largest fish on grounds of spiritual precedence. The dish has become an excellent test of how hungry theology can be.

choices.label: Agree piously

outcome.text: The bishop takes the fish and a second helping of the argument that got it for him. He blesses you between mouthfuls and has forgotten your name by the fruit.

choices.label: Argue theology

success.text: You prove the smallest fish is humblest and therefore holiest. The bishop loses appetite and argument, in that order.

failure.text: You confuse a psalm with a recipe. The bishop keeps the fish and the moral high ground.

events.title: THE SINGING LAWYER
events.text: A lawyer presents a boundary claim in rhyme. The verse is impeccable, which is awkward because the measurements are not.

choices.label: Join the rhyme

success.text: Your couplet wins the room and, somehow, the argument. The clerk copies it into the roll, where it will embarrass someone for a century.

failure.text: You rhyme "acre" with "baker." The judge ages visibly and rules against everyone present.

choices.label: Demand plain speech

outcome.text: Everyone thanks you except the lawyer, who was halfway to rhyming "ditch." The case is decided in an hour instead of a season.

events.title: THE COURT PORTRAIT
events.text: A painter has rendered your face with dismaying honesty. The clothes are splendid, so no one can claim the same mistake affected the whole canvas.

choices.label: Praise the honesty

outcome.text: The court admires your humility. The painter admits he painted the cabbage from memory. It hangs in the great hall for the rest of your life.

memory.note: A famously unflattering portrait hangs where everyone can see it.

choices.label: Demand beauty (10g)

outcome.text: The new version has heroic cheekbones and no known relation to you. The first one is not destroyed, merely moved somewhere with worse light.

events.title: HONOUR OF THE TURNIP
events.text: A knight mocks the root on your crest. The insult might be harmless if he were not waiting so eagerly to see what you will pay for a reply.

choices.label: Challenge him

success.text: You strike his shield so hard the turnip becomes fashionable.

failure.text: He knocks you into a cart of actual turnips. The symbolism is unbearable.

choices.label: Embrace the turnip

outcome.text: You declare the turnip humble, nourishing, and hard to kill. The crowd cheers despite itself.

events.title: THE SQUIRE'S HELMET
events.text: A squire has polished your helmet through a thin patch. You can now admire the work from both sides of the metal.

choices.label: Praise the work

outcome.text: The squire beams and drops the helmet on your foot.

choices.label: Teach discipline

outcome.text: You lecture on care, duty, and not blinding allies with shine.

events.title: THE PUDDING PRIZE
events.text: The tourney offers a spur for skill and a pudding for endurance. Competitors are becoming suspicious about which contest is expected to produce more casualties.

choices.label: Fight for the spur

success.text: You win the spur and only a modest limp. Chivalry smiles.

failure.text: You lose the bout and land face-first in the prize pudding. The heralds will describe this for years, always at feasts.

memory.note: Unhorsed into a pudding before the whole tourney field.

choices.label: Fight for the pudding

outcome.text: You win the pudding by terrifying everyone with sincerity, then eat a third of it standing up.

events.title: THE HORSE SERMON
events.text: The chaplain blesses the warhorses. One bows its head at exactly the right moment, creating an unfortunate comparison with the riders.

choices.label: Pray beside it

outcome.text: The horse sneezes on you at the amen. The chaplain calls it a sign, and the stable hands start calling you Blessed of the Bay Mare.

choices.label: Question its piety

outcome.text: It steps on your boot. The debate is settled, and the chaplain writes down that you doubted publicly.

events.title: A RANSOM IN POULTRY
events.text: A captured knight’s proposed ransom contains poultry, buttons and an account of why ready coin would be beneath the dignity of his house.

choices.label: Accept the ransom

outcome.text: The ducks arrive furious. The promise not to sing proves priceless, and the knight leaves owing you a courtesy he will one day be asked to repay.

memory.note: A knight ransomed himself in poultry and still owes a favour.

choices.label: Demand proper coin

success.text: His family pays in coin and apologizes for the ducks. They do not forget being made to apologize.

failure.text: His family sends more ducks. You have negotiated poorly and now keep five ducks.

events.title: THE RUSTY SWORD RELIC
events.text: A monk identifies your rusty practice sword as a martyr’s relic. You remember the smith making it, but the monk says certainty can be a spiritual obstacle.

choices.label: Donate it

outcome.text: Pilgrims kiss the rust. You feel pious and slightly worried about tetanus.

choices.label: Keep your sword

outcome.text: You keep it. The monk asks if your boot has any sacred blisters.

events.title: THE DUCKING STOOL HONOUR
events.text: A village asks you to settle a dispute by ducking both parties. The stated advantage is that nobody needs to listen to them finish.

choices.label: Dunk both equally

outcome.text: Justice splashes. Everyone leaves wet, offended, and weirdly satisfied. The village adds your name to the custom.

choices.label: Hear the case properly

outcome.text: You listen for an hour and discover the true villain is a missing cheese. Word spreads that you will actually hear a case, which is going to cost you every future afternoon.

events.title: THE BAD HERALD
events.text: Your herald announces a title from the rehearsal notes rather than the approved roll. The mistake describes your damp estate with painful accuracy.

choices.label: Accept the damp title and laugh first

outcome.text: You make the mistake safe to laugh at and gain household loyalty. The herald retains a job that suddenly feels much less secure.

memory.note: A herald’s joke became a title you chose to keep.

choices.label: Correct the roll without inventing a punishment

outcome.text: You have the proper title read and lose a little charm. The household learns you value precision even when everyone has heard the alternative.

events.title: THE FEAST DISASTER
events.text: At your feast, sauce catches fire just as a guest praises the kitchen’s originality. The cook waits to hear whether this is a compliment or a charge.

choices.label: Call it entertainment

outcome.text: You declare it a new French fashion. No one knows enough French to disagree.

choices.label: Blame the cook

outcome.text: The cook bows and points out you ordered "something memorable." Treason by accuracy.

events.title: YOUR FACE IN GLASS
events.text: A proposed chapel window gives you a halo and very prominent ears. The glazier says the ears will be less noticeable once people start praying.

choices.label: Praise the piety

outcome.text: You praise the holy light. At sunset, your ears glow across the nave.

choices.label: Pay for smaller ears (15g)

outcome.text: The glazier reduces them. The saint beside you now looks disappointed.

events.title: THE OVERPROUD COUSIN
events.text: A relative insists the family has always been noble while hiding the household’s old tools. The tools have a more convincing account of the past.

choices.label: Let him boast

outcome.text: He invents an ancestor who conquered a ditch. The room chooses to believe it, which means someone will eventually check.

choices.label: Mention the mud

outcome.text: You speak warmly of Swineford mud. Half the court laughs; the other half checks its boots. Your cousin does not speak to you until Candlemas.

events.title: THE REEVE'S PETITION
events.text: The reeve asks to tax smoke because it passes through your air. His calculation makes a cold, poor household look like a wilful tax evader.

choices.label: Reject the foolish tax

outcome.text: The villagers cheer. The reeve sadly scratches "cloud rent" from his next proposal. The whole village now knows what sort of lord it has, which is worth more than the four shillings.

choices.label: Allow a tiny tax

outcome.text: The treasury gains coin. Every chimney now smokes accusingly, and the reeve begins drafting cloud rent in earnest.

memory.note: You put a tax on chimney smoke and the village has not forgotten.

events.title: THE FRIAR AND THE PUDDING
events.text: A friar condemns appetite while concealing a pudding under his robe. A dark patch is developing exactly where the argument is weakest.

choices.label: Expose the pudding

outcome.text: The pudding drops at the word "temptation." The sermon ends early and sticky, and the friar remembers precisely who was pointing.

choices.label: Protect his dignity

outcome.text: You cough loudly while he rescues dessert. He blesses you with grateful crumbs and, more usefully, owes you a silence of your own one day.

memory.note: A friar owes you a kindness for a pudding nobody mentioned.

events.title: THE UPSIDE-DOWN FLAG
events.text: A sickness flag hangs the wrong way up. Two factions are arguing over the meaning of a knot nobody has offered to untie.

choices.label: Set it right

outcome.text: You fix the flag. The argument moves to whether you used the blessed ladder, and will still be running at Lammas.

choices.label: Declare both sides wrong

outcome.text: You declare the flag cannot read itself. This is called wisdom by three people and heresy by one, and it is the one who writes letters.

events.title: THE PARDONER'S BUNDLE
events.text: A pardoner offers forgiveness among the combs and trinkets on his stall. He recommends buying it before the afternoon prices rise.

choices.label: Buy forgiveness (6g)

outcome.text: He forgives you for sins you had not planned yet. Efficient, if troubling. You keep the paper, which is the part that will matter.

memory.note: You hold a pardoner’s letter for sins not yet committed.

choices.label: Ask for a receipt

outcome.text: He flees at the word "receipt." The crowd learns a valuable theology of paperwork, and repeats the story at every fair for a decade.

events.title: THE HEIR'S FIRST WORD
events.text: A young child in your household offers an early word that sounds like “goat.” You are asked to judge whether this demonstrates genius or somebody else’s example.

choices.label: Call it genius

outcome.text: You declare the child prophetic. The family begins watching goats for omens.

choices.label: Blame your spouse

outcome.text: Your spouse blames you back with better evidence.

events.title: FATHER'S TALL TALE
events.text: {{father}} tells a story in which the enemy gets larger every time the bowl is refilled. {{mother}} remembers being present and is finding the new numbers difficult.

choices.label: Believe Father

outcome.text: Your father glows with pride and retells it as eight taxmen.

choices.label: Ask Your mother for truth

outcome.text: Your mother describes the goose victory in brutal detail. Your father studies the floor.

events.title: SLEEPING THROUGH SERMON
events.text: {{spouse}} nods off during the sermon and snores into a pause designed for moral reflection. The reflection spreads to your bench.

choices.label: Wake them gently

outcome.text: They wake, nod gravely, and pretend the snore was theological agreement.

choices.label: Let it happen

outcome.text: The priest takes it personally. The pew takes it loudly.

events.title: THE WRONG DOOR
events.text: A marker has mistaken your door for one under sickness watch. The apology is being delivered from a distance the mistake itself has made unnecessary.

choices.label: Scrub it off

outcome.text: You scrub until the door is cleaner than your soul.

choices.label: Use the privacy

outcome.text: No one visits for weeks. Peaceful, except for the screaming outside.

events.title: THE BELL ARGUMENT
events.text: The bell ringer asks what a sickness warning ought to sound like. Everyone wants a warning that is accurate and not intended for them.

choices.label: Choose hopeful

outcome.text: The bells ring bright over a frightened village. For a moment people breathe easier, and afterwards they remember who chose the sound of that year.

choices.label: Choose frightening

outcome.text: The bells terrify everyone except the sickness, which has poor manners. Three households leave Swineford rather than hear them again.

events.title: THE BACKWARDS BANNER
events.text: Your unit’s banner has been sewn backwards. The commander says the enemy must not be allowed to learn how literally the company can face the wrong way.

choices.label: Fix it before muster

outcome.text: You fix the banner and earn respect from everyone who can read cloth.

choices.label: Call it strategy

outcome.text: The captain loves it. Confusion, he says, is half of war and most of command.

events.title: COUNTING ARROWS
events.text: The quartermaster’s arrow count changes every time a bundle is opened. He proposes blessing the total rather than counting the shafts.

choices.label: Count them properly

outcome.text: You count thirty-seven arrows and one suspicious knitting needle.

choices.label: Pray over the bundle

outcome.text: The arrows remain thirty-seven. The needle seems holier.

events.title: THE COWARDLY DRUM
events.text: The war drum splits before the muster. The drummer gives it an honourable speech and asks whether a barrel might be promoted into the vacancy.

choices.label: Praise the drum

outcome.text: The men laugh, then cheer. Morale is a strange stew.

choices.label: Find a barrel

outcome.text: You beat a barrel into service. It sounds terrible, but so does war.

events.title: A VACANT BARONY
events.text: A border barony lacks a lord. The council wants coin, manners, and someone foolish enough to live near raiders.

choices.label: Buy the claim (90g)

outcome.text: The seal is yours. Your patent is entered in the royal register; your household now holds a barony.

choices.label: Wait for a better chance

outcome.text: You smile, bow, and keep your purse closed. The chance may come again, if death does not get bored first.

events.title: OATH DAY
events.text: Your tenants gather to swear loyalty. They look hungry, hopeful, and very aware of your boots.

choices.label: Promise fair rule

outcome.text: You promise justice first and coin second. The crowd cheers like people who have heard promises before, but want to believe.

choices.label: Demand proper dues

outcome.text: You remind them that loyalty has fees. The strong nod. The poor stare at the mud.

events.title: A FACE FROM SWINEFORD
events.text: An old neighbor asks for mercy after stealing grain from your storehouse.

choices.label: Forgive the theft

outcome.text: You send them home with grain enough for winter. Nobles call it weakness. Everyone else calls it dinner.

choices.label: Make an example

outcome.text: The stocks fill by sunset. Your barns remain full, and your halls grow quieter.

events.title: RAIDERS AT THE BORDER
events.text: Smoke rises from the edge of your lands. Your steward asks whether to muster riders or count losses.

choices.label: Ride out yourself

success.text: You drive the raiders off and return with a dented helm and a louder legend.

failure.text: The raid breaks your line. You survive, but the songs do not flatter your horse.

choices.label: Pay scouts and guards (20g)

outcome.text: Paid guards do paid work. The raiders find easier prey, and your villagers sleep.

events.title: TAX SEASON
events.text: The ledgers are thin. Your steward suggests squeezing the villages. He says squeezing with a smile helps.

choices.label: Keep taxes light

outcome.text: The treasury groans, but the people bless your name in every bakehouse.

choices.label: Fill the coffers

outcome.text: Coin pours in. So do complaints. You discover complaints cannot be minted.

events.title: A POWERFUL MATCH
events.text: A neighboring house offers marriage ties. The portrait is flattering. Suspiciously flattering.

choices.label: Accept the match

outcome.text: The wedding is grand, costly, and full of relatives counting your plates.

choices.label: Politely decline

outcome.text: You decline with such grace that only half the family vows revenge.

events.title: LESSONS FOR AN HEIR
events.text: A child in your household asks how to rule. A dangerous question from someone holding a wooden sword.

choices.label: Teach mercy

outcome.text: You teach that power is lent, not owned. The child nods, then pardons a biscuit thief.

choices.label: Teach strength

outcome.text: You teach that crowns are held by steady hands. The child immediately orders the spoon drawer inspected.

events.title: THE COURT POET
events.text: A poet offers to make you immortal in verse. The first draft rhymes "baron" with "barren."

choices.label: Fund better rhymes (12g)

outcome.text: The second draft flatters your jaw, your wisdom, and a battle you barely attended.

choices.label: Banish the poem

outcome.text: The poet leaves, loudly comparing you to damp porridge. Annoying, but accurate in meter.

events.title: ROYAL FAVOR
events.text: A royal messenger praises your household. Praise from above is rarely free.

choices.label: Send a lavish gift (35g)

outcome.text: The crown remembers your generosity, which is the polite word for payment.

choices.label: Send loyal words

outcome.text: Your letter is loyal, cheap, and only slightly damp from panic.

events.title: SICKNESS IN THE VILLAGES
events.text: A fever moves through your lands. The physician asks whether the poor are worth expensive herbs.

choices.label: Open the stores (30g)

outcome.text: Herbs, bread, and clean straw save more lives than any sermon. People remember.

choices.label: Seal the manor

outcome.text: Your household survives behind locked gates. Outside, the bells do not stop.

events.title: A CLAIM TO THE CROWN
events.text: Your documented claim reaches the council while the reigning monarch’s mandate falters. The genealogist recommends bringing witnesses rather than fresh ink.

choices.label: Press the claim (140g)

success.text: Banners rise. Rivals kneel. Somehow, impossibly, the crown rests on your head.

failure.text: The claim collapses under laughter and steel. You flee with fewer friends and lighter coffers.

choices.label: Keep the secret

outcome.text: You tuck the family tree away. Some branches are best left unclimbed.

events.title: FIRST DAY WITH THE CROWN
events.text: Everyone bows. Everyone wants something. The crown is heavier than it looked on other heads.

choices.label: Speak of peace

outcome.text: You promise peace, bread, and fewer public hangings. The hall applauds cautiously.

choices.label: Speak of obedience

outcome.text: You promise order. The hall applauds very quickly, which is almost the same as love.

events.title: THE EMPTY TREASURY
events.text: The royal treasury contains 250 gold, two moths, and a note blaming the previous ruler.

choices.label: Seek gifts from wealthy households

outcome.text: Wealthy households contribute coin and grain to the royal appeal. The kingdom eats, and the donors keep very careful receipts.

choices.label: Raise royal taxes

outcome.text: The treasury fattens overnight. So does the list of people muttering near tavern doors.

events.title: REBELLION
events.text: A duke declares you unfit to rule. Rude, dangerous, and annoyingly well funded.

choices.label: Meet them in battle

success.text: The rebellion breaks. You return with torn banners and a kingdom that suddenly remembers its manners.

failure.text: Your army scatters. The council recognises a rival, removes your seal and sends you into exile.

choices.label: Offer pardon

outcome.text: You offer mercy with one hand and hold guards behind the door with the other. It works.

events.title: ROYAL PROGRESS
events.text: You ride through the kingdom so people may cheer, complain, or throw root vegetables from a patriotic distance.

choices.label: Hear every petition

outcome.text: Your ears ache, but your people feel seen. Even the beet-thrower bows.

choices.label: Wave from the carriage

outcome.text: The route is shorter, cleaner, and less informative. Royal wrists are delicate things.

events.title: THE HEIR QUESTION
events.text: Courtiers whisper about succession. They do this loudly enough to be helpful and insulting.

choices.label: Name an heir publicly

outcome.text: The court exhales. A named heir is a shield against chaos, and a target for everyone ambitious.

choices.label: Keep them guessing

outcome.text: Mystery has power. It also has daggers.

events.title: A GRAND FEAST
events.text: Foreign envoys arrive. The cook asks whether to serve modest dignity or edible showing off.

choices.label: Feast like legend (45g)

outcome.text: The tables groan, the envoys beam, and someone writes a ballad about the pudding.

choices.label: Serve simple fare

outcome.text: The meal is plain, honest, and described by envoys as "educational."

events.title: JUSTICE DAY
events.text: Two nobles argue over land. Both have witnesses. Both witnesses look purchased.

choices.label: Judge by evidence

outcome.text: You untangle lies until truth limps into view. The court hates how long fairness takes.

choices.label: Favor the richer house

outcome.text: The richer house wins, naturally. Justice wears a very expensive hat today.

events.title: SWINEFORD REMEMBERS
events.text: Your birth village sends a gift: a turnip wearing a tiny crown.

choices.label: Laugh and reward them

outcome.text: You laugh until the court dares to join in. Swineford receives a new well and unbearable pride.

choices.label: Ban the joke

outcome.text: The turnip is removed. Unfortunately, jokes grow better underground.

events.title: THE HOLY CROWN
events.text: A bishop suggests your rule needs divine polish. He has incense, hymns, and a very large invoice.

choices.label: Hold a sacred rite (35g)

outcome.text: The rite dazzles the realm. Even skeptics bow while checking where the smoke comes from.

choices.label: Rule without incense

outcome.text: You decline. The bishop looks wounded, which is a skill bishops practice.

events.title: A KNIFE IN THE CURTAIN
events.text: At midnight, a curtain sneezes. Curtains should not know how.

choices.label: Trust your guards

success.text: Your guards seize the assassin. Loyalty, it turns out, is cheaper than a funeral.

failure.text: The guards are late. The knife is not.

effects.death: Assassinated behind a curtain. A poor review for the guards.

choices.label: Sleep in armor

outcome.text: You survive the night and wake shaped like a soup pot.

events.title: YEARS UPON THE THRONE
events.text: You have ruled long enough that young courtiers think you were born wearing the crown.

choices.label: Celebrate the realm

outcome.text: Bells ring from coast to border. For one bright day, even your enemies pretend to enjoy you.

choices.label: Take the praise quietly

outcome.text: You accept the praise with a small nod. The crown has taught you the value of neck muscles.

events.title: THE WEARY CROWN
events.text: Your bones ache. Your heir is ready enough. The throne looks more like a chair every year.

choices.label: Abdicate with grace

outcome.text: You lay the crown down and live to hear people miss you. A rare royal victory.

choices.label: Cling to power

outcome.text: You grip the throne until your knuckles pale. The court smiles the way knives smile.

events.title: A LAW FOR COMMONERS
events.text: A clerk proposes a law protecting common folk from noble whims. Nobles call this the end of civilization.

choices.label: Sign the law

outcome.text: The common folk cheer. The nobles sulk. This is how you know the ink mattered.

choices.label: Shelve it forever

outcome.text: The law vanishes into a drawer deep enough to have weather.

events.title: WHAT WILL THEY SAY?
events.text: A chronicler asks how history should remember you. A dangerous thing, history.

choices.label: As a beloved ruler

outcome.text: The chronicler writes of mercy, bread, and a crown that remembered the mud.

choices.label: As a feared ruler

outcome.text: The chronicler writes carefully. Very carefully. Your enemies are described in the past tense.

choices.label: As truth allows

outcome.text: The chronicler sighs with relief and begins with the turnip fields.

events.title: AT THE CHURCH DOOR
events.text: a familiar face asks you to stand witness while two households marry off children who have met twice. The dowry is read out at the porch: eight ewes, a brass pot, and four shillings at Michaelmas.

choices.label: Stand witness and say the words

outcome.text: You say the words. Four households now consider you party to the bargain. In Swineford that is as binding as a seal and rather harder to break.

memory.note: You stood witness at a betrothal made between households, not people.

choices.label: Ask aloud whether the bride consents

outcome.text: The porch goes quiet. Canon law is on your side and nobody in the lane thanks you for it. She says yes, eventually, and everyone hears how long it took.

choices.label: Refuse to put your name to it

outcome.text: You walk back up the lane. They find another witness inside the hour, and remember that they had to.

events.title: THE FOUR SHILLINGS THAT NEVER CAME
events.text: Michaelmas passes and the four shillings do not appear. a familiar face is fairly sure an uncle used them to settle an older debt, and has begun praying about providence at considerable volume.

choices.label: Quietly make up the shortfall (4g)

outcome.text: You put four shillings on the table and let them believe it came from the uncle. Two people know otherwise, and one of them is the uncle.

memory.note: You secretly paid a dowry that was owed by somebody else.

choices.label: Name the uncle at the hallmote

outcome.text: You say it in front of the steward. The uncle is amerced sixpence and swears he will remember your face longer than the debt.

choices.label: Let them work it out themselves

outcome.text: You say nothing. They work it out in March, badly, in front of the whole lane.

events.title: ONE DOOR BARRED
events.text: The bride’s people demand the marriage go ahead. The groom’s people have barred their door and are shouting the missing shillings through it. a familiar face is stood in the lane between them holding the brass pot.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE FOUR SHILLINGS THAT NEVER CAME

choices.label: Broker a smaller dowry before witnesses

outcome.text: Six ewes, the pot, and the shillings forgiven. Both households sign because you made it hard to refuse in public.

choices.label: Send it to the church court

outcome.text: The consistory court will hear it at Easter, or the Easter after. The bride will be nineteen by then and the pot will have been sold.

choices.label: Let the match die in the lane

outcome.text: Everyone goes indoors. The ewes stay where they are, the pot comes back to you, and two households stop speaking for a generation.

events.title: LETTERS FROM AN EARLIER LOVE
events.text: A carter brings a bundle of letters a familiar face wrote to somebody else three summers ago. Read in the right room they are a precontract, which voids the marriage outright and disgraces every household named in it on the way out.

choices.label: Burn them in the hearth

outcome.text: They go up quickly. {{other.name}} watches the whole time and neither of you says anything about it ever again.

memory.note: You burned letters that would have voided a marriage.

choices.label: Carry them to the priest

outcome.text: The priest takes the letters as evidence for a church hearing. You gain standing for submitting them and lose {{other.name}}’s trust; no marriage is dissolved simply because a witness has arrived.

choices.label: Keep them somewhere you can find them

outcome.text: You put them under the floor of the byre. They are worth nothing until the day they are worth a great deal.

memory.note: You hold letters that could dissolve a marriage whenever you choose.

events.title: THE CHILDREN OF BOTH HOUSES
events.text: At the Lammas ale, children of the two houses ask you what the quarrel was actually about. Nobody living now agrees on the sum, and two people have already said "ten shillings" with total confidence.

choices.label: Tell them the whole of it

outcome.text: You give them the ewes, the pot, the uncle and the debt. They are disappointed by how small it all was. Nothing you could have said would have taught them more.

choices.label: Give them the kind version

outcome.text: You tell them about eight ewes and a brass pot and leave the uncle out. It is a better story and it will hold for another generation.

choices.label: Tell them to mind the harvest

outcome.text: They go back to the sheaves. The quarrel keeps its teeth for whoever asks next.

events.title: THE LAST WITNESS AT THE PORCH
events.text: The last person living who stood at that church door offers to say what really happened, but only if both households sit at one table to hear it. Everyone involved is now old, and not one of them is sorry.

choices.label: Set the table and sit them down

outcome.text: It takes most of an afternoon and two jugs. Nobody apologises, but by the end they are arguing about sheep prices instead, which is as close to peace as Swineford gets.

memory.note: You got two feuding households to sit at one table and hear the truth.

choices.label: Let it die with the witness

outcome.text: The witness is buried in spring and takes it with them. Both houses go on believing the version that suits them, and both are wrong.

events.title: A CHILD AT THE THRESHOLD
events.text: a familiar face carries an orphaned child to your door on the eve of Martinmas. The child owns a blanket, a wooden spoon, and no surname anyone will admit to.

choices.label: Give the child a place at your fire

outcome.text: You clear a corner by the hearth. The parish is relieved, your stores are not, and the child sleeps for fourteen hours.

choices.label: Find them a place at the mill

outcome.text: The miller takes the child for the work in them. It is a roof, and it is not a kindness, and you knew both when you arranged it.

choices.label: Turn them away

outcome.text: You shut the door. The child is taken in three doors down by people with less than you, and Swineford counts the doors.

events.title: THE BIRTH KIN COME BACK
events.text: The child’s blood family appears at the gate. They do not want the child back. They want it acknowledged that the child owes them service for the roof they gave first.

choices.label: Pay them to go away (6g)

outcome.text: Six shillings and they are gone by dusk. They will be back in three years, having spent it, with the same argument.

choices.label: Take it to the hallmote

outcome.text: The steward rules the claim has no standing, the birth kin are amerced fourpence for troubling the court, and the whole village now knows the child’s business.

choices.label: Put it to the child

outcome.text: The child stands in the gateway and picks. It takes a long time and everybody has to watch.

events.title: THE LOAVES THAT WALKED
events.text: You find the lardarium lighter than it should be. The child has been carrying bread out to a household that has not eaten since Tuesday, and has got quite good at it.

choices.label: Send more, and openly

outcome.text: You put a basket on their step yourself. It costs you a fortnight of stores and buys you something the stores could not.

choices.label: Explain what a theft costs, then look away

outcome.text: You explain leyrwite, amercement and the pillory in some detail, then go to bed early and stop counting loaves.

choices.label: Put a lock on the lardarium

outcome.text: The bread stops walking. So does the child’s habit of looking at you when you come in.

events.title: A PLACE AT THE FORGE
events.text: A smith offers the child a seven-year indenture. The premium is two marks, and the child leaves the household the day it is sealed and does not come back.

choices.label: Pay the indenture (14g)

outcome.text: The indenture is cut in two and you keep the ragged half. The child is a smith’s apprentice by Whitsun and cries on the way out of the gate.

memory.note: You paid two marks to put your foster child into a trade.

choices.label: Keep them home for the harvest

outcome.text: You need the hands and you say so honestly, which does not make it land any better. The smith takes another boy.

choices.label: Send them to the priest for letters instead

outcome.text: Cheaper than a forge and slower to pay. The child learns to read a rent-roll, which in Swineford is very nearly a weapon.

events.title: WHICH NAME AT THE VIEW OF FRANKPLEDGE
events.text: Grown now, the ward must give a surname at the view of frankpledge, in front of the tithing and the steward’s clerk, and it will be written down and kept.

choices.label: Offer them your name

outcome.text: The clerk writes it without looking up. Your family gains a member and a set of complications, in that order.

memory.note: Your foster child took your surname at the frankpledge view.

choices.label: Tell them to keep their own

outcome.text: They give the name they were born with, in a clear voice, and the tithing writes it down as though it had never been in doubt.

events.title: THE UNEQUAL BOWLS
events.text: a familiar face says at supper what the family has arranged silently for two generations: the eldest takes the land, and everybody else takes goodwill and a place to sleep until they marry.

choices.label: Say aloud that it is not fair

outcome.text: You agree, at volume, in front of everyone. The eldest puts down the bread and does not pick it up again that evening.

choices.label: Defend the custom of the manor

outcome.text: You point out that a divided holding feeds nobody. That is true. You then say it is why the thing has always been done, and that is a different argument wearing the same coat.

choices.label: Change the subject to the pig

outcome.text: You raise the matter of pannage in the lord’s wood. It works, for about a year.

events.title: THE CHRISTENING SPOON
events.text: A silver christening spoon goes missing after supper. Four siblings remember four separate deathbed promises about it, all made in the same room, apparently on the same afternoon.

choices.label: Search every chest in the house

outcome.text: You find no spoon, one hidden purse, and a letter nobody wanted read. The spoon turns up in June behind the salt.

choices.label: Buy a second spoon and say nothing (8g)

outcome.text: The silversmith asks no questions for an extra penny. Two spoons now exist and the family peace rests on nobody ever putting them side by side.

memory.note: You forged family peace with a duplicate christening spoon.

choices.label: Let the accusation lie where it fell

outcome.text: The blame settles on the sibling least able to argue back, which is why it settled there. Everyone is relieved and nobody says so.

events.title: A LINE IN A DIFFERENT HAND
events.text: a familiar face produces the parish copy of the will, and a witness who says the priest’s clerk took twopence to change one line of it after the sealing.

choices.label: Sue in the church court (5g)

outcome.text: Probate belongs to the church and the church takes its time. Two years later a ruling arrives that pleases nobody and costs more than the land.

choices.label: Have a quiet word with the clerk

outcome.text: He is very frightened and very forthcoming. You leave with six shillings of his money and a permanent hold on him.

choices.label: Let the will stand as written

outcome.text: One line stays changed. The family stops shouting and starts keeping accounts of who owes whom, which lasts considerably longer.

events.title: AT THE LAMMAS ALE
events.text: The quarrel follows the family to the Lammas ale, where the whole village is within earshot and saying nothing looks exactly like admitting it.

hasWorldMemoryType: A LINE IN A DIFFERENT HAND

choices.label: Say the grievance in the open

outcome.text: You lay it out in front of forty people and a barrel. It is true, it is satisfying, and the family will be explaining it at every ale for a decade.

choices.label: Toast the family and lie beautifully

outcome.text: You give a short speech about your parents that is almost entirely false and genuinely moving. Three people weep. The quarrel goes back under the table intact.

choices.label: Leave before the second barrel

outcome.text: You walk home in the light. Everything said after you go is worse than anything you would have said, and all of it is attributed to you.

events.title: WHAT THE DEAD ACTUALLY LEFT
events.text: The last of the elder generation is buried and the heriot is paid: the best beast, gone to the lord before the family sees a penny. What is left is the land, the spoon, and every word said while fighting over both.

choices.label: Divide it evenly, whatever custom says

outcome.text: You split a holding that was never meant to be split. Each share feeds one household badly instead of one household well, and nobody has to leave.

memory.note: You split the family land against custom rather than turn kin out.

choices.label: Take what the custom gives you

outcome.text: You take the whole of it, lawfully, and two of your siblings are cottars by Michaelmas. The custom is on your side every single day of it.

memory.note: You took the whole inheritance by custom and left your siblings landless.

events.title: SICKNESS AT THE MILLRACE
events.text: a familiar face takes a fever after a week clearing the wet millrace. Within four days nobody in Swineford will buy flour, and the miller is standing in his own doorway watching the queue not form.

choices.label: Buy a sack in front of everyone

outcome.text: You carry it home on your shoulder past the whole market. Three households buy after you and one of them tells you it was foolish.

choices.label: Keep well clear of the mill

outcome.text: You grind by hand for a season and stay entirely well. The miller notices which neighbours crossed the lane to avoid his door.

choices.label: Fetch the herb-wife for them (2g)

outcome.text: She comes for tuppence and stays two nights. The fever breaks on the second, and she is honest enough to say she may have had nothing to do with it.

events.title: THE MILL HOUSE FALLS
events.text: Three more in the mill house take it. Swineford argues over which kills faster, an empty belly or a wet cough, and grinds its corn by hand in the meantime, badly.

choices.label: Organise shared querns and shared labour

outcome.text: Six households, four hand-querns, and a rota you have to referee twice a week. Everyone eats and everyone complains about the rota.

choices.label: Grind your own and say nothing

outcome.text: Your household eats well and quietly. The smoke from your oven is visible from most of the lane.

choices.label: Argue for burning the mill’s stock

outcome.text: You get your way and a great deal of grain goes up in the yard. The sickness stops. So does the flour, three months before harvest.

events.title: THE CHARGE OF CONCEALMENT
events.text: a familiar face mends. A customer swears at the hallmote that the mill hid the sickness for a fortnight to keep selling, and asks for an amercement and the loss of the mill’s suit.

choices.label: Swear for the mill

outcome.text: You stand as an oath-helper and say the fortnight never happened. It probably did. The mill keeps its suit and you keep a debt you cannot name.

choices.label: Swear against it

outcome.text: You say what you saw. The mill is amerced two shillings, the customer buys you a drink, and the miller’s family stops speaking to yours entirely.

choices.label: Swear you saw nothing at all

outcome.text: The steward looks at you for slightly too long and writes it down anyway. Both sides now consider you unreliable, which is at least even-handed.

events.title: FORTY DAYS AND THE LAST GOOD GRAIN
events.text: A physician from the town wants the mill house shut up for forty days. The last sound grain in Swineford is inside it, and there are five weeks until harvest.

choices.label: Shut the door and go hungry

outcome.text: The door is nailed and the grain sits behind it. Nobody else takes the fever and everybody else is thinner by Whitsun.

choices.label: Grind it out first, then shut the door

outcome.text: Two days of grinding with the sick upstairs. Swineford eats through the summer and two more households take the fever in June.

choices.label: Pay the physician to find them well (5g)

outcome.text: He writes what you paid for and rides out before dusk. The mill opens, the grain sells, and in August the parish clerk starts a longer burial list than usual.

memory.note: You paid a physician to certify a plagued house as sound.

events.title: THE WHEEL TURNS AGAIN
events.text: The mill runs. Swineford keeps an unusually exact memory of who carried bread up that lane and who carried accusations, and both lists are still current.

hasWorldMemoryType: FORTY DAYS AND THE LAST GOOD GRAIN

choices.label: Buy the first sack of the new grinding (4g)

outcome.text: You take it at the old price in front of the market. The miller does not thank you, which is how you know it landed.

choices.label: Take your custom to the next village’s mill

outcome.text: It is a four-mile walk each way and a penny more a bushel. You make it every month for a decade and never once explain why.

events.title: A HAND ON THE WINTER ROAD
events.text: a familiar face has caught half the children born in Swineford. On the ice by the ford she puts her hand through a hurdle, and by the time she reaches the village she cannot close it.

choices.label: Take her in until it mends

outcome.text: She stays nine weeks and is a terrible guest. Every woman in the parish comes to your door to ask her things. It ruins your mornings and puts your household at the centre of the lane.

choices.label: Pay the barber-surgeon to set it (6g)

outcome.text: He sets it badly and charges well. The hand works, mostly, and neither of you says which two fingers do not.

choices.label: Send to the next parish for a midwife

outcome.text: One comes over for the worst of it and charges by the mile. It is sensible, it works, and {{other.name}} understands exactly what it means.

events.title: THE APPRENTICE ASKS FOR A HEARTH
events.text: The apprentice has attended four births and watched seven. She asks to use your hearth as the place she learns the rest properly, where there is light and clean water and somebody sober.

hasWorldMemoryType: A HAND ON THE WINTER ROAD

choices.label: Give her the hearth

outcome.text: Your main room becomes the place Swineford is born for the better part of a decade. It costs you firewood, sleep and privacy, and the parish burial list for infants gets noticeably shorter.

choices.label: Refuse. A birth is not a lesson

outcome.text: You say it plainly and she does not argue. She just looks at the fire until you leave. She learns anyway, on kitchen floors, in the dark.

choices.label: Give it, and charge for it

outcome.text: A penny a birth, payable by the household concerned. It is entirely reasonable and the entire village finds it repulsive.

events.title: THE HAND THAT WILL NOT WAIT
events.text: a familiar face goes back to work far too early and hides how the fingers lock in cold weather. You watch her drop a bowl in your own kitchen and blame the frost.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE APPRENTICE ASKS FOR A HEARTH

choices.label: Say it aloud in front of the apprentice

outcome.text: You name it in the room, once. She does not forgive you for a long time, and she stops going out alone in January.

choices.label: Keep it between the two of you

outcome.text: You say nothing to anyone and she knows you saw. It holds until the winter she cannot hide it, and then it does not hold at all.

choices.label: Quietly take the heavy work off her

outcome.text: You start turning up at the right moments with the right excuses. It costs you sleep and she pretends not to notice for both your sakes.

events.title: A HARD BIRTH AT CANDLEMAS
events.text: A birth turns bad past midnight. Master and apprentice stand on either side of the bed accusing each other of pride, and the woman on it is past caring which of them is right.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE HAND THAT WILL NOT WAIT

choices.label: Back the master

outcome.text: Forty years of hands against two. It goes badly for an hour and then it does not, and nobody afterwards can say which of them turned it.

choices.label: Back the apprentice

outcome.text: She does the thing the master called proud, and it works. The master leaves before dawn and does not attend another birth in that house.

choices.label: Put both out and send for the physician (8g)

outcome.text: He arrives at first light, charges a mark, and does almost exactly what the apprentice had proposed at midnight.

events.title: WHOSE HANDS SWINEFORD SENDS FOR
events.text: The next child is coming and the village has already quietly decided which pair of hands it wants at the door. You had rather more to do with that than you meant to.

choices.label: Speak for the old hands

outcome.text: They send for the master, as they always have. She is grateful, she is slower than she was, and everyone agrees not to mention the second thing.

choices.label: Speak for the new

outcome.text: They send for the apprentice. The master hears about it the same afternoon, from someone who enjoyed telling her.

events.title: THE MARKS ON THE MOULD
events.text: a familiar face has cast every bell in three parishes and can no longer see the tuning marks scratched on the mould. The workshop opens at dawn exactly as it always has.

choices.label: Read the marks aloud for them

outcome.text: You go down before the pour and call the numbers. It becomes a habit neither of you ever names, and it lasts five years.

choices.label: Tell the guild wardens

outcome.text: The wardens are correct, thorough and merciless. The workshop keeps its licence and loses its commissions, which amounts to the same thing more slowly.

choices.label: Say nothing to anyone

outcome.text: You leave it alone. Somebody else will see it eventually, and you will remember that you saw it first.

events.title: THE CORRECTIONS MADE AT NIGHT
events.text: The apprentice has been re-cutting the master’s moulds after dark and receiving neither credit nor thanks. He shows you once, by candle, and asks you to look away.

choices.label: Look away

outcome.text: You go home. The bells keep ringing true and the wrong name keeps going on them, and everyone concerned has agreed to this.

choices.label: Make the master see it

outcome.text: You put both of them in front of the same mould in daylight. It is a bad hour and the workshop is better run afterwards.

choices.label: Tell the apprentice to sign his own work

outcome.text: He starts cutting his mark into the crown of each bell where only the founder would look. Within two years the wardens have noticed.

events.title: THE BELL THAT CRACKED ON THE THIRD PEAL
events.text: The new bell splits on its third ringing. The parish blames failing eyes. You have seen the guild’s bill of metal for that pour and the tin in it was cheap and poor.

choices.label: Produce the bill of metal

outcome.text: You read the weights out in the churchyard in front of the wardens. The guild pays for the recast and does not forget who made them.

memory.note: You proved a guild sold bad tin and made them pay for the recast.

choices.label: Let the old eyes take the blame

outcome.text: The wardens are relieved, the parish is satisfied, and the workshop is finished. You are paid a mark for a silence nobody names as such.

choices.label: Pay for the recast yourself (12g)

outcome.text: Twelve shillings and no explanation offered to anyone. The parish gets its bell and spends a decade guessing why.

events.title: THE DEED ON THE BENCH
events.text: a familiar face pushes a parchment across the bench and asks you to read it out. It keeps the workshop open and puts the name over the door into somebody else’s hand entirely.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE BELL THAT CRACKED ON THE THIRD PEAL

choices.label: Read it plainly, clause by clause

outcome.text: You read every line including the one about the moulds. They sign anyway, but they sign knowing, which was the only thing you could give them.

choices.label: Buy the foundry yourself (30g)

outcome.text: Thirty shillings, the moulds, the debts and the apprentice. The name over the door is now yours and half the parish thinks you circled it for years.

memory.note: You bought a failing bell foundry from the man who built it.

choices.label: Tell them to sign and take the pension

outcome.text: They sign. There is a clause about a chair by the fire and the right to watch the pours, and it is honoured until the second winter.

events.title: WHOSE NAME GOES ROUND THE SHOULDER
events.text: The next bell rings clean over four fields. The inscription cut round its shoulder will be read by people who have not been born for three hundred years.

choices.label: The old master’s name

outcome.text: It goes up with his mark on it and he is helped out to hear the first peal. He says it is a little flat. It is not.

choices.label: The apprentice’s name

outcome.text: His mark, on the crown, in daylight, at last. The master does not come to the ringing and everyone notices the empty place.

choices.label: Yours, for paying for it

outcome.text: Your name, round the shoulder, in letters a hand high. It is entirely accurate and it sounds worse every time the bell rings.

memory.note: You put your own name on a bell somebody else spent a life learning to cast.

events.title: THE CHALICE IS GONE FROM THE AUMBRY
events.text: The parish chalice is missing from the aumbry, and a familiar face was seen coming out of the north door before first light with something under a coat.

choices.label: Ask them yourself, first

outcome.text: They say it was a lamb they were hiding from the reeve, and produce a lamb. The lamb is real. The timing is not.

choices.label: Raise the hue and cry

outcome.text: The whole tithing turns out, as the law requires, and finds nothing. {{other.name}} spends the night in the reeve’s outhouse on the strength of your word.

choices.label: Keep what you saw to yourself

outcome.text: You go home. Six people saw them come out of that door and you are the only one who has decided to be no help whatsoever.

events.title: A SLIVER OF GILT IN THE MARKET
events.text: A scrap of gilded rim turns up in a pedlar’s tray at market. a familiar face says flatly that it was planted by a man who owes them seventeen shillings and would like the debt to die with them.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE CHALICE IS GONE FROM THE AUMBRY

choices.label: Trace where the pedlar got it

outcome.text: Three days of asking ends at a tinker who bought it at Stourbridge fair from a man he cannot describe. It proves nothing and unproves nothing.

choices.label: Buy the scrap and pocket it (3g)

outcome.text: Threepence and no questions asked. You now own the only piece of evidence in the parish. It sits in your purse for a month before you understand what you are carrying.

choices.label: Take it straight to the reeve

outcome.text: He puts it in the box with the writs and thanks you formally. The pedlar is arrested and is very obviously not the man anyone is looking for.

events.title: A NEW ROOF AND SEVERAL FAT HENS
events.text: The one witness who was certain has changed his account. He also has a new roof this month, and considerably more hens than his yard can honestly explain.

hasWorldMemoryType: A SLIVER OF GILT IN THE MARKET

choices.label: Count the hens aloud at the hallmote

outcome.text: You do the arithmetic in public: a roof, nine hens, and a labourer’s wage. The steward strikes the testimony and the witness leaves the parish before Advent.

choices.label: Offer him more to change it back (10g)

outcome.text: He takes it, changes his story a third time, and is now worth precisely nothing as a witness to anybody at all, yourself included.

memory.note: You paid a witness to change his testimony back.

choices.label: Let the new roof stand

outcome.text: You say nothing about the hens. The case bends round the bribe the way water bends round a stone, and everyone can see the shape of it.

events.title: THE REEVE AND THE ARCHDEACON DISAGREE
events.text: The reeve is preparing a trial at the manor court. The archdeacon holds that a consecrated vessel is the Church’s business, and wants the relic recovered before anybody is judged for taking it.

hasWorldMemoryType: A NEW ROOF AND SEVERAL FAT HENS

choices.label: Back the reeve and the manor court

outcome.text: Secular justice, and quickly. The archdeacon writes a letter about jurisdiction that is still being quoted in that parish forty years later.

choices.label: Back the archdeacon

outcome.text: It goes to the church court, where the penalty is penance and the object comes before the person. The reeve does not speak to you until Lady Day twice over.

choices.label: Tell {{other.name}} to claim sanctuary

outcome.text: Forty days in the chancel, then abjure the realm and walk to the coast barefoot carrying a cross. It is not mercy. It is not the gallows either.

events.title: THE CHALICE COMES BACK IN A MEAL SACK
events.text: The chalice reappears on the church step in a meal sack, undamaged, with no note. Everybody has now been accused of something and nobody has been cleared of anything.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE REEVE AND THE ARCHDEACON DISAGREE

choices.label: Declare the matter closed

outcome.text: You say it loudly and often until it becomes true. Three households never speak again, and the parish is content to call that a resolution.

choices.label: Keep asking who carried the sack

outcome.text: You ask for twelve months and get an answer nobody wanted. By then the parish had stopped wanting one and rather resents being given it.

events.title: THE SILVERSMITH’S CONFESSION
events.text: A silversmith two towns over confesses he copied that chalice fourteen years ago for a churchwarden who wanted the original sold. Which vessel was actually stolen is now an open question.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE CHALICE COMES BACK IN A MEAL SACK

choices.label: Have the confession read in church

outcome.text: The parish learns it nearly hanged a neighbour over pewter under gilt. The churchwarden’s tomb is in the chancel and cannot be asked about it.

choices.label: Pay him for his silence (8g)

outcome.text: Eight shillings for his trouble and his quiet. The parish keeps its relic, its story and its grudges, and every one of them is false.

events.title: THE ACCOUNT READ BEFORE THE PARISH
events.text: The whole business is read out at the annual view: every accusation, every retraction, every hen. Silence from the innocent will cost as much today as speech from the guilty.

choices.label: Stand and say your own part in it

outcome.text: You give your account including the parts that do you no credit at all. Two others follow you up. It is the closest the parish comes to a reckoning.

memory.note: You gave a full public account of your part in the chalice affair.

choices.label: Stay on the bench

outcome.text: You keep your seat. The reading ends, everyone files out, and the whole business settles into the parish like damp into a wall.

events.title: VENISON IN THE WRONG HOUSES
events.text: a familiar face knows exactly who has been taking deer out of the lord’s wood, and knows which six households have eaten meat this winter because of it.

choices.label: Want no part of it

outcome.text: You say so plainly and are not asked twice. You are also not told anything, by anybody, for a very long time afterwards.

choices.label: Take a share of the meat

outcome.text: A shoulder, wrapped in sacking, left in your byre before dawn. Your household eats, and you are now inside something with no obvious door out.

choices.label: Warn the forester there is a gang

outcome.text: You tell him there is a gang without telling him who. Patrols double, the poaching stops for six weeks, and somebody works out where the warning came from.

events.title: A SNARE TAKES A FORESTER’S LEG
events.text: A hidden snare opens a forester’s leg to the bone. Poaching the parish quietly tolerated has become a hunt for blood, and the verderers are riding for the eyre.

choices.label: Carry him in and pay the herb-wife (4g)

outcome.text: You get him to the village on a hurdle and he keeps the leg. He remembers who took the front end, which turns out to matter enormously.

choices.label: Go out at night and clear the snares

outcome.text: Fourteen snares in one night by moonlight. Nobody thanks you, both sides suspect you, and no forester loses a leg in that wood again.

choices.label: Be somewhere else entirely

outcome.text: You are seen at the alehouse from noon to dark by nine reliable witnesses, which is the most suspicious alibi in the history of Swineford.

events.title: A SHARE OF THE SILVER
events.text: The gang offers you a cut of what the venison earns at market, if you can pull the village patrol off the coppice road for a single night.

hasWorldMemoryType: A SNARE TAKES A FORESTER’S LEG

choices.label: Take the silver and move the patrol

outcome.text: You send them the long way on a story about a broken hurdle. Six shillings arrive wrapped in cloth two days later.

memory.note: You were paid to divert the village patrol for poachers.

choices.label: Refuse, and tell them why

outcome.text: You tell them a leg is already open and the next thing opened will be a neck. They call you soft. Two of them privately agree with you.

choices.label: Take the silver and send the patrol anyway

outcome.text: Three of them are taken on the coppice road with your six shillings still in your purse. It is the cleverest thing you have ever done and you sleep badly for a decade.

events.title: THE APPROVER’S PARDON
events.text: One of the gang is offered a pardon for turning approver: he names every accomplice from the dock, a familiar face among them, and fights in the lists any man who denies it.

choices.label: Stand surety for {{other.name}}

outcome.text: You pledge your own goods against their appearance. If they run you are ruined, and every man in that court does the arithmetic while you are still speaking.

choices.label: Petition the lord for a common fine instead

outcome.text: You argue that hanging four tenants costs the manor four tenants. The steward finds this persuasive in a way that justice had not been.

choices.label: Let the approver name whoever he names

outcome.text: He names sixteen people, two of whom were nowhere near the wood. Three hang. His pardon is honoured in full and he is gone by spring.

events.title: THE WOOD GOES QUIET
events.text: After the eyre the wood is silent. Several households still eat because of venison buried in salt two winters ago, and loyalties considerably older than the forest law.

choices.label: Keep the buried stores moving

outcome.text: You shift salt meat between four byres for another three winters. It is a small crime conducted with enormous administrative care.

choices.label: Dig it up and end it

outcome.text: You burn what has gone over and return the rest. Two households go hungry in March who did not have to, and they know which choice did it.

events.title: THE NEW FORESTER OFFERS AN AMNESTY
events.text: A new forester offers to forget every snare in that wood, provided the village names who organised the gang. They have until Michaelmas to settle it among themselves.

choices.label: Give him the one who has already fled

outcome.text: You name a man who took ship at Boston two winters back. The forester writes it down, everyone knows exactly what has happened, and the amnesty holds.

choices.label: Let the village name nobody

outcome.text: Michaelmas passes in total silence. The amnesty lapses, the patrols double, and Swineford holds together in a way that costs it a great deal.

choices.label: Name who actually did it

outcome.text: You say the name in the open. The amnesty holds for everybody else, and you are the man who said it for the rest of your life.

events.title: WHEN THE DEER COME BACK TO THE COPPICE
events.text: The deer return in numbers nobody has seen in a generation. The poorest households ask, out loud, whether the law made the wood safer or merely emptier of them.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE NEW FORESTER OFFERS AN AMNESTY

choices.label: Say the law kept the wood

outcome.text: You make the case for forest law to people whose grandparents cleared that coppice. It is a sound argument and it persuades nobody who is hungry.

choices.label: Petition for a common right of pannage

outcome.text: Not deer. Pigs, in the wood, in autumn, by right. It is a smaller thing to ask for, it is granted, and it feeds Swineford every October after.

memory.note: You won Swineford a standing right of pannage in the lord’s wood.

events.title: AN ALIBI THAT IS PARTLY TRUE
events.text: a familiar face asks you to swear they were at your hearth on the night in question. They were. For roughly half of it.

choices.label: Swear to the whole night

outcome.text: You give the oath entire and they walk free. The half you invented sits in the court roll in a clerk’s beautiful hand for good.

choices.label: Swear only to the hours you had them

outcome.text: You give the court exactly what you know: not enough to clear them, not enough to hang them. Both sides find you useless and entirely honest.

choices.label: Refuse the oath entirely

outcome.text: You will not stand up at all. They find two oath-helpers elsewhere inside a day, neither of whom was anywhere near your hearth.

events.title: THE SECOND WITNESS IS TOO TIDY
events.text: The accuser’s family produces a second witness whose account is cleaner than any real memory has a right to be. He has the hour, the weather, and the colour of a coat.

hasWorldMemoryType: AN ALIBI THAT IS PARTLY TRUE

choices.label: Ask him what the rain did that night

outcome.text: You ask in front of the steward. He answers with total confidence and gets it wrong, and the court goes very quiet indeed.

choices.label: Produce a tidier witness of your own

outcome.text: You find somebody willing to be equally certain of the opposite. The court now holds two immaculate lies and no means of choosing between them.

choices.label: Let the clean story stand

outcome.text: It stands, and it wins. It was the best-told story in the room, and that is what the room was always going to decide on.

events.title: THE CLERK STILL HAS THE FIRST DRAFT
events.text: The steward’s clerk lets slip that the testimony was rewritten after the hearing, that he kept the original, and that he is a poor man with a great fondness for being helped.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE SECOND WITNESS IS TOO TIDY

choices.label: Buy the original (9g)

outcome.text: Nine shillings for one sheet of parchment that says something quite different from the roll. You are now a man who buys evidence.

choices.label: Report the clerk to the steward

outcome.text: He is dismissed inside the week and the roll stands uncorrected, because correcting it would mean admitting it was wrong. Justice, administratively.

choices.label: Tell him to hide it and say nothing

outcome.text: It goes into the church chest under the tithe books. It will surface in fifteen years at the worst possible moment. Neither of you says so, and both of you are counting on it.

memory.note: A rewritten testimony still exists, hidden in the church chest.

events.title: THE LIE WAS FOR SOMEBODY ELSE
events.text: a familiar face finally admits the lie was never about them at all. It was covering a third person, and naming that person now would do far more damage than the original charge ever could.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE CLERK STILL HAS THE FIRST DRAFT

choices.label: Name the third person

outcome.text: You say it and the whole shape of the case turns over. The damage is exactly as large as promised, and it lands on people who had done nothing.

choices.label: Carry the name yourself

outcome.text: You carry it. It is heavier than you expected and gets no lighter, and the wrong person stays under a shadow for years because you are decent.

choices.label: Make {{other.name}} say it themselves

outcome.text: You give them a month, then you stop giving them months. They say it badly, to the wrong people, and it costs them everything it would have cost you.

events.title: THE WRONGED HOUSEHOLD ASKS FOR THE RECORD
events.text: Years on, the household that lost the case asks the parish to correct the roll. Everybody who could be embarrassed by it is still alive, and most of them hold some kind of office.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE LIE WAS FOR SOMEBODY ELSE

choices.label: Get the roll corrected (6g)

outcome.text: Nineteen months, two petitions and a fee. One line struck and one line added, and the family read it aloud to each other every evening for a week.

memory.note: You got a false judgment struck from the manor roll years after the fact.

choices.label: Pay them instead (15g)

outcome.text: Fifteen shillings, and the record stands. They take it because they need it, and both parties understand precisely what has been bought.

choices.label: Tell them it is too late

outcome.text: It is too late, factually. They knew that when they asked, and the asking was the whole of the point.

events.title: NO HERO IN THE CORRECTED ROLL
events.text: The finished record names no hero. It names a great many people who found a small lie easier than a difficult morning, and it names them in a clerk’s immaculate hand.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE WRONGED HOUSEHOLD ASKS FOR THE RECORD

choices.label: Read it aloud at the view

outcome.text: You read every name, including your own. Nobody enjoys it. It is entered in the roll as read, which is the only monument the business ever gets.

choices.label: File it in the chest unread

outcome.text: It goes in with the writs and the tithe books, entirely accurate and entirely unread for the rest of the century.

events.title: THE COPE-CHEST COMMISSION
