events.text: a familiar face brings the guild wardens’ commission: a carved cope-chest in seasoned oak, delivered by Michaelmas. No honest craftsman in the shire could promise that date, and the alderman’s own son wants the work.

choices.label: Promise Michaelmas and worry later

outcome.text: You give them the date they wanted. The alderman’s son is furious, the wardens are delighted, and you have nine months to become somebody who can do this.

memory.note: You promised a masterpiece by a date no honest craftsman could meet.

choices.label: Give them the honest date

outcome.text: You say Candlemas and explain about seasoning oak. They take it to the alderman’s son, who promises Michaelmas within the hour.

choices.label: Ask to share it with another shop

outcome.text: Two shops, one mark, half the fee. The wardens dislike the arrangement and cannot fault the reasoning.

events.title: THE OAK ARRIVES SPLIT
events.text: The timber comes in with three boards split along the grain. The supplier stands in your yard and explains at length that your shop dried it wrong, which is not possible, because it has been in your yard for six hours.

choices.label: Take him before the guild court

outcome.text: You bring the carter, the tally and the six hours. He replaces the boards and adds your shop to a list he keeps of difficult customers.

choices.label: Swallow it and buy more oak (12g)

outcome.text: Twelve shillings out of your own purse and no argument in front of the apprentices. The work stays on time and the supplier does it again in spring.

choices.label: Work round the splits and say nothing

outcome.text: You hide two splits inside the carcase where nobody will look for thirty years. Somebody will look in thirty years.

memory.note: There are split boards concealed inside your masterpiece.

events.title: THE APPRENTICE HAS A BETTER JOINT
events.text: Your apprentice proposes a housed dovetail nobody in the shire cuts. It would save five weeks and put his hand permanently beside yours in the finished work.

choices.label: Cut it his way and say whose it is

outcome.text: You use the joint and tell the wardens whose idea it was. Your standing with the guild improves, and {{other.name}} trusts you with the next suggestion.

choices.label: Cut it his way and say nothing

outcome.text: You take the payment and the credit. {{other.name}} knows where the joint came from and loses trust in you; no journey is needed to carry that grievance.

memory.note: The joint your masterpiece is famous for was your apprentice’s idea.

choices.label: Cut it the way it has always been cut

outcome.text: Five weeks longer, the old joint, no argument with the wardens. It is the safe decision and the apprentice stops offering things.

events.title: THE PATRON WANTS IT CHEAPER
events.text: With six weeks left the patron asks for elm instead of oak and paint instead of carving, while still describing the piece to everyone in the county as a masterpiece.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE APPRENTICE HAS A BETTER JOINT

choices.label: Refuse and finish it properly

outcome.text: You finish it in oak at your own cost. The patron pays the reduced fee, tells everyone he commissioned it, and you are thirteen shillings poorer and correct.

choices.label: Give him exactly what he is paying for

outcome.text: Elm, paint, and a bill that matches. It looks well from six feet and you make certain the wardens know which decisions were his.

choices.label: Take it to the wardens

outcome.text: The guild rules a master may not be made to put his mark on elm. The patron pays in full, loudly, and never commissions anything in this town again.

events.title: THE UNVEILING AT THE GUILD HALL
events.text: The cope-chest stands in the hall with the wardens, the parish and the alderman’s son around it. Somebody is about to say aloud whose work it actually is.

choices.label: Tell the whole history of it

outcome.text: The oak, the splits, the joint, the elm, the apprentice. It is a very strange speech for an unveiling. They are still repeating it in that hall forty years later, and getting the ending wrong.

memory.note: You gave a full public account of how your masterpiece was really made.

choices.label: Accept the praise and go home

outcome.text: You bow, you are admired, and you leave early. The chest is beautiful and everything anybody says about it is slightly wrong.

events.title: FOUR CARTS TO STOURBRIDGE
events.text: a familiar face proposes a shared venture to Stourbridge fair: four carts, four partners, one purse. The profit is real and so are the roads between here and Cambridge.

choices.label: Put in a full share (20g)

outcome.text: Twenty shillings into a common purse held by a man you have known nine years. The others put in the same and everyone shakes on it in the alehouse.

choices.label: Put in a quarter share and keep the rest

outcome.text: You take a small stake and a small risk, and {{other.name}} notes exactly how small before agreeing very pleasantly.

choices.label: Lend them the money at interest instead

outcome.text: You are not a partner, you are a creditor, and the difference will matter enormously in about nine months.

events.title: ONE CART GONE IN THE NIGHT
events.text: A cart vanishes overnight outside Huntingdon with goods belonging to every partner except a familiar face, whose bales were moved onto another cart the previous evening for reasons that were entirely sensible at the time.

choices.label: Say the obvious thing aloud

outcome.text: You put it to them in front of the other partners. They have an answer for the bales and no answer at all for the timing.

choices.label: Insist the loss is shared four ways

outcome.text: You argue it through half a night and win. Everyone loses the same amount and the partnership survives, slightly bent.

choices.label: Say nothing and start keeping notes

outcome.text: You write down dates, bales and names in a little book. By Candlemas you have a very complete picture and nobody knows you have it.

events.title: THE DRIVER COMES BACK
events.text: The missing driver walks into Swineford three weeks later with a story about soldiers, mud, and a bargain struck at knifepoint. Roughly half of it can be checked and roughly half of it checks out.

hasWorldMemoryType: ONE CART GONE IN THE NIGHT

choices.label: Believe him and pay his wages

outcome.text: You pay him for the weeks he was gone. He works for you for eighteen years and never once mentions it, which is either gratitude or discipline.

choices.label: Ride to Huntingdon and check it

outcome.text: Four days and a lame horse. Half the story is true. That is the worst answer he could have brought back, and you have to act on it anyway.

choices.label: Hand him to the constable

outcome.text: He is held six weeks and released without charge. He does not come back to Swineford and his family stops speaking to yours entirely.

events.title: SAFE PASSAGE, MINUS ONE
events.text: A rival merchant offers the partnership armed escort on the Cambridge road for the rest of the season. His condition is that the poorest partner is dropped from the venture first.

choices.label: Refuse and travel unescorted

outcome.text: You go without the escort and nobody is dropped. It costs you two more losses that season and the partnership never once discusses breaking up.

choices.label: Take the escort

outcome.text: The poorest partner is out by Lady Day. The roads are safe, the season is excellent, and there is now an empty chair at every meeting.

memory.note: You traded a partner for safe passage on the Cambridge road.

choices.label: Buy the poor partner’s share yourself (14g)

outcome.text: You buy him out at a fair price, take the escort, and hold his stake in your own name. It is generous, it is profitable, and it is not the same as loyalty.

events.title: WHAT COMES BACK DOWN THE ROAD
events.text: The carts come home with less silver than anyone hoped and a reputation that may prove worth more. Every merchant between here and Cambridge now knows how this partnership behaved when it went wrong.

choices.label: Renew the partnership for another season

outcome.text: The same four names, or the three that are left. They sign again, which after this year is a considerably more serious thing than it was.

choices.label: Dissolve it and trade alone

outcome.text: You divide the purse on the table and shake hands. It is amicable, it is final, and you are considerably richer and slower for the next ten years.

events.title: HOURS BEYOND THE ORDINANCE
events.text: a familiar face speaks for the apprentices of three shops. The guild ordinance sets the working day from dawn bell to curfew; the masters have been quietly adding two hours at each end since Lady Day.

choices.label: Back the apprentices openly

outcome.text: You put your name to their complaint. Two masters stop sending you work the same week and the apprentices remember it for thirty years.

choices.label: Read the ordinance to both sides

outcome.text: You find the clause, copy it, and nail it to three shop doors. Nobody can claim not to know now. That was the point, and it costs you three friendly shops by Whitsun.

choices.label: Keep out of it

outcome.text: It is not your shop and not your quarrel. It becomes your quarrel by Candlemas, on worse terms.

events.title: A CONTRACT OFFERED QUIETLY
events.text: A master dismisses the complaint in public. In private he offers you the good commissions, first refusal, for a year, on the understanding that you have no further opinions.

choices.label: Take the contracts

outcome.text: The work is genuinely good and the silence is genuinely purchased. Both facts are true at once and only one of them is discussed.

memory.note: You were paid in commissions to stop speaking for the apprentices.

choices.label: Refuse, and say what was offered

outcome.text: You describe the offer word for word at the next guild meeting. The master denies it, everyone believes you, and nothing whatsoever is done about it.

choices.label: Take the contracts and speak anyway

outcome.text: You take the work and go on saying exactly what you said before. He cannot withdraw it without admitting what it was for, and you both know it.

events.title: TOOLS DOWN IN THREE SHOPS
events.text: The apprentices lay down their tools. Three shops are silent, the unfinished orders are somebody’s wedding chest and somebody’s coffin, and the town starts losing money on the second day.

choices.label: Get both sides in one room

outcome.text: Four hours, one barrel, and a written agreement about bells. It holds because everybody had to say their terms out loud in front of the other side.

choices.label: Finish the urgent orders yourself

outcome.text: You work nine days straight and deliver the coffin on time. The masters are grateful and the apprentices watch you undercut the only pressure they had.

choices.label: Feed the apprentices out of your own stores

outcome.text: Bread and pottage for nine young men for three weeks. It empties your lardarium and it is the reason the strike lasts long enough to win anything.

events.title: ONE NAME OR ALL OF THEM
events.text: The guild threatens to strike every apprentice from the register unless one of them accepts the blame in writing and is expelled for it. a familiar face is the obvious name and knows it.

choices.label: Put your own name on it instead

outcome.text: You sign as the instigator. You are barred from guild work for two years and nine apprentices keep their indentures, and everybody in the trade knows why.

memory.note: You were struck off the guild register to save nine apprentices.

choices.label: Let {{other.name}} take it

outcome.text: They sign, they are expelled, and they leave for Bristol in April. The eight who stayed are careful never to say the name out loud again.

choices.label: Tell the guild to strike off all fifteen

outcome.text: You point out that nine expelled apprentices is nine shops without hands in July. The threat is quietly withdrawn and never referred to again.

events.title: THE NEW CHARTER READ ALOUD
events.text: A revised shop charter is read out in the guild hall: hours, bells, holidays, and the price of a broken indenture. Everybody present can hear exactly whose bad year became a permanent rule.

hasWorldMemoryType: ONE NAME OR ALL OF THEM

choices.label: Put your seal to it

outcome.text: You seal it with the rest. It is worse than what was asked for and enormously better than what there was, and it outlives everyone in the room.

choices.label: Refuse to seal it

outcome.text: You say it gives back less than it took and decline. The charter passes without you, and in eight years somebody quotes your refusal in a very different argument.

events.title: THE BUSHEL THAT WEIGHS SHORT
events.text: a familiar face says the great tithe was taken this year with a bushel measure that does not match the one chained in the market house. In a lean year, one-tenth measured wrong is a fortnight of somebody’s bread.

choices.label: Carry both measures to the market house

outcome.text: You set them side by side in front of thirty people. The rector’s bushel is short by better than a quart and there is nothing anybody can say about it.

choices.label: Have a quiet word with the rector

outcome.text: He is embarrassed, blames a servant, and the measure is corrected before Lady Day without one word said in public. Nobody is punished and everybody eats.

choices.label: Pay the tithe as measured

outcome.text: You give the tenth as demanded and say nothing. Four households follow your example. The rector had been waiting all morning for exactly that.

events.title: THE GRANARY OPENS, WITH CONDITIONS
events.text: The rector opens the church granary and requires each household receiving grain to make its submission in writing first. The clerk has the roll ready and the grain is behind him.

choices.label: Sign first and openly

outcome.text: You put your name at the head of the roll so that poorer households do not have to be the first to bend. It costs you nothing but the sight of your own signature.

choices.label: Refuse to sign and go hungry

outcome.text: You walk out past the grain. Nine households sign, two do not, and the parish spends the rest of the winter deciding which of you was the fool.

choices.label: Buy grain elsewhere and share it out (12g)

outcome.text: Twelve shillings of Cambridge wheat, distributed from your own yard with no roll and no clerk. The rector’s granary stays remarkably full.

events.title: THE BISHOP’S CLERK COMES TO COUNT
events.text: A clerk arrives from the bishop to inspect the tithe accounts. Within a day it is plain that he is much more interested in who has been loyal than in whether the arithmetic works.

choices.label: Give him the accounts, all of them

outcome.text: You hand over every roll including the ones that embarrass the parish. He reads for two days and writes down four names, none of them about arithmetic.

choices.label: Coach the parish on what to say

outcome.text: You spend an evening in the alehouse making sure everybody tells the same true story. He finds nothing and reports the parish sullen. A parish with nothing to hide does not close ranks.

choices.label: Give him the name he came for

outcome.text: You name the churchwarden who has been selling tithe hay on the side. It is entirely true, it satisfies the clerk completely, and it ends a family in this parish.

events.title: THE NEXT COLLECTION REFUSED
events.text: The parish prepares to refuse the next collection outright. The rector has begun using the word excommunication in sermons, which means no burial ground and no marriages for anyone who holds out.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE BISHOP’S CLERK COMES TO COUNT

choices.label: Broker a modus: a fixed sum in place of the tenth

outcome.text: A money payment, fixed by agreement, entered in the book. Both sides lose the argument and gain a number, which is what a settlement is.

memory.note: You settled the tithe dispute with a fixed money payment.

choices.label: Hold the refusal

outcome.text: The refusal hardens religious tension and lowers public order. Your standing with the Commons rises, while the rector’s authority remains a matter for the church rather than a victory you can announce.

choices.label: Pay in full and break the refusal

outcome.text: You pay the whole tenth on the first day. The refusal collapses within a week and the parish is very clear about who collapsed it.

events.title: THE TITHE AS IT IS NOW TAKEN
events.text: A new arrangement is proclaimed at the church door and written into the book. Every threat, bargain and short bushel of the last six years is somewhere in the wording of it.

choices.label: Have the terms read out every year

outcome.text: You get it entered that the modus is to be read aloud each Lady Day. It is read for a hundred and forty years, long after nobody remembers why.

choices.label: Let it lie in the book

outcome.text: It goes into the parish chest. Within a generation both sides are quoting it inaccurately and with total confidence.

events.title: THE COMMISSION OF ARRAY
events.text: a familiar face brings the writ down the lane: men, carts and grain for the king’s host, assessed at a figure Swineford could meet in a good year. This is not a good year.

choices.label: Draw up an honest assessment

outcome.text: You go house by house with the tax roll and set what each can actually bear. It takes nine days and everybody hates the number and pays it.

choices.label: Plead the village down

outcome.text: You take the murrain, the flood and the burial list to the commissioners in person. They cut the assessment by a third and mark Swineford as difficult.

choices.label: Offer money instead of men (20g)

outcome.text: You raise twenty shillings and buy the village out of the array. No Swineford man marches, and the money is gone in a way the grain would not have been.

events.title: NAMES OFF THE MUSTER ROLL
events.text: Five names vanish from the roll between the drafting and the reading. All five households have made private payments to somebody, and everyone can guess to whom.

choices.label: Put the four names back

outcome.text: You write them in again in front of the constable. Two of the five never speak to you again and the roll is honest for the first time in nineteen years.

choices.label: Take a payment to leave your own name off (10g)

outcome.text: Ten shillings changes hands and your name is not read out. It is precisely what the five households did, and you were a great deal angrier about it in March.

memory.note: You paid to keep your own name off the muster roll.

choices.label: Read the roll as it stands

outcome.text: You read out what is written. Five men who should be marching are at home, and the rest of the column noticed exactly which five.

events.title: LOTS DRAWN IN FRONT OF THE HALL
events.text: The Commons demand a public drawing of lots for who marches. The lord’s retainers are stood along the hall wall in mail, which is not a coincidence and is not quite a threat.

choices.label: Hold the drawing, and draw first

outcome.text: You put your own hand in the bag before anybody else. You draw a short straw and it is the single most useful thing you do all year.

memory.note: You drew a lot for the levy before anyone else and lost.

choices.label: Let the steward choose the men

outcome.text: He picks twelve and the retainers stay against the wall. The fourteen are the sixteen you would have expected, and the hall empties in complete silence.

choices.label: Take the place of a man with children

outcome.text: You march in place of a father of four. His wife brings your household bread for six years and never explains why to anybody who asks.

events.title: THE ESCHEATOR ASKS ABOUT THE NUMBERS
events.text: A royal officer arrives on a rumour that Swineford falsified both its population and its harvest returns. He has the old rolls with him and a great deal of time.

hasWorldMemoryType: LOTS DRAWN IN FRONT OF THE HALL

choices.label: Give him the true figures

outcome.text: You lay out what the village actually has. The assessment goes up by a fifth, permanently, and no one is ever hanged for it.

choices.label: Stand by the returns as filed

outcome.text: Every man in the village tells him the same figure. He does not believe a word of it and cannot prove otherwise, and he says so in writing.

choices.label: Blame the dead reeve

outcome.text: You put it all on a man buried three years ago who cannot argue. The officer accepts it because it is convenient, and his widow hears about it by Friday.

events.title: THE LEVY MARCHES OUT
events.text: They go up the Cambridge road with the carts behind them. Swineford now has to decide, out loud and for the record, whether the burden was shared or merely hidden well.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE ESCHEATOR ASKS ABOUT THE NUMBERS

choices.label: Say plainly how it was shared

outcome.text: You give the full account at the view: who paid, who marched, who bought their way clear. It is entered in the roll and read at every array afterwards.

choices.label: Let the village forget it

outcome.text: Nobody says anything. By the next array the story has quietly rearranged itself so that everyone behaved rather better than they did.

events.title: TWO SEALS, ONE MATRIX
events.text: a familiar face discovers that two guild officers are issuing orders under impressions of the same seal. One matrix, two men, and a fortnight of contradictory instructions already out on the roads.

choices.label: Seize the matrix and lock it in the chest

outcome.text: You take it, put it under three keys held by three men, and no order goes out for twenty days. The town is furious and the forgery stops dead.

choices.label: Recognise one officer and ignore the other

outcome.text: You pick the one who is more likely to win and start honouring his orders. Half the guild does the same and the other half does the opposite.

choices.label: Take orders from whichever suits you

outcome.text: For a season you have written authority for absolutely anything you care to do. It is extremely profitable and it cannot possibly last.

events.title: THE MERCHANTS STOP TAKING SWINEFORD PAPER
events.text: Merchants at Lynn and Stourbridge refuse anything sealed out of Swineford until somebody proves which council is lawful. Three carts of wool are sitting on a wharf accruing nothing but charges.

choices.label: Ride to Lynn and vouch for the wool yourself

outcome.text: You stand surety in person for three carts on nothing but your own name. It works, it takes nine days, and your name is worth more at Lynn afterwards than it is at home.

choices.label: Sell the wool at whatever it fetches

outcome.text: It goes for two-thirds and the charges eat a third of that. Everybody is paid something and nobody is paid enough.

choices.label: Leave it on the wharf and wait them out

outcome.text: Eight weeks of charges and the wool is worth less than the storage. The dispute is settled the following spring, far too late for that wool.

events.title: A CHARTER FRAGMENT IN A FAMILY CHEST
events.text: Half a charter turns up in a dead man’s chest, granting the guild rights that neither faction had thought to claim and that the borough would very much prefer stayed lost.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE MERCHANTS STOP TAKING SWINEFORD PAPER

choices.label: Produce it before both councils

outcome.text: It is read out and it changes the argument completely. Both factions immediately begin claiming they always knew about it.

choices.label: Sell it to the borough (25g)

outcome.text: The borough pays well for a document that ceases to exist the moment it is paid for. You are twenty-five shillings richer and the guild is smaller forever.

memory.note: You sold a guild charter to the borough and it was never seen again.

choices.label: Go looking for the other half

outcome.text: Two years of chests, priories and one very unhelpful archdeacon. You never find it, and everybody now knows there is half a charter somewhere.

events.title: THE CROWN OFFERS RECOGNITION
events.text: The Crown will recognise one council and settle the whole business tomorrow. The fee is an annual payment that will bind the guild for a generation and be described in the writ as a free gift.

hasWorldMemoryType: A CHARTER FRAGMENT IN A FAMILY CHEST

choices.label: Take the recognition and the debt

outcome.text: Sealed by Whitsun. The guild is lawful, undisputed, and paying the Crown eight marks a year in 1390 for a quarrel settled in 1352.

choices.label: Refuse and settle it yourselves

outcome.text: Four more years of argument, two ruined merchants, and a settlement written by the guild for the guild that costs it nothing annually forever.

choices.label: Go to the borough instead

outcome.text: The borough will recognise the guild for less money and considerably more interference. It is a smaller collar and it is a collar.

events.title: ONE SEAL RETURNS TO THE HALL
events.text: A single matrix goes back into the guild chest under three keys. Its authority now rests entirely on a history that every man in the hall remembers differently and none of them wrongly.

choices.label: Have the whole history written into the book

outcome.text: Four pages, both factions, the wool on the wharf, the charter. It is read to every new warden at their swearing-in for two hundred years.

choices.label: Turn the key and get back to trade

outcome.text: Nobody writes it down. Inside a generation the guild is confidently telling a version in which nothing much went wrong at all.

events.title: THE THATCH WILL NOT SEE ANOTHER WINTER
events.text: a familiar face pushes a thumb through the thatch above the hearth end and it goes in to the knuckle. There are seven weeks to Martinmas and a thatcher wants nine shillings.

choices.label: Pay the thatcher properly (9g)

outcome.text: Nine shillings, three days, and new reed over the whole hearth end. It is the correct decision and it empties the purse before winter.

choices.label: Patch it yourself with what you have

outcome.text: Two days on the roof with old reed and borrowed spars. It will hold. It will hold in the way that things hold when you are the one who fixed them.

choices.label: Move the bed and leave it

outcome.text: You shift the beds to the dry end and put a pot under the wet one. Everybody sleeps in one room until March and nobody says a word about it.

events.title: ROT UNDER A RECENT REPAIR
events.text: The carpenter strips back the hearth end and finds the main tie-beam soft as bread. Somebody patched over this within living memory and charged for a sound repair.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE THATCH WILL NOT SEE ANOTHER WINTER

choices.label: Find out who did it and make him pay

outcome.text: It was the man who is now the churchwarden. He pays for the beam rather than have it discussed, and he is never civil to you again.

choices.label: Buy the beam and say nothing (16g)

outcome.text: Sixteen shillings for oak and two men to raise it. The house will stand for two hundred years and nobody will ever know why it needed to.

choices.label: Prop it and hope

outcome.text: A post under the beam and a prayer. It holds for thirteen years. Nobody who signed it expected five.

memory.note: The main beam of your house is rotten and propped.

events.title: RAIN IN THE BEDDING
events.text: A week of rain comes through before the work is done and ruins the stored bedding. Two households are now sharing one dry room and both have opinions about who sleeps nearest the fire.

choices.label: Give up your own place by the fire

outcome.text: You sleep by the door for six weeks and take a cough that lasts into April. The other household never forgets which side of the room you chose.

choices.label: Draw lots for it each week

outcome.text: A rota, drawn publicly, changed every Sunday. It is fair, everybody grumbles about it, and there is not one serious quarrel all winter.

choices.label: Keep your place; it is your roof

outcome.text: It is your roof, factually. You are warm all winter and the arrangement is discussed in the lane for considerably longer than the winter lasts.

events.title: THE TIMBER GOES TO THE LORD’S GRANARY
events.text: The oak promised to your roof is diverted to repair the lord’s granary. The steward is apologetic and entirely immovable, and the carpenter is stood in your yard with nothing to raise.

choices.label: Petition the steward at the hallmote

outcome.text: You cite the custom of the manor on timber-right for repairs. It is real, and he had plainly assumed nobody in Swineford could quote it. Half the oak comes back.

memory.note: You quoted manorial custom at the steward and got your timber back.

choices.label: Buy timber from the next parish (18g)

outcome.text: Eighteen shillings and a two-day haul. The roof is finished a fortnight before Martinmas and the purse is emptier than it has been in years.

choices.label: Take what you need off the granary pile at night

outcome.text: Three spars, moved after dark, from a pile of forty. Nobody counts them and you spend the next five years expecting somebody to.

events.title: THE SACKS COME UP LIGHT
events.text: a familiar face finds three sacks gnawed open at the seam. The loss is larger than any rat could account for, and the granary door has a good lock on it.

choices.label: Set traps and count every sack weekly

outcome.text: You catch nine rats and establish, by arithmetic, that the rats account for about a third of it. The other two-thirds have a key.

choices.label: Blame the rats and get a better cat

outcome.text: A good mouser from the mill, fed on scraps, worth every one of them. The loss halves and the half that remains keeps quietly happening.

choices.label: Sit in the granary all night

outcome.text: Four nights in the cold before you see who has the key. You know, now, and knowing turns out to be considerably harder than not knowing was.

events.title: A CHILD CARRYING FLOUR AT DUSK
events.text: A child is stopped in the lane with flour under a coat, going to a household that has had nothing since Tuesday. The child is nine and does not attempt to lie about it.

choices.label: Fill the coat properly and send them on

outcome.text: You put a full measure in and walk them to the door yourself. Four households know by morning and two of them start doing the same.

choices.label: Take the child to the reeve

outcome.text: The reeve is obliged to record it and does so with visible reluctance. The child is amerced twopence their family cannot pay, and everyone involved feels precisely as bad as they should.

choices.label: Take the flour back and say nothing

outcome.text: The child goes home with an empty coat. Nothing is recorded, nothing is said, and nothing is eaten in that house until Friday.

events.title: DAMP GRAIN BEHIND A NEW WALL
events.text: Somebody has walled up a section of the granary with grain still damp behind it. By the time the smell reaches the yard, a quarter of the winter store has gone to mould.

hasWorldMemoryType: A CHILD CARRYING FLOUR AT DUSK

choices.label: Break the wall out and salvage what is sound

outcome.text: Two days of shovelling and sorting in a stench that gets into your clothes. You save rather more than anyone expected and lose the rest.

choices.label: Sell the doubtful sacks at market

outcome.text: It goes at a good price to a buyer three villages off who does not open the sacks in your presence. You are paid and you are not proud of it.

memory.note: You sold spoiled grain at market to a buyer three villages away.

choices.label: Burn the lot in the yard

outcome.text: A quarter of the winter store, on a fire, in front of the household. Nobody in Swineford is poisoned that year and nobody in your house forgives you until March.

events.title: THE RECKONING AT WINTER’S END
events.text: The household counts what is left in March: what was eaten, what was stolen, what was shared out and what was quietly saved. All four numbers are known and only two of them are ever said aloud.

hasWorldMemoryType: DAMP GRAIN BEHIND A NEW WALL

choices.label: Say all four numbers out loud

outcome.text: You read the whole account to the household including the sharing and the theft. It is a difficult evening and the granary is never short again.

choices.label: Say the two that are easy

outcome.text: Eaten and spoiled. The other two numbers stay in your head, where they go on being true and go on being expensive.

events.title: SPARKS ON YOUR OWN THATCH
events.text: a familiar face is in the lane shouting that the roof next door is gone. The wind is coming your way and there are already sparks landing on your thatch.

choices.label: Wet your own roof first

outcome.text: Every bucket in the house onto your own thatch. Your roof survives, theirs does not, and both of those facts are noted in the lane.

choices.label: Pull the burning roof down with hooks

outcome.text: You get the fire-hooks off the church wall and drag the whole roof into the lane. It is the right answer, it saves the row, and it takes the skin off your hands.

choices.label: Get the people out and let it burn

outcome.text: Three children and an old man out through the smoke, and the row goes up behind you. Everyone lives. Nothing else does.

events.title: THREE HOUSEHOLDS, TWO ROOMS
events.text: The fire is out. Three households now have between them two rooms with roofs on, and the frost is a fortnight off.

choices.label: Take a household into your own room

outcome.text: Six people where six lived. The food goes twice as fast, nobody sleeps well, and not one of them is out of doors when the frost comes.

choices.label: Let out your byre at a fair rent

outcome.text: A penny a week for the byre, which is honest, sheltered and cold. They take it and they pay it and something between you never quite comes back.

choices.label: Get the church house opened for them

outcome.text: You badger the churchwardens until they open the church house, which has stood empty for six years for no reason anybody can defend.

events.title: A STRONGBOX IN THE ASHES
events.text: Raking the burnt row turns up a small iron box with fifteen shillings and a ring in it. Nobody living in that row will admit to owning it, which is the most interesting thing about the box.

choices.label: Have it cried in church three Sundays

outcome.text: Three Sundays and no claimant. It goes to the parish chest for the rebuilding, lawfully, and everybody knows you could have kept it.

choices.label: Keep it

outcome.text: Nine shillings and a ring you never wear. Whoever it belonged to knows it was in that row, and one day may work out who did the raking.

choices.label: Split it between the three households

outcome.text: Three shillings and eightpence each and the ring drawn for. It is not lawful and nobody in that lane ever raises the point.

events.title: WHO GETS A ROOF FIRST
events.text: The rebuilding begins and there is timber for one house before the frost. The poorest of the three families has the most children and the least claim on anybody.

choices.label: The poorest family first

outcome.text: They are under a roof by Martinmas. The other two wait until spring and say, mostly, that it was right, and mean it, mostly.

memory.note: You had the poorest burnt-out family roofed before the others.

choices.label: Whoever can pay toward the timber

outcome.text: The family that can find twelve shillings is roofed first, which is how it is normally done and is the reason the poorest family is the poorest family.

choices.label: Split the timber three ways and rough-roof all three

outcome.text: Three bad roofs instead of one good one. All three leak, all three stand, and nobody spends the winter in somebody else’s byre.

events.title: A RAIN-SOAKED MAP FOR FOURPENCE
events.text: a familiar face buys a ruined sheet of vellum off a pedlar for fourpence. Under the water damage is a line running beneath Swineford’s oldest boundary stones, and a cross where no cross should be.

choices.label: Dry it out and read it properly

outcome.text: Three days over a low fire and most of it comes back. It is a genuine survey, badly copied, of something under the mere field.

choices.label: Buy it off {{other.name}} for a shilling

outcome.text: A shilling for fourpence of vellum. They take it happily and tell nine people about the profit. By Sunday the whole village knows there is a map.

choices.label: Tell them to burn it

outcome.text: Maps of things under boundary stones have a way of becoming inquests. They do not burn it. They put it somewhere you cannot find it.

events.title: BONES, TOOLS, AND A NEWER FOOTPRINT
events.text: A night in the mere field with a spade opens a sealed chamber under the third boundary stone. There are bones in it, iron tools of a shape nobody uses, and one bootprint considerably fresher than the rest.

choices.label: Seal it up again and tell the priest

outcome.text: The priest has it consecrated and blessed and firmly closed. He also asks, twice, who else had been down there, and you do not have an answer.

choices.label: Take the tools

outcome.text: Five iron pieces of a make no smith in the shire recognises. They are worth money to the right person and questions to everybody else.

choices.label: Go looking for whose boot it was

outcome.text: You measure it against every man in Swineford over the next month, entirely without explaining why. You find the match and you very much wish you had not.

events.title: THE MISSING CORNER IN THE REEVE’S ARCHIVE
events.text: The torn-off corner of the map turns up in the reeve’s own chest, filed among records of land confiscated from a family that stopped existing in this parish some ninety years ago.

hasWorldMemoryType: BONES, TOOLS, AND A NEWER FOOTPRINT

choices.label: Ask the reeve about it directly

outcome.text: He goes grey, says it was there when he came, and is entirely honest about that. He is much less honest about why he never mentioned it.

choices.label: Take the corner out of the chest

outcome.text: You now have the whole map and a theft from the manor archive on your conscience and, potentially, on the record.

choices.label: Trace the family that stopped existing

outcome.text: Ninety years of rolls and one very reluctant priory. They did not die out. They were dispossessed, and there are descendants, and they are three miles away.

memory.note: You found living descendants of a family dispossessed ninety years ago.

events.title: THE PATH ENDS UNDER A LIVING HOUSE
events.text: The line on the map runs out beneath a house with a family asleep in it. Whatever is down there and whoever owns the ground are now precisely the same argument.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE MISSING CORNER IN THE REEVE’S ARCHIVE

choices.label: Tell the family what is under their floor

outcome.text: You tell them everything and let them decide. They decide to do nothing at all, and they sleep on it for another forty years, and they are grateful you asked.

choices.label: Dig at night from the byre side

outcome.text: Ten nights of quiet digging under somebody else’s floor. You find it. Whatever it is worth, you can never once explain how you came by it.

memory.note: You dug treasure out from under a sleeping family’s house.

choices.label: Declare it as treasure trove

outcome.text: You report it to the coroner as the law requires. The Crown takes the whole of it, you are thanked in writing, and the family gets the hole in their floor filled in.

events.title: A RELIQUARY AND A LARGE CLAIM
events.text: a familiar face arrives with a small enamelled reliquary and the assertion that the finger-bone inside belonged to a saint that nobody in this diocese has heard of.

choices.label: Look at the reliquary rather than the bone

outcome.text: The enamel is Limoges work and eighty years old at least. Whatever is inside it, the box is real and the box is worth more than the parish makes in a year.

choices.label: Take it to the rector at once

outcome.text: He is cautious, delighted, and writing to the bishop before you are out of the door. It is out of your hands inside a week.

choices.label: Tell them to keep it in a box and say nothing

outcome.text: It goes under a floorboard. It stays there for nine years and then somebody’s child finds it, at the worst possible moment, in front of a visiting archdeacon.

events.title: PILGRIMS ON THE SWINEFORD ROAD
events.text: Word gets out. Pilgrims come, and bring with them coin, sickness, and five competing accounts of miracles performed within sight of the reliquary.

hasWorldMemoryType: A RELIQUARY AND A LARGE CLAIM

choices.label: Sell them beds, bread and badges

outcome.text: Swineford makes more in one summer than in the four years before it. It also buries nine people in August who came in already coughing.

choices.label: Limit them to the churchyard and the well

outcome.text: You organise where they sleep, where they wash and where they do not go. It makes half the money and buries nobody, and the alehouse never forgives you.

choices.label: Ask the miracle-witnesses some questions

outcome.text: Of six miracles, eight are weather, two are recovery from things people recover from, and one is genuinely unaccountable. You write all seven down anyway.

events.title: THE SCHOLAR WILL NOT SPEAK OF THE BONE
events.text: A scholar from Cambridge examines the reliquary and certifies the enamel as genuine and old. Asked directly about the bone inside it, he changes the subject three times and then leaves.

choices.label: Follow him to the gate and press him

outcome.text: He tells you, quietly, that it is a sheep’s. He also tells you he will deny having said so, and that he is not the first man to have found this out.

memory.note: A scholar told you privately that the parish relic is a sheep bone.

choices.label: Let him go and publish the certificate

outcome.text: The certificate says the reliquary is genuine. That is true, and it is not what anybody who reads it will think it says.

choices.label: Ask him the question in front of the parish

outcome.text: He gives a beautiful eight-minute answer about the limits of scholarly method that says nothing whatsoever, and the parish is entirely satisfied by it.

events.title: TWO CHURCHES AND AN ARMED GUARD
events.text: A priory and a cathedral both claim the relic. There are now armed men sleeping in the church porch, and the poor of Swineford are asking loudly why holiness needs a guard.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE SCHOLAR WILL NOT SPEAK OF THE BONE

choices.label: Give it to whichever house will take it furthest away

outcome.text: It goes to the cathedral with an escort. The pilgrims follow it inside a twelvemonth and Swineford goes back to being a village with a wet field.

choices.label: Fight to keep it in the parish

outcome.text: Two years of proctors and letters and one shoving match in the nave. Swineford keeps it, keeps the trade, and keeps the armed men in the porch indefinitely.

choices.label: Put the offerings to the poor and say so loudly

outcome.text: Every penny in the box goes to the burnt-out and the widowed, published at the church door each quarter. Both claimant houses lose interest remarkably quickly.

memory.note: You put every penny of the relic offerings to Swineford’s poor, publicly.

events.title: THE CHILD WHO DESCRIBED THE FLOOD
events.text: a familiar face reports that a child in the lane described the mere coming over the causeway four days before a cloud was seen. It came over the causeway.

choices.label: Write down exactly what was said and when

outcome.text: You take it in the child’s own words with the date and two witnesses. It is either the most valuable page in the parish or a piece of paper.

choices.label: Tell the priest at once

outcome.text: He is far more worried than impressed and says three things about discernment of spirits that the family does not understand and does not like.

choices.label: Call it a coincidence, loudly

outcome.text: You say the obvious thing about a wet spring and a low causeway. Half the lane agrees with you and the other half remembers, in detail, that you said it.

events.title: A SECOND DREAM NAMES SOMETHING PRIVATE
events.text: The child describes a thing about a household that they could not possibly have known and that two adults have spent five years making sure nobody knew.

hasWorldMemoryType: THE CHILD WHO DESCRIBED THE FLOOD

choices.label: Get the child out of the lane for a while

outcome.text: You send them to kin at Barton for the summer. The household concerned calms down, and the two who are protecting the secret work out exactly who moved the child.

choices.label: Ask the child how they knew

outcome.text: They say a woman told them, and describe somebody who has been dead since before they were born, accurately, including the limp.

choices.label: Use what the child said

outcome.text: You go to the household concerned and let them understand that you know. They are extremely accommodating from that day and they hate you for the rest of their lives.

memory.note: You used a child’s vision to blackmail a household.

events.title: CROWDS AT THE DOOR ASKING ABOUT HARVESTS
events.text: People come from three parishes to ask about weather, marriages and the price of wool. The child is eight, is frightened of them, and the family is asking for it to stop.

hasWorldMemoryType: A SECOND DREAM NAMES SOMETHING PRIVATE

choices.label: Shut the door and stand in front of it

outcome.text: You turn away sixty people in a month, some of them angry and more of them desperate. The child sleeps properly for the first time since Lady Day.

choices.label: Let them come, but on your terms

outcome.text: You limit the questioning to one morning a week and refuse payment. Religious tension still rises a little; the smaller gathering is a boundary, not proof that the child is no longer frightened.

choices.label: Charge a penny a question

outcome.text: You collect twenty gold and increase household wealth. Existing debts are not erased by the takings, and {{other.name}} trusts you less for pricing the frightened child’s answers.

events.title: A DREAM THAT SUITS NOBODY
events.text: The final dream contradicts what the priest has been preaching and what the lord has been planning, in the same sentence. Everybody in the parish now has to say out loud what they actually believe.

hasWorldMemoryType: CROWDS AT THE DOOR ASKING ABOUT HARVESTS

choices.label: Say you believe the child

outcome.text: You say it in the nave with both of them present. It costs you the rector’s goodwill, the steward’s goodwill, and absolutely nothing that you needed.

choices.label: Say the child is ill and needs quiet

outcome.text: It is the answer that ends the matter without anybody being burned or believed. The child is left alone and grows up ordinary, which was possibly the point.

choices.label: Side with the rector

outcome.text: You say what the rector needs said. The dream is condemned from the pulpit, the family leaves the parish by spring, and you are on very good terms with the church.

events.title: THE DREAMER COMES BACK GROWN
events.text: Years on, the grown dreamer walks back into Swineford to find out which parts of the story the parish decided to keep. They are entirely ordinary now, and they want to know.

choices.label: Tell them what actually happened

outcome.text: The flood, the secret, the crowds, the penny a question, what you did about each. They listen the whole way through and thank you, and they do not stay.

choices.label: Tell them the version the parish tells

outcome.text: It is a better story than the truth and considerably kinder to everybody in it, including you. They know it is not right and do not press.

events.title: THE BISHOP ADMIRES THY FALCON
events.text: The bishop stops mid-procession to admire your hunting falcon, and asks its breeding in a tone that is not entirely about birds.

choices.label: Give him the falcon

outcome.text: He is delighted and slightly embarrassed, and a bishop in that condition is worth a great deal. Your name reaches the diocese before you do.

choices.label: Fly her for him instead

outcome.text: She takes a heron in front of the whole procession. The bishop talks about it for years and never once offers to buy her.

choices.label: Name a price

outcome.text: He pays it without blinking, which tells you the price was too low. You have coin and he has a story about a grasping fellow from Swineford.

events.title: A HORSE WORTH TAKING
events.text: The muster clerk looks at your destrier, then at his roll, and informs you that a man with a warhorse serves mounted, at his own cost, for twice the term.

choices.label: Serve mounted and be seen doing it

outcome.text: You ride out at the head of the Swineford contingent, which is four men and a cart. It is absurd and it is remembered.

choices.label: Swear the horse is lame

outcome.text: You keep the horse and the clerk keeps a note. Both of you know the horse is sound and neither of you says so.

events.title: THEY HAVE HEARD ABOUT THE RELIC
events.text: Three pilgrims are at your gate before Prime, having walked from Ely on the strength of a rumour about what you keep in your house.

choices.label: Let them see it, and take nothing

outcome.text: They stay an hour and leave weeping. By Lammas there are thirty of them, and by Michaelmas the road past your door is a road.

choices.label: Ask a penny a head

outcome.text: They pay it. Word of the penny travels exactly as fast as word of the relic, and arrives in the same conversation.

choices.label: Send them on to the abbey

outcome.text: You point them up the road and shut the gate. They go, and they tell the abbey where they were sent from.

events.title: A MAN WHO KEEPS A LEDGER
events.text: Word has got round that you keep written accounts. The reeve arrives with a box of tallies, an apologetic expression, and no intention of leaving with the box.

choices.label: Do the parish accounts

outcome.text: Nine evenings of somebody else’s arithmetic. You find two errors in the parish’s favour and one very much not, and you report both.

choices.label: Do them for a fee

outcome.text: Four shillings and the work is done properly. The reeve pays and thereafter treats you as a tradesman rather than a neighbour.

choices.label: Do them, and improve them

outcome.text: The accounts balance beautifully and two of the entries are yours. It will hold until somebody else learns to read a tally.

events.title: A STONE OF THINE OWN
events.text: Your own millstone means your own flour, and half the lane has worked that out. They arrive with sacks and a hopeful manner.

choices.label: Grind for them, and take no toll

outcome.text: You grind for nine households and take nothing. The miller hears about it within the day and is not amused.

choices.label: Take a toll, honestly measured

outcome.text: A twentieth, measured in front of them. The mill takes a tenth and everybody knows it, so you are paid and nobody feels robbed.

choices.label: It is your stone

outcome.text: You shut the door on them. It is entirely your stone and they go back to the mill, past your house, every week, for years.

events.title: THE ONE WITH THE MASK
events.text: Sickness is in the row by the ford and you own the only beaked mask in the parish, which in everyone else’s eyes makes you the nearest thing Swineford has to a physician.

choices.label: Put it on and go in

outcome.text: The mask does nothing at all and the vinegar-soaked rag inside it may do a little. You bring four people through and take a cough that lasts till spring.

choices.label: Lend it to the herb-wife

outcome.text: She takes it without comment and uses it for nine years. You never get it back and never ask.

choices.label: Keep it, and keep indoors

outcome.text: You are well all season. The lane knows exactly what is hanging on your door and exactly who did not come.

events.title: A MAN WITH A SWORD IS ASKED
events.text: A carter is being beaten in the market by two men over a debt. You are wearing a sword, which the whole market has noticed, and which changes what standing still means.

choices.label: Draw it

outcome.text: They go. Nobody is cut and everybody saw the steel come out, and you will be answering for that at the tourn.

choices.label: Put a hand on the hilt and say nothing

outcome.text: They look at the hand, then at your face, and decide the debt can wait. Not one word is spoken and it works completely.

choices.label: Walk on

outcome.text: You walk on wearing a sword past a man being beaten. The market watches you do it and draws the obvious conclusion.

events.title: THE FORESTER LOOKS AT THY HOUND
events.text: The forester stops you on the coppice road and looks a long time at your hunting hound. Under forest law a dog that can run down a deer must be lawed: three claws off the forefoot.

choices.label: Have the dog lawed

outcome.text: It is done at the next swanimote with a mallet and a chisel. The dog lives, limps, and never runs anything down again.

choices.label: Pay the fine instead (12g)

outcome.text: Twelve shillings buys the dog its claws and buys the forester a new opinion of your purse. He will be back.

choices.label: Keep the dog out of the wood

outcome.text: The hound never goes near the coppice again and neither do you. It is a small life for a good dog and it keeps all four feet.

events.title: THE COUNCILLOR’S CREATIVE ACCOUNTS
events.text: Your councillor, your official, has diverted 0 treasury gold. The account describes national security. The receipt describes decorative horses. A family ally asks whether the horses could be classified as cavalry.

choices.label: Demand a public investigation

outcome.text: The inquiry removes the responsible official and recovers half the missing funds. The household’s supporters take the dismissal personally.

choices.label: Cover up the accounts

outcome.text: The official keeps the seal and owes you a favour. The original receipts remain in someone else’s hands.

choices.label: Blame the treasurer

outcome.text: The treasurer loses the seal. The guilds recognise an injustice considerably faster than the council recognises a sum.

choices.label: Dismiss the official quietly

outcome.text: The seal returns to your keeping. The missing gold does not. The dismissed official takes the grievance home.

events.title: THE CONTESTED SEAL
events.text: The court has already recorded this petition.

choices.label: Present your learning and service

outcome.text: The ruler considers your service against the vacancy, incumbent and rival candidates. The court record gives the decision.

choices.label: Ask your patron to speak for you

outcome.text: Your patron addresses the council. Their support helps; the incumbent still has a case to answer.

choices.label: Offer further service before a new petition

outcome.text: The ruler records a condition of further professional service. You receive a target rather than a seal.

choices.label: Withdraw the request

outcome.text: The request is withdrawn. The existing officeholder remains responsible.

events.title: THE OPPOSING HOUSEHOLDS
events.text: An opposing household brings a coalition before the council. Their strength is 0. They have withheld cooperation and demand an answer.

choices.label: Fund a negotiated settlement (15 treasury)

outcome.text: A recorded settlement reduces the coalition’s strength. Rival claims remain in the family record.

choices.label: Hear the households’ grievances

outcome.text: The hearing earns some respect and eases opposition while leaving the dispute open.

choices.label: Assert royal authority and dismiss them

outcome.text: The rejected petition becomes a rallying point. The coalition gains strength and public order falls.

events.title: THE DYER’S BLUE DEBT
events.text: {{client}} offers a winter’s cloth on credit. The blue dye washes out in rain. {{rival}} has already promised to sell it as royal indigo.

choices.label: Test the dye before signing

outcome.text: You test the cloth in clean water and retain the sample. The contract now names the dye.

choices.label: Sell it before the weather turns

outcome.text: You sell the cloth without a rain clause. The counting house keeps an unusually thin copy of the warranty.

choices.label: Pay a dyer to fix the cloth

outcome.text: Eight gold retains a dyer to fix the cloth before delivery.

events.title: THE DYER’S BLUE DEBT · THE RECKONING
events.text: The first rain has arrived. Your buyers bring their sleeves to the counting house as evidence.

choices.label: Defend the cloth contract

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the dyer’s blue debt. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Refund the disputed dye charges (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the dyer’s blue debt. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE RIVAL’S LAST BALE
events.text: {{rival}} claims that {{client}}’s wool bears a stolen mark. The guild may seize the entire consignment, including your stake.

choices.label: Call the shepherd as witness

outcome.text: You record the shepherd’s testimony beside the wool marks before the bales leave the yard.

choices.label: Buy the rival’s silence

outcome.text: You pay for silence about the wool marks. Your rival keeps the original receipt.

choices.label: Hire a clerk to trace the sales

outcome.text: Eight gold retains a clerk to trace the flock and its sales.

events.title: THE RIVAL’S LAST BALE · THE RECKONING
events.text: The guild opens the bales before both households. Inside one lies a very indignant living lamb.

choices.label: Present the wool title

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the rival’s last bale. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Settle the wool claim openly (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the rival’s last bale. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE FUNERAL BELL WARRANTY
events.text: {{client}} orders a bell guaranteed to outlive the abbot. The mould is cracked. {{rival}} offers a coat of paint and a quiet blessing.

choices.label: Recast the faulty bell

outcome.text: You break the faulty mould and begin a sound casting. The parish witnesses the decision.

choices.label: Conceal the crack beneath the inscription

outcome.text: You order the crack painted beneath the inscription. The painter keeps a charcoal rubbing.

choices.label: Hire an apprentice for a second casting

outcome.text: Eight gold retains an apprentice to help cast the bell again.

events.title: THE FUNERAL BELL WARRANTY · THE RECKONING
events.text: The bell is raised above the churchyard. Your maker’s mark sits where the whole parish can read it.

choices.label: Answer for the bell’s casting

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the funeral bell warranty. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Compensate the parish for the bell (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the funeral bell warranty. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE WIDOW’S WORKSHOP
events.text: {{client}} keeps a workshop after the master’s burial. {{rival}} petitions the guild to confiscate the tools before the candles burn down.

choices.label: Defend the household’s charter

outcome.text: You bring the widow’s charter before the guild before its officers seize the tools.

choices.label: Take the disputed commissions yourself

outcome.text: You take the widow’s commissions. The guild clerk records who collected them.

choices.label: Pay a clerk to establish the succession

outcome.text: Eight gold retains a clerk to establish the workshop’s succession.

events.title: THE WIDOW’S WORKSHOP · THE RECKONING
events.text: The guild court hears whether a dead master’s tools must become a living rival’s property.

choices.label: Submit to the workshop hearing

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the widow’s workshop. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Restore the disputed workshop fees (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the widow’s workshop. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE PHYSICIAN’S GREAT SUCCESS
events.text: {{client}} asks you to organise care for a household. {{rival}} advertises expensive bloodletting without first asking who is ill. Your own record must distinguish actual symptoms from preventive advice.

choices.label: Select the difficult cases

outcome.text: You accept the difficult patients and record their symptoms before proposing a treatment.

choices.label: Accept every patient and every fee

outcome.text: You promise every household a visit. Your treatment ledger fills faster than your days.

choices.label: Hire a medical apprentice

outcome.text: Eight gold retains an apprentice for dressings and routine attendance.

events.title: THE PHYSICIAN’S GREAT SUCCESS · THE RECKONING
events.text: Three new patients arrive with identical complaints and contradictory instructions from the same cousin.

choices.label: Present your treatment record

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the physician’s great success. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Pay the patients and correct the record (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the physician’s great success. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE WELL OF SAINT ITCH
events.text: Fever follows the water sold by {{client}} as a saint’s blessing. {{rival}} proposes charging double for blessed leeches.

choices.label: Inspect the well and separate the sick

outcome.text: You inspect the well, record the privy’s position and separate the fever beds.

choices.label: Sell the fashionable treatment

outcome.text: You sell the fashionable treatment. Your patient keeps the bottle and its contents.

choices.label: Pay an assistant to boil cloth and water

outcome.text: Eight gold pays an assistant to boil water and prepare clean cloth.

events.title: THE WELL OF SAINT ITCH · THE RECKONING
events.text: The parish asks why the blessed well stands downhill from the privy. The well keeper invokes mystery.

choices.label: Give evidence about the fever well

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the well of saint itch. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Refund the fever treatment and publish the evidence (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the well of saint itch. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE TITHE OF THE DEAD
events.text: {{client}} discovers that the abbey charges burial tithe on bones washed out of last year’s graves. {{rival}} calls this recurring revenue.

choices.label: Seek restitution for the households

outcome.text: You suspend the duplicate burial fees while the parish records are checked.

choices.label: Defend the abbey’s profitable custom

outcome.text: You collect the disputed tithes. The households retain the burial tallies.

choices.label: Pay a clerk to reconcile the burial roll

outcome.text: Eight gold pays a clerk to reconcile each burial against the parish roll.

events.title: THE TITHE OF THE DEAD · THE RECKONING
events.text: The archdeacon summons you to explain why one parish has buried the same tanner five times.

choices.label: Answer for the burial tithe

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the tithe of the dead. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Repay the duplicate burial fees (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the tithe of the dead. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE SAINT’S HORSE TOOTH
events.text: {{client}} seeks a ruling on the priory’s newest relic. {{rival}} has already sold indulgences for venerating what looks remarkably like a horse’s tooth.

choices.label: Submit the relic to an honest inquiry

outcome.text: You seal the relic until an open inquiry establishes its provenance.

choices.label: Protect the priory’s profitable reputation

outcome.text: You permit the horse tooth’s veneration to continue. The stable boy declines to pray.

choices.label: Hire a scholar to examine its provenance

outcome.text: Eight gold retains a scholar to compare the reliquary account with the stable inventory.

events.title: THE SAINT’S HORSE TOOTH · THE RECKONING
events.text: The bishop requests the relic, its history and an explanation for the stable boy’s recognition of it.

choices.label: Report to the relic inquiry

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the saint’s horse tooth. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Compensate the petitioners at the relic hearing (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the saint’s horse tooth. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE COMPANY AT THE BROKEN BRIDGE
events.text: {{client}} brings orders to cross a broken bridge before dawn. {{rival}} proposes sending the levy first to test its strength.

choices.label: Find a ford and protect the levy

outcome.text: You scout the ford before ordering the levy forward. The company waits under cover.

choices.label: Force the crossing before the enemy arrives

outcome.text: You order the crossing despite the split timbers. The muster clerk records the order.

choices.label: Pay engineers to shore the bridge

outcome.text: Eight gold pays engineers to shore the bridge before the convoy arrives.

events.title: THE COMPANY AT THE BROKEN BRIDGE · THE RECKONING
events.text: The supply train arrives as enemy scouts appear on the far bank. The company waits for your command.

choices.label: Accept responsibility for the crossing

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the company at the broken bridge. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Pay restitution and revise the crossing report (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the company at the broken bridge. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE CAPTIVES’ EMPTY PURSES
events.text: {{client}} brings three captured scouts. {{rival}} insists they are noblemen in unusually convincing poverty.

choices.label: Exchange them for your missing soldiers

outcome.text: You send the prisoners’ names with an exchange proposal before anyone sets a price.

choices.label: Extort a ransom from their families

outcome.text: You demand ransom from the prisoners’ households. The messenger keeps the demand.

choices.label: Hire a clerk to verify their names

outcome.text: Eight gold retains a clerk to verify the names before the exchange.

events.title: THE CAPTIVES’ EMPTY PURSES · THE RECKONING
events.text: A messenger offers peace on the road if the prisoners return alive. Your soldiers recognise one missing man’s belt.

choices.label: Answer for the prisoners’ exchange

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the captives’ empty purses. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Return the disputed ransom (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the captives’ empty purses. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE CHANCELLOR’S SALTED CAMEL
events.text: {{client}} sends a draft levy taxing every salt camel. The realm has no camels. {{rival}} recommends retaining the revenue estimate.

choices.label: Rewrite the levy around actual trade

outcome.text: You amend the levy around actual cargoes and circulate a corrected draft.

choices.label: Sell exemptions before anyone notices

outcome.text: You sell exemptions from the camel levy. The port keeps the exemption register.

choices.label: Hire a clerk to survey the ports

outcome.text: Eight gold pays a clerk to survey the ports before the decree is sealed.

events.title: THE CHANCELLOR’S SALTED CAMEL · THE RECKONING
events.text: The council demands the promised revenue. The treasurer presents a drawing of a camel in place of payment.

choices.label: Defend your salt-levy advice

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the chancellor’s salted camel. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Repay the exemption fees before the council (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the chancellor’s salted camel. The record includes the correction.

events.title: THE DEAD FALCONER’S WAGES
events.text: {{client}} pays a falconer dead these nine years. {{rival}} claims the hawks remain loyal enough to justify his wages.

choices.label: Expose the accounts to the council

outcome.text: You submit the falconer’s burial entry beside the nine years of wages.

choices.label: Sell your silence to the beneficiary

outcome.text: You sell your silence to the account’s beneficiary. A second copy of the burial entry survives.

choices.label: Hire an auditor to follow the payments

outcome.text: Eight gold retains an auditor to follow the falconer’s payments.

events.title: THE DEAD FALCONER’S WAGES · THE RECKONING
events.text: The council calls for the falconer. Someone sends a glove on a cushion. The accounts are rather more talkative.

choices.label: Submit the falconer audit

outcome.text: Your account enters the record: the dead falconer’s wages. The recorded agreement determines who pays and who is believed.

choices.label: Return the hush money and publish the audit (6g)

outcome.text: You pay six gold in restitution over the dead falconer’s wages. The record includes the correction.

events.title: ROTATE THE STRIPS
events.text: {{client}} brings a thin harvest from exhausted strips. {{rival}} has offered a new rotation without testing the soil.

choices.label: Test a small strip first

outcome.text: You mark a trial strip and record the soil before committing seed.

choices.label: Replant the whole field now

outcome.text: The whole strip is planted under your new plan; the harvest will test its ambition.

choices.label: Plan around the tenants’ observations

outcome.text: The tenants compare their observations with yours before the rotation is agreed.

events.title: NEGOTIATE A TENANCY
events.text: {{client}} needs a rent agreement that survives a poor harvest. The landlord wants a fixed payment even if the seed fails.

choices.label: Bring the recorded harvest

outcome.text: The harvest tally becomes the basis of your proposed rent.

choices.label: Demand a lower rent outright

outcome.text: Your demand for a lower rent puts the landlord’s agent on the defensive.

choices.label: Negotiate through a trusted neighbour

outcome.text: The neighbour brings both parties’ accounts to the negotiation.

events.title: INSPECT THE LIVESTOCK
events.text: {{client}} brings news of coughing livestock. No one has yet established whether the illness has spread beyond one stall.

choices.label: Inspect and isolate the sick animals

outcome.text: You examine the coughing animals separately and record what you find.

choices.label: Return the herd to work quickly

outcome.text: The owner is asked to return the herd to work before every uncertainty is settled.

choices.label: Ask a herder to review the symptoms

outcome.text: A second herder compares the animals’ signs with your notes.

events.title: ACCEPT A COMMISSION
events.text: {{client}} orders hinges before a funeral date has been agreed. The metal, dimensions and delivery promise are yours to settle.

choices.label: Measure and test before delivery

outcome.text: The customer receives a delivery plan with measured dimensions and a test piece.

choices.label: Promise a quick, expensive delivery

outcome.text: You offer an earlier delivery for a larger fee, accepting a smaller margin for error.

choices.label: Share the work with an apprentice

outcome.text: The apprentice receives a defined part of the commission under your supervision.

events.title: TEACH AN APPRENTICE
events.text: {{client}} asks you to train a workshop apprentice. The learner needs supervision, wages and a piece suited to their ability.

choices.label: Teach a supervised trial piece

outcome.text: The learner starts a trial piece with your hand close enough to stop an error.

choices.label: Set a difficult independent job

outcome.text: You give the learner an independent job that will test their present limits.

choices.label: Pay for a second master’s advice

outcome.text: The second master is paid to inspect the learner’s work alongside yours.

events.title: CHALLENGE THE GUILD
events.text: {{client}} disputes a guild assay. {{rival}} wants the hearing held over the inspecting master’s private wine.

choices.label: Submit a witnessed assay

outcome.text: A witnessed assay enters the guild record before the hearing.

choices.label: Challenge the guild officers publicly

outcome.text: You challenge the officers in public, making their pride part of the dispute.

choices.label: Seek support from a respected master

outcome.text: A respected master agrees to examine the claim before supporting your petition.

events.title: NEGOTIATE A GRAIN DEAL
events.text: {{client}} offers a grain shipment with a disputed measure. Price, quality and the partner’s share must be agreed before loading.

choices.label: Negotiate price against honest measures

outcome.text: The buyer and seller compare the grain against a witnessed measure.

choices.label: Press for a high margin and rapid shipment

outcome.text: You press for a higher margin and accept the risks of a hurried shipment.

choices.label: Share the shipment with a trading partner

outcome.text: The partner’s cargo and share are written into the shipment agreement.

events.title: SETTLE THE BRIDGE TOLL
events.text: {{client}} has a cart held at a bridge charging for six wheels. There are two on the cart, and armed men beside the toll board.

choices.label: Check the toll charter and escort

outcome.text: The keeper receives the toll charter and the convoy’s actual wheel count.

choices.label: Run the disputed crossing at speed

outcome.text: Your cart approaches the crossing quickly enough to limit time for negotiation.

choices.label: Negotiate a shared convoy

outcome.text: The convoy partners present a joint toll offer with a shared escort.

events.title: CONTEST A RIVAL’S CLAIM
events.text: {{rival}} claims the mark on {{client}}’s wool. The shepherd remembers the shearing and expects someone to ask.

choices.label: Present witnesses and the wool marks

outcome.text: The shepherd and wool marks enter the disputed sale’s record.

choices.label: Undercut the rival’s price

outcome.text: Your lower offer challenges the rival’s custom as well as their claim.

choices.label: Offer a witnessed settlement

outcome.text: Both counting houses receive a proposed settlement in writing.

events.title: DELIVER A SERMON
events.text: {{client}} asks for a sermon after counterfeit relics divide the parish. Their neighbours disagree about who should be named.

choices.label: Address the parish’s actual distress

outcome.text: The sermon begins with the parish’s needs and the evidence about the relics.

choices.label: Condemn the offenders by name

outcome.text: Your sermon names the suspected offenders before the whole congregation.

choices.label: Ask the parish elder to help reconcile them

outcome.text: The parish elder helps frame a sermon that leaves room for restitution.

events.title: MEDIATE THE TITHE DISPUTE
events.text: {{client}} disputes another household’s goose tithe. The old custom is unclear and the archdeacon dislikes an empty purse.

choices.label: Hear both households openly

outcome.text: Both households give their account of the goose tithe in the same hearing.

choices.label: Back the more influential household

outcome.text: Your support for the stronger household makes their influence part of the settlement.

choices.label: Seek a private settlement with the elder

outcome.text: The elder carries a private proposal between the disputing households.

events.title: SEEK PARISH RESPONSIBILITY
events.text: {{client}} can bring your parish work before the archdeacon. {{rival}} has already requested the same responsibility.

choices.label: Submit the parish work record

outcome.text: The archdeacon receives an account of the parish work you actually completed.

choices.label: Press your patron for precedence

outcome.text: Your patron is asked to press your claim ahead of competing candidates.

choices.label: Accept a supervised parish assignment

outcome.text: You offer to take a supervised parish task before receiving wider responsibility.

events.title: LEAD A ROAD PATROL
events.text: {{client}} reports bandits on the road. The reeve’s nephew insists they cannot be there; a familiar tent suggests otherwise.

choices.label: Scout the dangerous road first

outcome.text: Scouts return with observations before the patrol takes the road.

choices.label: Ride a direct armed patrol

outcome.text: The armed patrol moves directly toward the reported camp.

choices.label: Coordinate with local watchmen

outcome.text: Local watchmen compare routes and signals with your patrol.

events.title: ORGANISE THE COMPANY
events.text: {{client}} brings the company muster. Spears, boots and soldiers appear in three different totals, and the next march is approaching.

choices.label: Inspect equipment and practise formations

outcome.text: The equipment list is checked against the soldiers present at drill.

choices.label: Demand an immediate forced drill

outcome.text: The company is ordered into a forced exercise before every shortage is repaired.

choices.label: Give experienced soldiers a voice

outcome.text: Experienced soldiers identify the failures they will have to carry on the march.

events.title: COMMAND A CONVOY ESCORT
events.text: {{client}} needs an escort for a supply convoy. A fast route crosses an exposed ford; the longer road needs ration stops.

choices.label: Scout the convoy route and ration stops

outcome.text: The convoy plan names water, cover and ration stops along the scouted road.

choices.label: Race the convoy through the threat

outcome.text: You accept exposure at the ford in exchange for a faster crossing.

choices.label: Hire engineers and share command

outcome.text: Engineers and soldiers divide the work of protecting the convoy.

events.title: SEEK A NOBLE PATRON
events.text: {{client}} will consider patronage if you can offer a useful service. {{rival}} promises access to people neither of you has met.

choices.label: Offer a documented service

outcome.text: The proposed service is specific enough for a patron to judge your usefulness.

choices.label: Promise influence beyond your standing

outcome.text: Your promise of influence reaches beyond your established position.

choices.label: Seek an introduction from a colleague

outcome.text: A colleague carries an introduction and an account of your previous work.

events.title: ADVISE ON A DECREE
events.text: {{client}} brings a salt levy that counts the same barrel three times. Changing the draft may offend its author.

choices.label: Compare the decree with actual accounts

outcome.text: The salt draft is compared with the accounts of actual cargoes.

choices.label: Demand the council adopt your draft

outcome.text: You demand the council adopt your correction in front of the original author.

choices.label: Circulate a revised draft privately

outcome.text: A revised draft circulates privately before the council’s decision.

events.title: INVESTIGATE COURT ACCOUNTS
