events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · THE FIRST GREAT COUNCIL
events.text: someone once known in Swineford sets the order of business. Twenty items, and the one about the coinage is placed eleventh, where the council will be tired and will pass it without argument.

choices.label: Move the coinage to the front

outcome.text: Four hours of argument about the coinage with everybody awake. The council agrees on a sounder coinage, at a cost to the treasury.

choices.label: Leave it eleventh

outcome.text: It passes at dusk in four minutes with nobody attending. It is exactly what you wanted, but merchants question its value and the Commons record their objections.

events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · A FAVOURITE AND A FAMINE
events.text: The grain is short in four counties and the man you have raised highest is the one holding the export licences. Everybody in the room knows both facts.

choices.label: Revoke the licences yourself, in council

outcome.text: You do it in front of him, giving the reason plainly. His manner turns cold. With the licences revoked, grain reaches the markets and food supplies improve.

choices.label: Let the licences stand

outcome.text: They stand. He is loyal beyond anything money could buy and there are bread riots in two counties by Lent.

events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · PARLIAMENT WANTS REDRESS BEFORE SUPPLY
events.text: The Commons will vote the subsidy only after their petitions are answered. someone once known in Swineford points out that no king has ever conceded that order and that you need the money by Whitsun.

choices.label: Concede the order

outcome.text: Redress before supply, conceded in writing. You get your subsidy, and the Commons enter the concession in the roll as a precedent.

choices.label: Dissolve them and raise it another way

outcome.text: Forced loans, a benevolence, and the sale of thirteen offices. You get more than the subsidy would have been and you have taught the Commons what you think of them.

events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · THE WAR OR THE REALM
events.text: The claim abroad is genuinely good and pressing it will take every penny raised for a decade. someone once known in Swineford has the two accounts side by side and will not say which one to choose.

choices.label: Abandon the claim and spend it at home

outcome.text: You give up a legitimate claim and are called a coward in three chronicles. The roads are repaired, the coinage is sound, and nobody writes about that at all.

choices.label: Press the claim

outcome.text: You summon the retinue and fund the opening campaign. The court applauds your resolve, while levies and requisitions leave the realm poorer and food supplies strained.

events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · A DULL AND SOLVENT REIGN
events.text: The chronicles give your reign four lines and none of them are interesting. The realm is solvent, quiet, and rather better off than it was, which is not a thing chroniclers count.

choices.label: Take the four lines

outcome.text: You accept the short account and return to the council’s work. Sound coinage and repaired roads have brought the realm more benefit than a flattering chronicle.

events.title: THE WEIGHT OF THE CROWN · THE CHRONICLE ENTRY
events.text: A chronicler offers nineteen pages and a woodcut celebrating your rule. Outside the court, the cost of those campaigns weighs on the realm.

choices.label: Take the nineteen pages

outcome.text: They are magnificent pages. The county paying for the campaigns owns no copy of the chronicle, and its hardship continues.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · THE FIRST RULE OF THE BAND
events.text: someone once known in Swineford says the band needs a rule about what is not taken, and needs it before the first job rather than after the first mistake.

choices.label: Nothing from a household that works the land

outcome.text: It halves what is available and it means four villages will feed you rather than name you. It is the single most useful decision the band ever makes.

choices.label: Everything is taken from everybody

outcome.text: No rule, no argument, no limit. It is extremely profitable for fifteen months and the countryside turns out for the hue and cry in the twelfth.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · THE MAN WHO CANNOT KEEP QUIET
events.text: One of the band talks in alehouses. Everybody knows it, nobody has raised it, and someone once known in Swineford raises it in front of all of them and then looks at you.

choices.label: Put him out of the band and see him settled

outcome.text: He is out, with a share and a place found for him forty miles off. It costs money and it means nobody in the band ever fears being killed by it.

choices.label: Make an example of him

outcome.text: It is done in front of the band and it is entirely effective. Nobody talks in an alehouse again and three men leave inside a month.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · A PARDON FOR SERVICE
events.text: The Crown is offering pardons to outlaws who will serve in the array. It is a genuine offer, it is a genuine war, and roughly half of the men who take it do not come back.

choices.label: Put it to the whole band and let each choose

outcome.text: Six take it and five stay. You make sure the six leave with a share and the five are told exactly why the six went.

choices.label: Forbid it and keep the band whole

outcome.text: Nobody takes the pardon because nobody dares. The band is at full strength and every man in it now knows what he is not allowed to want.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · THE SHERIFF OFFERS TERMS
events.text: The sheriff offers you personally a pardon, a small office and a quiet life, on condition you deliver the band. someone once known in Swineford does not know the offer has been made.

choices.label: Refuse, and tell the band it was offered

outcome.text: You tell them what was offered and what you said. Some remain doubtful, but showing them the terms earns a measure of trust.

choices.label: Take the terms

outcome.text: Five men taken in one night on your word, a pardon under seal, and an office worth four pounds a year. Every part of it is honoured exactly as agreed.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · THE BAND THAT HELD
events.text: The band meets again with its members still free and its agreement intact. Your refusal has given them a reason to trust one another.

choices.label: Renew the agreement

outcome.text: The band renews its agreement: nobody is to be sold for a pardon. They share supplies and information, giving one another a better chance of staying free.

events.title: HONOUR AMONG THIEVES · THE OFFICE AND THE QUIET LIFE
events.text: The pardon is honoured, the office is real, and the quiet life is exactly as promised. It is a good outcome by every measure that can be written in a roll.

choices.label: Accept the official settlement

outcome.text: The authorities pay the agreed settlement and publicly accept your cooperation. Your household benefits; your former companions keep their distance.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · THE SURETY
events.text: someone once known in Swineford asks you to go surety for a debt of eight shillings. If they default, the bond falls on you, and they are asking in a doorway rather than in front of witnesses.

choices.label: Put your name to the bond

outcome.text: You sign. They pay the first three instalments early. You decide not to work out whether that is reassurance or a performance.

choices.label: Lend them the eight shillings yourself (8g)

outcome.text: Your money, no bond, no lender. It is cleaner and it makes you the creditor, which changes something between you that neither of you names.

choices.label: Say no in the doorway

outcome.text: You say no plainly. They find somebody else within a week and are perfectly civil to you for five years and never ask you for anything again.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · WHAT IS SAID AT THE ALEHOUSE
events.text: It gets back to you that someone once known in Swineford has been telling a story about you at the alehouse. It is funny, it is largely true, and it is the part you asked them never to repeat.

choices.label: Tell them you heard it

outcome.text: They go red and apologise properly, which is rare, and tell the story again eighteen months later.

choices.label: Tell a worse one about them

outcome.text: You tell a better story about them in the same room a week later. Honours are considered even by everybody except the two of you.

choices.label: Say nothing at all

outcome.text: You never mention it. It sits there, and every time they tell a story afterwards you are listening for it.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · THE OLD DEBT SURFACES
events.text: someone once known in Swineford finally says what has actually been wrong: something you did at seventeen that you had entirely forgotten and they have not, once, in twenty years.

choices.label: Apologise for the thing itself

outcome.text: Not for how they felt about it. For the thing. It takes a long time and it is the first honest hour the two of you have had in a decade.

choices.label: Say it did not happen that way

outcome.text: You are probably right about the facts. Being right about the facts turns out to have nothing whatever to do with it.

choices.label: Ask why they carried it for twenty years

outcome.text: The answer is longer and worse than the original grievance and involves three other people. You had no idea about any of it.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · MEND IT OR END IT
events.text: Twenty years of this is either about to become forty or about to stop. someone once known in Swineford is waiting and, for once, is not going to fill the silence.

choices.label: Say you would rather have them than be right

outcome.text: You say it out loud, which neither of you has ever done. It is excruciating and it works, and you are both slightly different people afterwards.

choices.label: Say it has run out

outcome.text: You say it kindly and completely. They do not argue, which tells you they had reached the same place, and you walk out of the same door separately.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · TWENTY MORE YEARS
events.text: It goes on, repaired and slightly reinforced at the join. Neither of you refers to the conversation and both of you behave differently because of it.

choices.label: Let it go on

outcome.text: They are at your table at Christmas for the next twenty years and at your burial at the end of it, and they tell that alehouse story at the wake.

memory.note: An old friendship survived being said out loud.

events.title: A FRIENDSHIP TESTED · THE SAME VILLAGE, SEPARATELY
events.text: You live four doors apart for the rest of your lives and are unfailingly polite. Both households know precisely how far the politeness goes.

choices.label: Be polite in the lane

outcome.text: Nineteen years of good mornings. At the end of it you carry one corner of their coffin because there was nobody else to do it.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · THE SAME STRIP OF GROUND
events.text: You and someone once known in Swineford hold strips that meet at a headland, and the headland has been ploughed a furrow the wrong way every year since your fathers were alive.

choices.label: Get the field jury to walk it and measure

outcome.text: Twelve men, a rope and an afternoon. The answer is that you are both wrong by about half a furrow, which satisfies neither of you.

choices.label: Plough it your way and see what happens

outcome.text: You take the furrow. They take it back in October. You take it again in spring, and by the fourth year the furrow is the only thing either of you still says to the other.

choices.label: Give them the furrow openly

outcome.text: You concede it in front of witnesses so that it cannot be conceded twice. They are graceless about it and they never touch it again.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · THE BEAST IN THE CORN
events.text: Their ox is in your corn, or your ox is in theirs. The accounts differ and the corn is equally flattened either way. The hayward is standing in the gap looking at both of you.

choices.label: Impound the beast and make them redeem it

outcome.text: Into the pound it goes, and they pay fourpence and a great deal of dignity to get it out. It is entirely lawful and it makes an enemy for a generation.

choices.label: Mend the gap together and say nothing about the corn

outcome.text: Two hours and a hurdle. Neither of you mentions whose beast it was and the gap does not open again while either of you is farming.

choices.label: Present them at the next hallmote

outcome.text: A formal presentment for a beast in the corn. The steward amerces them twopence and writes both your names in the roll next to each other.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · WHY IT ACTUALLY STARTED
events.text: An old woman mentions, without meaning anything by it, that the quarrel began over a marriage that did not happen in 1319 and has had nothing to do with land since.

choices.label: Go and tell {{other.name}}

outcome.text: They already knew. They have known since they were nine and assumed you did too, and the two of you stand in the lane feeling extremely stupid.

choices.label: Find out which family was jilted

outcome.text: It was theirs. It is a small, mean, useful piece of knowledge and you can hear yourself deciding to keep it.

choices.label: Decide it changes nothing

outcome.text: It is sixty years old and both principals are dead. Both the jilted and the jilter are sixty years in the ground. Every furrow since has been your own work.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · THE LOVEDAY OFFERED
events.text: The parish offers a loveday: both of you on the green, drink provided, and a formal end declared in front of everybody. It only works if you both actually turn up.

choices.label: Turn up

outcome.text: You are both there, both awkward, both drinking too fast. It is declared ended and, to the surprise of the whole parish, it is.

choices.label: Stay away

outcome.text: You are not there. They are, for an hour, in front of everybody, and that hour is the thing the parish remembers about the whole feud.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · THE HEADLAND SHARED
events.text: The headland is ploughed in alternate years by agreement, which is what any reasonable person would have suggested in 1319.

choices.label: Take your year

outcome.text: You alternate for thirty years without one word of disagreement, and your grandchildren have no idea there was ever anything in it.

events.title: A RIVAL RECKONING · INHERITED BY THE CHILDREN
events.text: Neither of you gives way and both of you die. The strips still meet at the headland and your children take up the furrow exactly where you left it.

choices.label: Leave it to them

outcome.text: It runs for two more generations on the same half-furrow. Nobody involved after 1360 can say what it was originally about.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · THE THIRD BAD HARVEST
events.text: Three lean years and someone once known in Swineford has stopped saying what they think about the decisions that got you here. The silence at the table is louder than the arguing was.

choices.label: Ask them directly what they would have done

outcome.text: They tell you, at length, and most of it is correct. It is not a pleasant evening and it is the first useful one in three years.

choices.label: Explain why the decisions were right

outcome.text: You give a good account of three bad harvests. They agree with all of it and go back to not saying anything.

choices.label: Give them the household accounts entirely

outcome.text: You hand over the tally and the purse and stop deciding. It is a considerable admission and the accounts are in better order by Lady Day.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · WHAT THE PARISH HAS NOTICED
events.text: The parish has noticed. Somebody asks you a kind question in the churchyard and you understand that it has been chewed over in at least seven households.

choices.label: Give an honest answer in the churchyard

outcome.text: You say it is a hard few years and leave it there. It is enough. The talk stops in five of the seven almost at once.

choices.label: Put on a very good show at the next ale

outcome.text: Two hours of visible warmth in front of sixty people. It works entirely and you both go home and do not speak.

choices.label: Let the parish talk

outcome.text: You do nothing about it and neither does {{other.name}}, which is the first thing you have agreed on in a year.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · THE THING THAT WAS NEVER SAID
events.text: someone once known in Swineford says the actual thing at last, on an ordinary Tuesday, about something that happened before the lean years and has nothing to do with money.

choices.label: Sit down and hear all of it

outcome.text: It takes until the fire is out. You do not defend yourself once. It is the hardest hour of your life and the only one that changes anything.

choices.label: Say your own version

outcome.text: You have one and it is fair. Both versions are now in the room and neither of you can put either of them away again.

choices.label: Go and see to the beasts

outcome.text: You go out to the byre for an hour. When you come back the fire is banked and they have gone up, and it is never raised again.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · WHAT THE NEXT TWENTY YEARS LOOK LIKE
events.text: Whatever is decided now is what the household is until one of you dies. There is no version of this where it simply carries on unaddressed.

choices.label: Start again, on stated terms

outcome.text: You agree, out loud, what each of you will actually do differently. It is unromantic and specific and it is the only kind that ever holds.

choices.label: Agree to live as two households under one roof

outcome.text: Separate work, separate purse, one table for the children’s sake. It is entirely functional and it is not a marriage.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · THE STATED TERMS HOLD
events.text: The terms hold, mostly, with two renegotiations and one very bad Christmas. The household comes out of the lean years intact and rather better run.

choices.label: Keep to the terms

outcome.text: Thirty more years. They are the ones who closes your eyes at the end of it and they are still cross about the second renegotiation.

events.title: STRAIN IN THE MARRIAGE · ONE ROOF, TWO HOUSEHOLDS
events.text: The arrangement works exactly as designed. The children grow up in a house that is warm, well-run and quiet in a way they cannot explain to anybody until they are forty.

choices.label: Keep the arrangement

outcome.text: It lasts. Both purses prosper, both of you are civil, and neither of you is ever asked by anybody whether it was worth it.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · WHO SAT UP WITH THE DYING
events.text: someone once known in Swineford sat up seven nights with your parent at the end. You were a day’s walk away with a holding to run, and neither of you has yet said one word about it.

choices.label: Say plainly that they did it and you did not

outcome.text: You say it without excuses. It does not make it even and it stops it becoming the thing that never gets said.

choices.label: Explain about the holding

outcome.text: It is a complete and accurate explanation. They listen to all of it and say, evenly, that they know.

choices.label: Make it up in goods (10g)

outcome.text: Ten shillings’ worth of things they need and did not ask for. They take it because they need it and it is not what was owed.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · THE DIVISION OF GOODS
events.text: The moveables have to be divided: two beds, a brass pot, the good cloak, and a psalter nobody in the family can read.

choices.label: Let {{other.name}} choose first, every time

outcome.text: They pick first on every item and take slightly less than half by weight, which you both notice and neither mentions.

choices.label: Have it appraised by two neighbours

outcome.text: Two men, an afternoon, and a written valuation. It is scrupulously fair and it turns the division of your parent’s bed into an accounting exercise.

choices.label: Take the psalter and give them the rest

outcome.text: They get everything of value and you get a book neither of you can read. In forty years your grandchild can, and it turns out to have names in the back.

memory.note: You took the family psalter over everything of value.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · WHAT WAS SAID AT THE END
events.text: someone once known in Swineford finally repeats what your parent said on the last night. It is about you, it is not kind, and there is no way of knowing whether it is being reported accurately.

choices.label: Take it as said

outcome.text: You accept it, entire, and do not ask them to soften it. It is the harder road and it removes the weapon from the argument permanently.

choices.label: Say you do not believe them

outcome.text: You may well be right. They will never forgive being called a liar about the seven nights, and that is what they heard.

choices.label: Ask what else was said

outcome.text: A great deal more, most of it about {{other.name}} and none of it kinder. They have been carrying all of it alone since the funeral.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · THE LAST OF THE FAMILY
events.text: You are the last two of your generation. Whatever the two of you settle now is what your children inherit as the family’s ordinary way of behaving.

choices.label: Settle it properly, in front of the children

outcome.text: You do it deliberately and where they can see: the nights, the goods, the words. Your children grow up in a family that repairs things.

choices.label: Divide the family and be done

outcome.text: Two households, one surname, no visits. Your children are told a version that makes sense and is not true.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · ONE FAMILY, TWO ROOFS
events.text: The families stay one family across two roofs. The cousins grow up in and out of each other’s doors and cannot imagine it having been otherwise.

choices.label: Keep the doors open

outcome.text: Both households come through two bad decades because there were always two households. Nobody afterwards can point to when it was decided.

events.title: BLOOD BETWEEN SIBLINGS · TWO FAMILIES, ONE NAME
events.text: The cousins grow up strangers with the same surname and meet properly for the first time at a funeral, where somebody has to introduce them.

choices.label: Let them be strangers

outcome.text: They are, thoroughly. In 1401 two of them marry the same family from opposite sides and neither knows the connection.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · THE ROAD ALREADY CHOSEN
events.text: someone once known in Swineford says, in the middle of an ordinary afternoon, that the life laid out for them is not the one they are going to have.

choices.label: Ask what they want instead

outcome.text: They have thought about it far more than you expected and the answer is specific, plausible and expensive.

choices.label: Explain why the road exists

outcome.text: The holding, the custom, the mouths. It is all true and they have heard it before and they were not asking about that.

choices.label: Say it can wait until after harvest

outcome.text: It waits until after harvest and then until after Christmas. By spring they have stopped raising it, which you briefly mistake for agreement.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · SOMEBODY ELSE IS ADVISING THEM
events.text: Somebody outside the household has been giving someone once known in Swineford advice, and it is better advice than yours, and they have started quoting it.

choices.label: Go and meet whoever it is

outcome.text: They are decent, competent, and have no designs on anything. It is a considerable relief and a small, specific injury.

choices.label: Forbid the connection

outcome.text: You forbid it clearly. It continues, considerably more carefully, and you are now outside a conversation you used to be inside.

choices.label: Find them a better teacher yourself

outcome.text: You spend three months and nine shillings finding somebody better. It works, and it is transparently an answer to the other one.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · WHAT THEY THINK YOU DID TO THEM
events.text: someone once known in Swineford tells you what they believe you did to them as a child. Two of the three things you have no memory of at all and one of them you remember exactly.

choices.label: Own the one you remember

outcome.text: You take that one entirely and say honestly that you do not remember the other two. It is the only answer that is not a negotiation.

choices.label: Say it did not happen like that

outcome.text: It probably did not. They have built half a life around it happening like that, and you have just told them the half life was a mistake.

choices.label: Take all three

outcome.text: You accept things you did not do to end an argument you are losing. It works immediately and it is a debt that comes due later.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · THEY ARE GOING EITHER WAY
events.text: They are leaving, or staying, and it is still genuinely open. What they are asking for is not permission. It is whether the door stays open behind them.

choices.label: Tell them the door stays open

outcome.text: You say it plainly and mean it, and you say it before they have decided, when it still costs you something to say.

choices.label: Tell them it is this house or the road

outcome.text: You put it as a choice because you are certain they will choose the house. They are on the Cambridge road inside a fortnight.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · THEY COME BACK IN MARCH
events.text: They go, and they come back in March, and they go again, and the door is open every single time. It is a considerably better arrangement than either of you expected.

choices.label: Keep the door open

outcome.text: They are at the burial and they bring their own children, who know the house and know the way in without being shown.

events.title: PARENT AND CHILD · A LETTER EVERY FOURTH YEAR
events.text: They write occasionally, briefly, and always at a distance that is carefully maintained on both sides. They are perfectly well and they do not come back.

choices.label: Keep the letters

outcome.text: Six letters in eighteen years, kept in the psalter. The last one arrives after you are already ill and you do not manage to answer it.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · WHAT YOU ARE FAIRLY SURE OF
events.text: You are fairly sure about someone once known in Swineford. Not certain. Fairly sure, on the evidence of three small things that would each be nothing on their own.

choices.label: Ask them outright

outcome.text: They deny it, well, and are careful for six weeks and then stop being careful. Now you are certain and you have used up the asking.

choices.label: Say nothing and watch

outcome.text: You watch through the summer and are entirely certain by Lammas. Four months of knowing and saying nothing changes you more than the fact does.

choices.label: Decide you do not want to know

outcome.text: You put it down deliberately. It is a real decision and it holds for three years. Most people cannot manage a fortnight.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · SOMEBODY ELSE KNOWS
events.text: A neighbour makes it clear that they know too, and that they are the sort of person who will mention it at the wrong moment for the pleasure of the thing.

choices.label: Buy their silence (10g)

outcome.text: Ten shillings and they are silent for a year and considerably more expensive after that. You have taught them exactly what it is worth.

choices.label: Tell somebody you trust first

outcome.text: You put your own version into the parish before theirs. It is a cold, effective thing to do and it works completely.

choices.label: Give them nothing to work with

outcome.text: You behave with total normality for as long as it takes them to get bored. It takes nine months and it is exhausting.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · THE CHURCH COURT SITS AT EASTER
events.text: The archdeacon’s court sits at Easter and takes presentments for adultery. A presentment means public penance in the market place, barefoot, with a candle.

choices.label: Get it ended before Easter

outcome.text: You do it yourself, quietly, with two conversations and no shouting. It ends. Whether it stays ended is another question and not one you can settle.

choices.label: Let the presentment go forward

outcome.text: The penance is performed in the market place in front of everybody who has ever known them. It is lawful, it is what the court is for, and you watched.

choices.label: Swear before the court that there was nothing in it

outcome.text: You perjure yourself in a church court to keep somebody out of the market place. It works. You are the only person in the building who knows what it cost.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · WHAT THE HOUSEHOLD IS NOW
events.text: Everything is known by everybody who matters. What remains is what the household is going to be for the next thirty years, and that is genuinely undecided.

choices.label: Rebuild it, knowing all of it

outcome.text: You start from what is actually true rather than from what should have been. It is slow, it is unglamorous, and it holds better than the first version did.

choices.label: Separate, formally and quietly

outcome.text: A separation from bed and board, done properly through the court, with the property divided. It is dignified, it is final, and the parish is disappointed by how little there is to watch.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · BUILT ON WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE
events.text: The household goes on and is, oddly, better. Nothing is assumed, which turns out to have been the trouble with it in the first place.

choices.label: Go on

outcome.text: Twenty-eight more years, one very bad month in 1371, and no more surprises of any kind. Neither of you ever explains it to anybody.

events.title: THE HIDDEN AFFAIR · SEPARATED FROM BED AND BOARD
events.text: The separation is entered in the court book and the property is divided to the halfpenny. Both households are solvent, quiet, and perfectly correct with each other.

choices.label: Sign the division

outcome.text: You sign. You see them at church every week for thirty years and exchange the same six words, and both of you mean them.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · THE FIRST HOUSE
events.text: someone once known in Swineford comes to say the sickness is in the row by the ford. Two dead in one house in a night, and the parish has to decide by morning whether that is a rumour or a fact.

choices.label: Go and see for yourself

outcome.text: You go into the house. It is a fact. You come out and say so, and the whole village believes you because you went in.

choices.label: Send for the physician before anyone says the word

outcome.text: You keep the word out of the alehouse for four days and get a man from the town who knows what he is looking at. Four days is not nothing, and it is not much.

choices.label: Buy every sound sack of grain in the parish first

outcome.text: You spend the morning buying and the afternoon telling people. By noon you own most of the food in Swineford and everyone knows what is coming.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · WHO CARRIES THE DEAD
events.text: The sexton is dead and there is nobody to carry. Bodies are going into the ground with no bearers, no bell and no words, and the households they came out of are watching from the doorways.

choices.label: Carry them yourself

outcome.text: Nine in seventeen days on a hurdle, with the words said badly from memory. You do not take it. Half the parish assumes you will.

choices.label: Pay men to carry (14g)

outcome.text: Fourteen shillings buys three men from outside the parish who do not ask questions and do not stay. Everyone is buried properly and nobody has to look at you doing it.

choices.label: Argue for a common pit outside the wall

outcome.text: It is sensible, it is quick, and it means twelve families never know which patch of ground is theirs. You win the argument on the second day.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · THE HOUSE THAT WAS PROMISED SHELTER
events.text: someone once known in Swineford took a household in on your word that it was safe to do so. It was not, and now there is sickness under a roof that had none before you spoke.

choices.label: Say plainly that it was your judgement

outcome.text: You say it in front of the household and the lane. It changes nothing about who is ill and it changes a great deal about what {{other.name}} can bear.

choices.label: Move in and nurse them yourself

outcome.text: Three weeks in a shut house. Two of the four live, which is better than the parish average, and you come out considerably worse than you went in.

choices.label: Say it was nobody’s doing

outcome.text: It is probably true and it is certainly convenient, and {{other.name}} watches you say it and does not argue.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · THE ORDER TO SHUT THE PARISH
events.text: An order comes to close Swineford entirely: no market, no road, no strangers, until the burials stop. It will hold the sickness and it will starve the poorest households by Candlemas.

choices.label: Shut the road but open the church granary

outcome.text: The parish is closed and fed at once, on the church’s stores and a great deal of shouting. It costs the rector his temper and everybody else their savings.

choices.label: Shut it completely and enforce it

outcome.text: Men on the ford with staves. The sickness stops in five weeks and three households are eating boiled nettles by the end of it.

choices.label: Refuse the order and keep the market open

outcome.text: Swineford eats all winter and buries fourteen more than it would have. You are the reason for both halves of that sentence.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · WHAT THE PARISH DID
events.text: The burials stop in March. Swineford came through with its poorest households alive and its granary empty, and both of those are somebody’s decision rather than anybody’s luck.

choices.label: Have the year written into the parish book

outcome.text: The dead, the shut road, the granary, the names of the bearers. It is read at every visitation for a century and it is entirely accurate.

memory.note: Swineford came through the pestilence with its poorest alive.

events.title: THE PESTILENCE YEAR · THE COUNT IN MARCH
events.text: The burials stop. The parish counts what it has left and finds the arithmetic came out in favour of the households that could already afford to shut their doors.

choices.label: Let the count stand

outcome.text: The names go in the book with no commentary. Two generations later the parish remembers the year and not one detail of how the burden fell.

events.title: THE CHARTER · A MARKET WITHOUT A LICENCE
events.text: Swineford has been holding a Thursday market for sixteen years without any right to. someone once known in Swineford points out that the town four miles off has finally noticed and has lawyers.

choices.label: Petition for a proper charter

outcome.text: A petition, a fee, and a great deal of standing about. It is the slow, expensive, correct road and half the parish thinks you are wasting their money.

choices.label: Find out whether an old right already exists

outcome.text: Two months in the priory’s muniments and there it is: a grant of 1204, unexercised for eighty years and never revoked. Nobody had thought to look.

choices.label: Hold the market anyway and dare them

outcome.text: Thursday comes and the market opens. The town sends a man to count the stalls and Swineford sells him a pie.

events.title: THE CHARTER · WHO PAYS THE FEE
events.text: The Crown wants forty marks for the charter. Swineford has perhaps twelve. someone once known in Swineford has begun listing which households could find the rest and how much they would want in return.

choices.label: Assess every household by what it holds

outcome.text: Nine days with the rent roll and the same argument in each doorway. Everyone pays something and nobody buys a controlling share of the market.

choices.label: Find one rich man to pay the lot

outcome.text: He pays thirty-eight marks and takes the market tolls for twenty years, which is precisely what thirty-eight marks buys.

choices.label: Put in everything you have (35g)

outcome.text: Thirty-five shillings of your own money into a charter with your name nowhere on it. Four people know. It does you no good at all and you would do it again.

events.title: THE CHARTER · THE TOWN SENDS ITS OWN PETITION
events.text: The town four miles off petitions against the grant and produces twenty merchants who will swear Swineford’s market is ruining them. someone once known in Swineford says two of the twenty have never traded there.

choices.label: Prove the two false witnesses

outcome.text: You get their own guild’s tally books and read them into the record. The petition survives and never recovers its authority.

choices.label: Offer to move Swineford’s market to Tuesday

outcome.text: A day’s difference and the whole objection evaporates. It costs Swineford the Thursday drovers and it costs nobody anything else.

choices.label: Petition against the town’s own liberties

outcome.text: You go through their charter looking for lapsed clauses and find three. It becomes a nine-year war of parchment that both sides eventually lose interest in.

events.title: THE CHARTER · WHAT GOES IN THE WORDING
events.text: The clerk is drafting. Every clause added now is law in Swineford for two centuries, and someone once known in Swineford wants a line about who may hold a stall and who may not.

choices.label: Write it open: any man of the parish may trade

outcome.text: One clause, six words, and no one is ever kept off the green for being the wrong kind of person. The wealthier stallholders argue about it for a decade and lose.

choices.label: Write it closed: freemen of the parish only

outcome.text: It protects the men who paid for the charter, exactly as they intended when they paid for it. Cottars and incomers trade from the verge for two hundred years.

choices.label: Leave the question out of the charter entirely

outcome.text: No clause at all, which means the argument is had fresh every generation by people with no document to point at.

events.title: THE CHARTER · THE SEAL COMES DOWN THE ROAD
events.text: The charter arrives with the great seal on it, and it is read at the cross in front of everybody. The wording is generous and it was fought for, clause by clause.

choices.label: Have it read aloud every Michaelmas

outcome.text: It is read at the cross every Michaelmas thereafter, in English, so that the people it protects can hear what it says.

memory.note: Swineford’s market charter was written open to every man of the parish.

events.title: THE CHARTER · SEALED AND LOCKED IN THE CHEST
events.text: The charter arrives, is read once in Latin, and goes into the parish chest. Swineford has a lawful market and a very precise list of who is allowed to stand in it.

choices.label: Lock the chest

outcome.text: The market prospers. So does the short list of families who paid for it, and in eighty years nobody can remember it was ever any other way.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · NO WRIT COMES
events.text: The quarter’s writs do not arrive. Neither does the escheator, the tax, or any word at all from Westminster. someone once known in Swineford says the last man down the road claimed there are two great seals in use.

choices.label: Call the tithings together and keep the peace locally

outcome.text: Watch, hue and cry, and a list of who is answerable for whom. Swineford governs itself from Lady Day and does it competently, which is faintly alarming.

choices.label: Send a man to find out who is actually king

outcome.text: Nine days, four shillings, and an answer that changes twice on the way home. There are two answers and both of them have armies.

choices.label: Stop paying anything to anyone

outcome.text: No tax, no tithe, no scutage, for as long as nobody is certain who to pay. Swineford is richer by Michaelmas than it has been in living memory.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · TWO COMMISSIONS, ONE ROAD
events.text: Two commissions of array arrive within a fortnight, each lawful, each demanding men, each promising to hang the parish for obeying the other.

choices.label: Answer neither and say the roads were bad

outcome.text: You send both a courteous letter about mud. It works until Whitsun. You had given it a fortnight.

choices.label: Answer whichever has the nearer army

outcome.text: Six men and a cart go north. It is the correct reading of the situation and it puts Swineford on a list held by the other side.

choices.label: Send a small party to each

outcome.text: Five men each way. Both sides are dissatisfied, neither is insulted, and two Swineford men end up on opposite sides of the same field in June.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · THE STEWARD STOPS COMING
events.text: The steward has not held a court in eight months and the manor’s business is simply stopping. someone once known in Swineford asks who is supposed to record a death, a transfer, or a marriage now.

choices.label: Hold the hallmote yourselves and keep the roll

outcome.text: You hold court, badly, with the old rolls as a guide. Every judgement is later confirmed as valid, which surprises everybody including you.

memory.note: Swineford ran its own manor court through the interregnum.

choices.label: Write it all down and wait for a steward

outcome.text: Eight months of business in one book, in order, with witnesses. When a steward finally comes he confirms the lot in an afternoon.

choices.label: Take the vacant holdings into your own hand

outcome.text: Four holdings with nobody to claim them and no court to stop you. It is defensible right up until somebody with a seal asks.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · SOMEBODY WINS
events.text: A king is proclaimed and it is the one Swineford did not answer. His officers are riding the shire asking, quite politely, what each parish did during the vacancy.

choices.label: Meet him at the boundary with the whole book

outcome.text: You hand over eight months of honest record including the parts that look bad. It is disarming, it is verifiable, and it is accepted.

choices.label: Say Swineford was loyal all along

outcome.text: You say it with total conviction and one very carefully edited roll. It holds. It holds for five years and then a clerk finds the other copy.

choices.label: Buy a pardon for the parish (30g)

outcome.text: Thirty shillings and a general pardon under seal for everything Swineford did or failed to do. It is expensive and it is completely final.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · THE WRITS COME BACK
events.text: The writs start arriving again as though they had never stopped. Swineford is back inside the realm, with its own record of the months it spent outside.

choices.label: Keep the interregnum book

outcome.text: It stays in the chest, unremarkable and complete. Twice in the next century somebody needs it, and twice it settles the matter.

events.title: THE EMPTY THRONE · THE PRICE OF BEING RIGHT LATE
events.text: Swineford is back inside the realm and firmly on the wrong side of somebody’s memory. The assessments come in high and stay high for a generation.

choices.label: Pay it and say nothing

outcome.text: The parish pays a fifth more than its neighbours for a generation and never once gets a straight answer about why.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · PRESENTED AT THE VIEW
events.text: Your name is presented at the view of frankpledge on the word of one man. The charge is small, the evidence is nothing, and the presentment is on the roll in ink.

choices.label: Find six oath-helpers and clear it at once

outcome.text: Compurgation: seven neighbours swearing to your word, not to the facts. You get twelve by noon and the presentment dies the same day.

choices.label: Find out who put your name forward and why

outcome.text: It takes three weeks and it is about a strip of headland your father ploughed wrong in 1338. Knowing this helps enormously and satisfies nobody.

choices.label: Ignore it and let it sit on the roll

outcome.text: You do nothing. It sits there, small and unresolved, and every future presentment against you is read next to it.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · THE CHARGE GROWS A SECOND HEAD
events.text: The small charge acquires a larger companion. someone once known in Swineford warns you that the second one carries the tourn rather than the manor court, and the tourn hangs people.

choices.label: Hire a man who knows the forms (12g)

outcome.text: Twelve shillings for someone who knows which words matter. He finds a defect in the presentment within an hour and looks bored doing it.

choices.label: Petition the lord for his protection

outcome.text: He gives it, in exchange for an understanding about your labour services that will cost you two days a week until you die.

choices.label: Go and stay with kin in the next hundred

outcome.text: You are outside the tourn’s reach and outside your own fields. The crop is somebody else’s problem and so, increasingly, is your reputation.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · WHAT {{other.name}} KNOWS
events.text: someone once known in Swineford can end this with one sentence in front of the steward. Saying it will put them exactly where you are standing now, and they know that better than you do.

choices.label: Ask them to say it

outcome.text: You ask, plainly, knowing what it costs. They say they will think about it and do not sleep for a week.

choices.label: Make sure they are never asked

outcome.text: You close that road off entirely and tell the pleader it does not exist. It is the most expensive decision in the whole business.

choices.label: Let the pleader call them as a witness

outcome.text: They are called, they are sworn, and they say it. You are clear by Friday and they are presented at the next view.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · THE STEWARD WANTS IT ENDED
events.text: The steward has no appetite for a hanging over a strip of headland and offers a way out that is neither acquittal nor conviction, and requires you to agree to something in public.

choices.label: Take the amercement and the loveday

outcome.text: A fine of two shillings and a public reconciliation with the man who accused you, on the green, with drink. Neither of you means a word of it and it holds for thirty years.

choices.label: Demand a full acquittal and a counter-charge

outcome.text: You get both. He is amerced, shamed, and ruined over five years, and the parish spends those five years deciding what that says about you.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · THE LOVEDAY ON THE GREEN
events.text: The reconciliation is performed on the green with the whole parish watching and a barrel provided. It is a legal fiction and it works exactly as intended.

choices.label: Drink the drink

outcome.text: You drink with him and neither of you ever refers to it again. Your children marry each other’s children, which nobody predicted at the time.

events.title: THE ACCUSED · CLEARED, AND NOT FORGIVEN
events.text: The roll records the acquittal in full. The parish records something rather different and passes it on with more care than the clerk ever managed.

choices.label: Let both records stand

outcome.text: You are clear in law and marked in memory, which turns out to be the record that gets consulted.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · MORE DOORS THAN HOURS
events.text: someone once known in Swineford has thirteen households asking and time for four. The other nine are watching to see which four, and drawing conclusions that will last decades.

choices.label: Send them to the poorest four

outcome.text: The four with nothing get seen. The seven with something remember precisely how that decision was made and by whom.

choices.label: Sort them by who is actually dying

outcome.text: You walk all thirteen doors in a morning and rank them honestly. Two of the four are people nobody would have chosen and both of them live.

choices.label: Let them be seen in order of payment

outcome.text: It is the arrangement everybody expects and nobody defends. The four who pay are seen and {{other.name}} stops meeting your eye.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · A DEATH THAT WAS PREVENTABLE
events.text: Somebody dies of a thing that could have been treated on the Tuesday. The family is not angry, which is considerably worse than if they were.

choices.label: Tell the family the truth about the Tuesday

outcome.text: They take it quietly and thank you for coming. You are never entirely sure whether it helped them and entirely sure it was owed.

choices.label: Make sure it never reaches {{other.name}}

outcome.text: You keep it from them entirely, which requires managing four other people’s conversations for a year. They find out anyway, in the worst way, from a stranger.

choices.label: Change how the doors are chosen

outcome.text: A written order of seeing, posted on the church door, argued over furiously and then simply used. Nobody dies on a Tuesday for that reason again.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · THE PHYSICIANS OBJECT
events.text: A licensed physician from the town informs the parish that someone once known in Swineford is practising unlawfully, and that he will lay it before the bishop’s court unless it stops.

choices.label: Fight the licence in the church court

outcome.text: You argue that surgery and physic are different things and win on a technicality about herbs. It is narrow and it holds for {{other.name}}’s whole life.

choices.label: Buy {{other.name}} a licence (25g)

outcome.text: Twenty-five shillings, a bishop’s clerk and an examination that is mostly Latin. They pass, barely, and are lawful for the rest of their life.

choices.label: Have them practise quietly and unpaid

outcome.text: No fee, no name, no record. It is lawful in the letter, it works, and it means {{other.name}} is poor for the rest of their life.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · MORE THAN ONE PAIR OF HANDS
events.text: It is plain that one healer for thirteen households is the actual problem, and it is equally plain that someone once known in Swineford has no intention of admitting that in public.

choices.label: Get them to take and teach two apprentices

outcome.text: It takes a winter of argument. Three pairs of hands by Whitsun, and {{other.name}} is furious about it for a year and grateful for twenty.

choices.label: Bring in a second healer over their head

outcome.text: You arrange it without asking. The parish is better served and {{other.name}} does not speak to you again for nine years.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · THREE PAIRS OF HANDS
events.text: Three healers where there was one. The burial list for the under-fives is the shortest it has been in the parish book, and nobody outside the three notices.

choices.label: Let the short list speak

outcome.text: It is entered in the book without comment. A vicar reads it in ninety years and works out what must have happened, and writes a note in the margin about it.

events.title: THE HEALER’S BURDEN · TWO HEALERS WHO DO NOT SPEAK
events.text: Swineford has two healers and they will not be in the same house. It works, in the sense that everybody gets seen, and it costs a friendship that had lasted since childhood.

choices.label: Let it be enough that it works

outcome.text: The parish is better doctored and quieter than it was. You did the right thing and it cost the wrong person.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · THE FIRE TAKES THE ROOF TREE
events.text: Your own roof goes up between vespers and dark. Everyone gets out. The roof tree, the stores, the tools and the year’s cloth do not.

choices.label: Count the people and stop counting anything else

outcome.text: You stand in the lane getting names until you have all of them. The stores are gone and every single person is standing in the road, and that is the whole account.

choices.label: Find out how it started before the ash is cold

outcome.text: You are in the wreck at first light. It started at the byre end, where nobody sleeps and nobody cooks and there is no reason on earth for a fire to begin.

choices.label: Save what will sell before the neighbours arrive

outcome.text: You get the ironwork and the good pot out and hidden before anybody comes to help. It is worth a fortnight of wages and it is watched from three doorways.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · WHERE EVERYONE SLEEPS NOW
events.text: The household is split across four other roofs. someone once known in Swineford says quietly that two of the four are being talked about as permanent, and asks what you intend.

choices.label: Insist the household stays one household

outcome.text: You get everyone under a borrowed byre roof rather than let them be absorbed. It is cold, cramped and correct, and the household exists in spring.

choices.label: Place the youngest where they will eat best

outcome.text: Two children go to households that can feed them. It is plainly right and there is a real chance they do not come back.

choices.label: Take the whole household to kin in the next parish

outcome.text: Four miles and a different manor. You keep everybody and you lose your holding, your suit of court and every claim Swineford owed you.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · IT STARTED AT THE BYRE END
events.text: Somebody in the household knows how it started. someone once known in Swineford has worked out who, has not said the name, and is waiting to see whether you ask.

choices.label: Ask, and hear the answer

outcome.text: It was carelessness by somebody who is fourteen and has not eaten properly since. You now know and can never quite unknow it.

choices.label: Say you do not want to know

outcome.text: You say it clearly enough that nobody ever raises it. The household rebuilds with one secret in it that everybody can feel and nobody can name.

choices.label: Let it be understood that a stranger did it

outcome.text: A convenient pedlar is blamed, in his absence, permanently. It protects the household and it is a lie the household has to keep for good.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · WHAT GETS REBUILT
events.text: There is timber for a smaller house or debt for the one you had. The decision is yours and everybody in the household is standing in the yard waiting to hear it.

choices.label: Build small, and build it debt-free

outcome.text: One room fewer and no money owed to anybody. It is a lesser house and the household holds it outright and sleeps.

choices.label: Borrow and rebuild exactly what was there

outcome.text: The same house, on the same footings, on twenty-two shillings of somebody else’s money at a rate you did not read carefully.

memory.note: You borrowed heavily to rebuild the house exactly as it was.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · A SMALLER ROOF, HELD OUTRIGHT
events.text: The new house is one room short of the old one and belongs to the household entirely. It is the first winter in years that nothing is owed to anybody.

choices.label: Sleep in it

outcome.text: Everybody sleeps under it and the year turns. In forty years somebody adds the missing room and nobody remembers why it was missing.

events.title: ASHES OF THE HOUSEHOLD · THE SAME HOUSE, AND THE DEBT
events.text: The house stands exactly as it did, on the same footings, and the interest falls due at Michaelmas for rather longer than anybody in the yard understood at the time.

choices.label: Make the first payment

outcome.text: It is paid, and the next, and the one after. The house is beautiful and the household works for it for five years.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · TWO SERMONS, ONE NAVE
events.text: The rector preaches obedience and the chantry priest preaches poverty, and the parish has begun sitting on two sides of the nave according to which they prefer. someone once known in Swineford asks which side your household sits on.

choices.label: Sit deliberately on the poorer side

outcome.text: You take your household across the nave in front of everybody. It is a small movement and the whole parish reads it correctly.

choices.label: Read what each of them is actually preaching

outcome.text: You get both men to write down what they hold. Neither text is heresy and neither man will say that about the other one.

choices.label: Sit with the rector and take the churchwardenship

outcome.text: You sit where the power is and are made warden by Lady Day. It is the correct move and everybody watching knows exactly what it was.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · THE ROOD SCREEN MONEY
events.text: Nine shillings collected for a new rood screen. The rector wants a rood screen. Half the parish wants it spent on the six households that lost everything in the flood.

choices.label: Get it spent on the four households

outcome.text: You take it to a vote at the parish meeting and win by three. The screen is not built and there is no argument in the parish for six years about anything else.

choices.label: Build the screen

outcome.text: It is beautiful, it is still there, and six households spent that winter in a byre looking at it every Sunday.

choices.label: Build it cheaply and give the difference away

outcome.text: A plainer screen and nine shillings to the flooded. Neither party is satisfied and both can live with it. That is what a settlement is for.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · SOMEBODY WRITES TO THE BISHOP
events.text: A letter goes to the bishop naming four parishioners as holding dangerous opinions. someone once known in Swineford has seen the list. Your household is not on it, and working out why is worse than being on it would have been.

choices.label: Warn the four

outcome.text: All four have time to think about what they will say. Two of them are very careful and two of them are not, and the difference shows.

choices.label: Find out who wrote it

outcome.text: It was the churchwarden, in the rector’s hand, over the chantry priest’s signature. All three of them are involved and none of them expected anyone to check.

choices.label: Be glad you are not on it

outcome.text: You say nothing to anybody. The four are cited, two do penance in the market place, and you watch from a doorway with everyone else.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · THE ARCHDEACON’S VISITATION
events.text: The archdeacon comes to settle it and asks the parish, formally and in writing, to state what the quarrel is. The answer given now is the one that goes into the diocesan record.

choices.label: Answer that the parish quarrelled over money and is done

outcome.text: It is true, it is unflattering to everybody equally, and it deprives both priests of a cause. The archdeacon accepts it with visible relief.

choices.label: Answer with the whole of it, names included

outcome.text: The letter, the screen money, the wardens, the lot. One priest is removed, one warden is ruined, and the parish talks about nothing else until the next rector dies.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · ONE SIDE OF THE NAVE AGAIN
events.text: People stop sitting in sides. Nothing has been resolved doctrinally and everything has been resolved practically, which is how parishes actually work.

choices.label: Sit where you always sat

outcome.text: The parish goes back to arguing about the churchyard wall, which is the correct thing for a parish to argue about.

events.title: THE DIVIDED PARISH · WHAT THE RECORD SAYS
events.text: The diocesan record contains every name and every accusation, permanently, in a fair hand. Swineford is a parish that had trouble, officially, for as long as the register survives.

choices.label: Let the record say it

outcome.text: It says it. Three families leave the parish inside eighteen months, and the two sides of the nave are still visible in where people sit in 1450.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · TWO NAMES FOR ONE WARDENSHIP
events.text: The wardenship falls vacant. someone once known in Swineford wants it and so does a man with more money, more relatives in the livery, and a rather better cellar.

choices.label: Back {{other.name}} openly

outcome.text: You put your name behind theirs early and in public, while it is still an open question and your name is still worth wagering.

choices.label: Read the guild’s own ordinances on the election

outcome.text: It turns out the wardenship is elected by all sworn brethren, not by the livery, and has been since 1311. Nobody has done it that way in thirty years.

choices.label: Let both of them bid for your support

outcome.text: You are courted for six weeks by two men with cellars. It is extremely pleasant and it costs you the respect of everyone who is watching.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · A DINNER FOR THE LIVERY
events.text: The other candidate gives a dinner for the livery three days before the vote: nine dishes, a swan, and no mention whatsoever of the election.

choices.label: Give a dinner for the whole brotherhood (24g)

outcome.text: You feed sixty men badly instead of nine men well. It costs twenty-four shillings and it makes an argument that the swan cannot answer.

choices.label: Have the dinner recorded as an election expense

outcome.text: You get it entered in the book as what it was. The ordinance against treating exists, it is read out, and the swan becomes the most famous bird in the trade.

choices.label: Go to the dinner

outcome.text: You eat the swan and vote as you had already decided. Both facts are noticed and only one of them is believed.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · THE SEARCHERS FIND FAULT
events.text: Three days before the vote, the guild searchers find fault with someone once known in Swineford’s work. It is a real fault, in a real piece, found for entirely dishonest reasons.

choices.label: Have them admit the fault and pay the fine

outcome.text: The fine is twopence and the admission is immediate. It takes the whole weapon away by refusing to pretend, and the searchers look ridiculous.

choices.label: Demand a search of the other candidate’s shop

outcome.text: They find four faults in an afternoon because there are always four faults. The election is now about searching and nobody remembers what it was about.

choices.label: Advise {{other.name}} to withdraw

outcome.text: They withdraw with the fault unadmitted, which the trade takes for guilt. It is the safe advice and it was the wrong advice.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · THE VOTE ITSELF
events.text: The brethren assemble. How the vote is taken has not been settled, and whoever settles it in the next ten minutes decides the result.

choices.label: Take it by written scrutiny, all brethren voting

outcome.text: Every sworn man votes and nobody sees how. It takes two hours, it is close, and no one afterwards can say the result was arranged.

choices.label: Take it by show of hands, livery first

outcome.text: The livery raise their hands, everyone sees who raised what, and the rest of the hall votes accordingly. It is over in four minutes.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · A WARDEN NOBODY CAN QUESTION
events.text: The warden takes the oath with a result behind them that nobody in the trade can call arranged. It is a smaller thing than it sounds and it changes how the guild runs for a generation.

choices.label: Get the scrutiny written into the ordinances

outcome.text: Written scrutiny, all brethren, every election. It survives four attempts to repeal it and outlasts everybody who voted that day.

events.title: THE GUILD ELECTION · A WARDEN AND A SHOW OF HANDS
events.text: The warden is sworn. Everybody in the hall knows how everybody else voted, and will know for the rest of their working lives.

choices.label: Let the hands speak

outcome.text: The trade runs perfectly well and rather quietly. Nobody proposes anything at a guild meeting for nine years without checking the room first.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · A CHILD AT THE PRIORY GATE
events.text: someone once known in Swineford brings word of a child boarded at the priory whose keep is paid quarterly from an account nobody will name, in coin nobody in this shire handles.

choices.label: Make sure the child is being decently kept

outcome.text: You go and look. The child is well fed, entirely alone, and has not been outside the precinct since it could walk.

choices.label: Follow the money instead of the child

outcome.text: Four quarters of payments through three hands, and the third hand is a clerk of the wardrobe. That is not a nobleman’s by-blow. That is closer than that.

choices.label: Let the right people know that you know

outcome.text: A word in the right ear and the quarterly payments acquire a small additional recipient. It is the easiest money you have ever made.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · THE PAYMENTS STOP
events.text: The quarterly payment does not come at Michaelmas, or at Christmas. The prior is a practical man and a child who costs money and earns none does not stay long.

choices.label: Pay the child’s keep yourself (20g)

outcome.text: Twenty shillings a year out of your own purse, quietly, with no explanation offered to the prior or anybody else.

choices.label: Take the child into your own household

outcome.text: One more at the table and a very large unanswered question living under your roof. The household adjusts and the question does not go away.

choices.label: Find out why the money stopped

outcome.text: Because the man who was paying it is dead, and because his executors are reading every account he kept. The child now appears in an executor’s inventory, listed between a bay gelding and thirteen yards of russet.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · MEN COME ASKING
events.text: Two men arrive who are polite, well-mounted, and entirely uninterested in Swineford. They want to know about a child boarded at the priory and they have a description.

choices.label: Tell them the child died in the winter

outcome.text: You say it steadily and the prior, to his eternal credit, says the same thing an hour later. They write it down and go, and you have just committed to something very large.

memory.note: You told the king’s men a living child was dead.

choices.label: Tell them the truth

outcome.text: The child is taken south within the week, well-horsed and well-attended, and is never heard of in this shire again by anybody.

choices.label: Ask what the child is worth to them

outcome.text: Rather a lot, it turns out, and they are willing to discuss it in a way that tells you exactly how frightened somebody in London is.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · THE CHILD ASKS
events.text: Old enough now to have worked out most of it, the child asks you directly what you know and what you intend to do with it.

choices.label: Tell them everything and let them decide

outcome.text: You give them the payments, the men, the lie, all of it. They think for three days and choose to stay exactly who they are, which was always the better claim.

choices.label: Tell them to press the claim

outcome.text: You put a young person with no friends into the path of people who employ men on good horses. It might work. It is not principally about them.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · THE CLAIM NEVER MADE
events.text: The claim is not pressed and the child grows into somebody ordinary in a village that has forgotten to be curious. It is the smallest possible ending and it was chosen.

choices.label: Let it be the small ending

outcome.text: They marry locally, hold four acres, and outlive most of the people who were frightened of them. Nothing whatever is written down.

memory.note: A royal claim was left unpressed and a life was left alone.

events.title: THE ROYAL BASTARD · THE CLAIM IN THE OPEN
events.text: The claim is made and the shire divides over it within a month. Swineford is now a place with a position, whether it wanted one or not.

choices.label: See where it goes

outcome.text: It goes a long way and not far enough. Retainers are quartered in the village for two winters and everybody is very careful about what they say at market.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · A LIST OF WHAT THE ABBEY LOST
events.text: someone once known in Swineford has a list, copied from an old inventory, of fifteen things an abbey lost in the fire of 1291. Four of them have since turned up in parish churches that have no business owning them.

choices.label: Warn the four parishes what they are holding

outcome.text: Three of them are grateful and one of them threatens you with a proctor. All four now know they may be sued in about eighteen months.

choices.label: Verify the inventory before doing anything

outcome.text: Two priories and a very unhelpful sacrist later, the inventory is genuine and the copy is not. Somebody has added a twelfth item in a newer hand.

choices.label: Go and find the remaining seven first

outcome.text: You are eight months ahead of anybody else who reads that list, and you spend all nineteen of them travelling.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · THE TWELFTH ITEM
events.text: The item added in the newer hand is not on any real inventory. Somebody wanted a thing to exist badly enough to write it into a document that everybody trusts.

choices.label: Prove the interpolation and say so

outcome.text: Ink, hand and parchment all disagree with the rest of the sheet. You are entirely right and you have just made a lot of expensive people look foolish.

choices.label: Go looking for the thing anyway

outcome.text: A forged entry does not prove the object never existed. It takes nine months and you find something, in a wall, that nobody can explain.

choices.label: Sell what you know to the abbey

outcome.text: They pay generously for the news that their own inventory was tampered with and rather more for your agreement to stop reading it.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · A COMPETITOR ON THE SAME ROAD
events.text: Somebody else is working the same list, three weeks ahead, and buying rather than asking. Two of the four parishes have already sold quietly and denied it.

choices.label: Buy the remaining two first (28g)

outcome.text: Twenty-eight shillings and both parishes are extremely relieved to deal with somebody who at least tells them what they are selling.

choices.label: Get the archdeacon to forbid all four sales

outcome.text: A monition under seal to four churchwardens. Nothing else moves, nothing is recovered either, and the competitor turns his attention to a different diocese.

choices.label: Propose you split the list

outcome.text: Six each and no bidding against one another. It is efficient, it is profitable, and it turns two searchers into one market.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · WHERE IT ALL GOES
events.text: Whatever has been gathered has to end up somewhere. The abbey that lost it in 1291 no longer exists, and four parishes, one collector and a bishop all have a case.

choices.label: Give it to the parishes it was found in, with a written history

outcome.text: Each piece goes back where it surfaced with a full account of how it got there attached. Nobody gets everything and every object gets its story.

choices.label: Keep the collection whole and keep it yourself

outcome.text: Thirteen objects in one chest under your floor, worth a very great deal and impossible to show to anybody.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · ELEVEN OBJECTS AND ELEVEN HISTORIES
events.text: Every piece sits where it was found with its own written account beside it. It is a very unusual thing to have done and two antiquaries write to you about it.

choices.label: Send them the copies

outcome.text: The histories are copied and outlive the objects by three hundred years. Nobody meant that, and it is the better half of the bargain.

events.title: THE RELIC HUNTER · THE CHEST UNDER THE FLOOR
events.text: The collection is complete, valuable beyond anything else you own, and can never be opened in front of another person for as long as you live.

choices.label: Put the boards back

outcome.text: You nail the floor down. Twice a year you take it up and look, alone, and put it back, and that is the entire use the collection ever gets.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · A CANDLE AND A COMMON BOX
events.text: someone once known in Swineford invites you into a fraternity that keeps a light burning in the church, buries its own, and pays a shilling a week to any brother too sick to work. It also meets behind a locked door.

choices.label: Join and pay your dues

outcome.text: Fourpence a quarter into the common box and your name in the brotherhood book. It is a burial club, a sick fund and, on the evidence, something else as well.

choices.label: Find out what happens behind the locked door

outcome.text: It is a burial club, a sick fund, and a meeting at which wages are discussed by men who are not allowed to discuss wages. That is precisely why the door is locked.

choices.label: Take note of who is in it

outcome.text: Seven names, and three of them work for men who would pay for that list. You do not sell it yet. You write it down.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · THE COMMON BOX IS LIGHT
events.text: The box is seven shillings short and three brothers are sick and unpaid. The steward of the box is a decent man in a bad year with a sick child of his own.

choices.label: Make the box up yourself (7g)

outcome.text: Seven shillings, replaced quietly, and the sick are paid on Friday. Two brothers work out what happened and neither of them ever says so.

choices.label: Put it to the brotherhood

outcome.text: He admits it in front of seven men, weeping, and is expelled by their own rule which does not allow for sick children. Everyone follows the rule and nobody defends it.

choices.label: Get the rule changed before anybody is accused

outcome.text: You propose relief for a brother’s household before you propose anything about the box. The rule passes, then the shortfall is raised, and it is a different meeting entirely.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · THE STATUTE AND THE LOCKED DOOR
events.text: The justices of labourers are riding the shire. A fraternity of working men meeting behind a locked door is, by the letter of the statute, a conspiracy, and the letter is what is enforced.

choices.label: Meet in the church porch with the door open

outcome.text: Everything the brotherhood does that is lawful is done in daylight where anyone may hear it. Everything else stops, and three brothers leave in disgust.

choices.label: Burn the brotherhood book

outcome.text: Fifteen names and forty years of burials, on the fire. There is now no evidence of anything, including of who is owed relief.

choices.label: Keep meeting behind the door

outcome.text: You go on exactly as before with a man watching the lane. It holds for two years, and then it holds for one more night than it should.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · A JUSTICE ASKS FOR THE NAMES
events.text: A justice of labourers asks you, under oath, for the names of every man in the fraternity. He already has four of them and wants to see whether you will give him the other three.

choices.label: Give him the brotherhood’s accounts instead

outcome.text: Forty years of burials, sick pay and candle wax, handed over entire. It is dull, it is complete, and it makes the conspiracy charge collapse under its own boredom.

choices.label: Give him the seven names

outcome.text: You say them under oath, correctly, one after another. Four are fined, two are ruined, and one of them was the man who let you in.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · THE LIGHT STILL BURNS
events.text: The fraternity survives as what it always mostly was: a light in the church, a box, and seven men who will bury each other. The other business is done elsewhere and not written down.

choices.label: Pay your quarter’s fourpence

outcome.text: You pay it for the rest of your life and the box pays your burial. The light is still burning in that church in 1520.

events.title: THE BROTHERHOOD · THE BOX IS BROKEN UP
events.text: The fraternity is dissolved, the box divided, and the light goes out. Three of the men live long enough to be old and none of them ever mentions it in your hearing.

choices.label: Take your share of the box

outcome.text: Elevenpence. You are entitled to it, you take it, and you cannot afterwards remember what you spent it on.

events.title: THE COMMON HEDGE
events.text: {{other.name}} moves a boundary hedge while you organise the village work. By dusk two households are shouting over a strip of common ground and everyone expects you to decide whether this was theft or a mistake.

choices.label: Measure the old boundary

outcome.text: You find the old stones beneath the nettles and put the hedge back where memory and mud agree it belongs.

choices.label: Back {{other.name}}

outcome.text: You declare the moved hedge reasonable. {{other.name}} remembers the loyalty; the other household remembers everything else.

choices.label: Put it before the reeve

outcome.text: The reeve restores the boundary, fines both households for wasting his morning, and thanks you by assigning next month’s ditch work.

events.title: THE MASTERS’ PRICE
events.text: {{other.name}} closes the guild-room door and lays out a simple proposal: every workshop will raise its prices together, and anyone who refuses will find supplies strangely unavailable.

choices.label: Refuse the pact

outcome.text: You keep your prices honest. Customers crowd your door, while three suppliers suddenly forget the road to your workshop.

choices.label: Join them

outcome.text: The new prices hold. Your purse grows heavier and the poorest customers begin repairing old things instead of buying yours.

choices.label: Demand a poor rate

outcome.text: You secure one price for noble orders and another for neighbours who arrive with mended sleeves. Nobody loves it, which is how you know it is a bargain.

events.title: WHAT WAS SAID IN DARKNESS
events.text: The voice behind the screen is {{other.name}}’s. The confession concerns a plan that may hurt innocent people, but repeating it would break the seal that made the truth possible.

choices.label: Keep the seal

outcome.text: You say nothing. {{other.name}} leaves knowing the secret is safe, while you spend the night wondering who may pay for that safety.

choices.label: Warn the threatened household
choices.hint: Prevent harm without naming the source

outcome.text: You deliver a warning wrapped in enough scripture to conceal its origin. The household prepares, and {{other.name}} watches you more carefully afterward.

choices.label: Report it openly

outcome.text: You name the danger and its source. The plan dies immediately, along with every honest confession likely to reach you for years.

events.title: THE FORBIDDEN GLOSS
events.text: {{other.name}} recognises the hand in a censored margin: a respected scholar condemned years ago. The erased argument is persuasive, useful, and dangerous to possess.

choices.label: Copy it in secret

outcome.text: You hide the argument inside an innocent commentary where a careful reader may recover it. Knowledge survives by learning to whisper.

memory.note: You preserved a forbidden argument inside an innocent manuscript.

choices.label: Finish the erasure
choices.hint: Protect the house; destroy the passage

outcome.text: Fresh scraping removes the last readable words. The manuscript is safe, the scriptorium is safe, and the thought exists only in your memory.

choices.label: Put it before the prior
