outcome.text: The prior reads the passage twice, locks the book away, and orders that no punishment follow. Half the house calls that mercy and half calls it fear.

events.title: ONE SPEAR MISSING
events.text: At roll call {{other.name}} is absent. You find them behind the tithe barn, shaking, with a widowed parent at home and no intention of marching toward a war they do not understand.

choices.label: Mark them sick

outcome.text: A fever appears in the roll beside {{other.name}}’s name. Their household keeps its last able pair of hands and your captain begins counting more carefully.

choices.label: Talk them back into line

outcome.text: You promise to place them in the rear rank and bring them home if promises survive battle. They return because you asked, not because the levy did.

choices.label: Make an example of them

outcome.text: {{other.name}} is bound before the whole levy. Nobody else deserts, and nobody meets your eye during the march.

events.title: TWO CLAIMS, ONE MEADOW
events.text: {{other.name}} arrives with a charter, while another household arrives with three generations of grazing and no parchment at all. Both claims are convincing. The meadow is not large enough to satisfy either.

choices.label: Uphold the old custom

outcome.text: The grazing continues as it always has. {{other.name}} folds the charter very carefully and begins asking who else doubts written law.

choices.label: Uphold the charter

outcome.text: The seal wins. The meadow changes hands before sunset, and an old household begins selling the animals it can no longer graze.

choices.label: Divide the grazing rights

outcome.text: You mark alternate grazing weeks. Both sides call it impossible and both follow the schedule once they think nobody is watching.

events.title: THE EMPTY GRANARIES
events.text: The council’s figures agree on one fact: there is not enough grain for the army, the towns, and the winter poor. {{other.name}} asks which promise should be broken first.

choices.label: Feed the poorest first

outcome.text: Army stores are opened at the church doors. The hungry eat, the captains protest, and every mother in the queue learns whose order did it.

choices.label: Keep the army supplied

outcome.text: The military granaries remain sealed. The levy will march well-fed past villages that are not.

choices.label: Buy foreign grain

outcome.text: Merchants empty your treasury and fill the quays. It is an undignified solution to hunger, which remains preferable to a dignified famine.

events.title: THE MISSING SHARE
events.text: The gang’s purse is light by twelve gold. {{other.name}} had the key, denies taking it, and offers three different explanations before anyone asks for one.

choices.label: Recover it quietly

outcome.text: You find six gold beneath a floorboard and accept that the other six purchased silence. The gang survives with a new lock and an old suspicion.

choices.label: Expel {{other.name}}

outcome.text: {{other.name}} leaves without the purse and with every name, route, and hiding place the gang has used this year.

choices.label: Forgive the debt once

outcome.text: You name the theft, forgive it, and make {{other.name}} earn the money back beside you. Half the gang calls it weakness; the other half would now follow you anywhere.

events.title: THE WRONG SEAT
events.text: Before the first loaf is cut, {{other.name}} objects to where you have seated them. The complaint is supposedly about precedence and unmistakably about an insult from twelve years ago.

choices.label: Move the whole table

outcome.text: Benches scrape, children carry trenchers, and everyone moves one place. The ancient insult survives but tonight’s supper does too.

choices.label: Give {{other.name}} the high seat
choices.hint: Win one ally; slight the rest

outcome.text: {{other.name}} receives the high seat and becomes gracious at once. Three other guests become historians.

choices.label: Make the quarrel ridiculous

success.text: You retell the old insult until even its victim laughs. By pudding, the rival households are correcting your version together.

failure.text: Your joke lands like a brick in a baptismal font. {{other.name}} leaves before supper and takes two cousins with them.

events.title: THE PARISH HEARS A NAME
events.text: Your sermon against hidden sin is still echoing when someone in the nave points at {{other.name}}. The congregation turns as one body and waits for you to confirm an accusation you never made.

choices.label: Preach mercy immediately

outcome.text: You turn the next half-hour toward mercy until pointing fingers lower. {{other.name}} remains shaken, but the parish leaves with nobody to punish.

choices.label: Let the accusation stand

outcome.text: You do not speak the name, but you do not deny it. By evening {{other.name}}’s door bears a mark in chalk and the collection plate is unusually heavy.

choices.label: Admit the sermon went too far

outcome.text: You say plainly that zeal outran wisdom. A few parishioners sneer, more look relieved, and {{other.name}} stays to help extinguish the candles.

events.title: JUDGMENT BEFORE SWINEFORD
events.text: The reeve reads the charge of an offence against local law. Evidence, reputation and old enemies now carry as much weight as truth.

choices.label: Answer every charge

success.text: Your defence exposes enough doubt for the charge to fail.

failure.text: The court rejects your defence and orders imprisonment.

choices.label: Confess and seek mercy

outcome.text: Your confession shortens the hearing, though not the memory of it.

choices.label: Purchase favourable testimony

success.text: Coin changes a witness’s certainty, and the charge collapses.

failure.text: The bribe is exposed before the court. The new charge proves easier than the old one.

beats.title: AT THE CHURCH DOOR
beats.text: {{other.name}} asks you to stand witness while two households marry off children who have met twice. The dowry is read out at the porch: eight ewes, a brass pot, and four shillings at Michaelmas.

choices.label: Stand witness and say the words
choices.text: You say the words. Four households now consider you party to the bargain. In Swineford that is as binding as a seal and rather harder to break.

memory.note: You stood witness at a betrothal made between households, not people.

choices.label: Ask aloud whether the bride consents
choices.text: The porch goes quiet. Canon law is on your side and nobody in the lane thanks you for it. She says yes, eventually, and everyone hears how long it took.

choices.label: Refuse to put your name to it
choices.text: You walk back up the lane. They find another witness inside the hour, and remember that they had to.

beats.title: THE FOUR SHILLINGS THAT NEVER CAME
beats.text: Michaelmas passes and the four shillings do not appear. {{other.name}} is fairly sure an uncle used them to settle an older debt, and has begun praying about providence at considerable volume.

choices.label: Quietly make up the shortfall (4g)
choices.text: You put four shillings on the table and let them believe it came from the uncle. Two people know otherwise, and one of them is the uncle.

memory.note: You secretly paid a dowry that was owed by somebody else.

choices.label: Name the uncle at the hallmote
choices.text: You say it in front of the steward. The uncle is amerced sixpence and swears he will remember your face longer than the debt.

choices.label: Let them work it out themselves
choices.text: You say nothing. They work it out in March, badly, in front of the whole lane.

beats.title: ONE DOOR BARRED
beats.text: The bride’s people demand the marriage go ahead. The groom’s people have barred their door and are shouting the missing shillings through it. {{other.name}} is stood in the lane between them holding the brass pot.

choices.label: Broker a smaller dowry before witnesses
choices.text: Six ewes, the pot, and the shillings forgiven. Both households sign because you made it hard to refuse in public.

choices.label: Send it to the church court
choices.text: The consistory court will hear it at Easter, or the Easter after. The bride will be nineteen by then and the pot will have been sold.

choices.label: Let the match die in the lane
choices.text: Everyone goes indoors. The ewes stay where they are, the pot comes back to you, and two households stop speaking for a generation.

beats.title: LETTERS FROM AN EARLIER LOVE
beats.text: A carter brings a bundle of letters {{other.name}} wrote to somebody else three summers ago. Read in the right room they are a precontract, which voids the marriage outright and disgraces every household named in it on the way out.

choices.label: Burn them in the hearth
choices.text: They go up quickly. {{other.name}} watches the whole time and neither of you says anything about it ever again.

memory.note: You burned letters that would have voided a marriage.

choices.label: Carry them to the priest
choices.text: The priest takes the letters as evidence for a church hearing. You gain standing for submitting them and lose {{other.name}}’s trust; no marriage is dissolved simply because a witness has arrived.

choices.label: Keep them somewhere you can find them
choices.text: You put them under the floor of the byre. They are worth nothing until the day they are worth a great deal.

memory.note: You hold letters that could dissolve a marriage whenever you choose.

beats.title: THE CHILDREN OF BOTH HOUSES
beats.text: At the Lammas ale, children of the two houses ask you what the quarrel was actually about. Nobody living now agrees on the sum, and two people have already said "ten shillings" with total confidence.

choices.label: Tell them the whole of it
choices.text: You give them the ewes, the pot, the uncle and the debt. They are disappointed by how small it all was. Nothing you could have said would have taught them more.

choices.label: Give them the kind version
choices.text: You tell them about eight ewes and a brass pot and leave the uncle out. It is a better story and it will hold for another generation.

choices.label: Tell them to mind the harvest
choices.text: They go back to the sheaves. The quarrel keeps its teeth for whoever asks next.

beats.title: THE LAST WITNESS AT THE PORCH
beats.text: The last person living who stood at that church door offers to say what really happened, but only if both households sit at one table to hear it. Everyone involved is now old, and not one of them is sorry.

choices.label: Set the table and sit them down
choices.text: It takes most of an afternoon and two jugs. Nobody apologises, but by the end they are arguing about sheep prices instead, which is as close to peace as Swineford gets.

memory.note: You got two feuding households to sit at one table and hear the truth.

choices.label: Let it die with the witness
choices.text: The witness is buried in spring and takes it with them. Both houses go on believing the version that suits them, and both are wrong.

beats.title: A CHILD AT THE THRESHOLD
beats.text: {{other.name}} carries an orphaned child to your door on the eve of Martinmas. The child owns a blanket, a wooden spoon, and no surname anyone will admit to.

choices.label: Give the child a place at your fire
choices.text: You clear a corner by the hearth. The parish is relieved, your stores are not, and the child sleeps for fourteen hours.

choices.label: Find them a place at the mill
choices.text: The miller takes the child for the work in them. It is a roof, and it is not a kindness, and you knew both when you arranged it.

choices.label: Turn them away
choices.text: You shut the door. The child is taken in three doors down by people with less than you, and Swineford counts the doors.

beats.title: THE BIRTH KIN COME BACK
beats.text: The child’s blood family appears at the gate. They do not want the child back. They want it acknowledged that the child owes them service for the roof they gave first.

choices.label: Pay them to go away (6g)
choices.text: Six shillings and they are gone by dusk. They will be back in three years, having spent it, with the same argument.

choices.label: Take it to the hallmote
choices.text: The steward rules the claim has no standing, the birth kin are amerced fourpence for troubling the court, and the whole village now knows the child’s business.

choices.label: Put it to the child
choices.text: The child stands in the gateway and picks. It takes a long time and everybody has to watch.

beats.title: THE LOAVES THAT WALKED
beats.text: You find the lardarium lighter than it should be. The child has been carrying bread out to a household that has not eaten since Tuesday, and has got quite good at it.

choices.label: Send more, and openly
choices.text: You put a basket on their step yourself. It costs you a fortnight of stores and buys you something the stores could not.

choices.label: Explain what a theft costs, then look away
choices.text: You explain leyrwite, amercement and the pillory in some detail, then go to bed early and stop counting loaves.

choices.label: Put a lock on the lardarium
choices.text: The bread stops walking. So does the child’s habit of looking at you when you come in.

beats.title: A PLACE AT THE FORGE
beats.text: A smith offers the child a seven-year indenture. The premium is two marks, and the child leaves the household the day it is sealed and does not come back.

choices.label: Pay the indenture (14g)
choices.text: The indenture is cut in two and you keep the ragged half. The child is a smith’s apprentice by Whitsun and cries on the way out of the gate.

memory.note: You paid two marks to put your foster child into a trade.

choices.label: Keep them home for the harvest
choices.text: You need the hands and you say so honestly, which does not make it land any better. The smith takes another boy.

choices.label: Send them to the priest for letters instead
choices.text: Cheaper than a forge and slower to pay. The child learns to read a rent-roll, which in Swineford is very nearly a weapon.

beats.title: WHICH NAME AT THE VIEW OF FRANKPLEDGE
beats.text: Grown now, the ward must give a surname at the view of frankpledge, in front of the tithing and the steward’s clerk, and it will be written down and kept.

choices.label: Offer them your name
choices.text: The clerk writes it without looking up. Your family gains a member and a set of complications, in that order.

memory.note: Your foster child took your surname at the frankpledge view.

choices.label: Tell them to keep their own
choices.text: They give the name they were born with, in a clear voice, and the tithing writes it down as though it had never been in doubt.

beats.title: THE UNEQUAL BOWLS
beats.text: {{other.name}} says at supper what the family has arranged silently for two generations: the eldest takes the land, and everybody else takes goodwill and a place to sleep until they marry.

choices.label: Say aloud that it is not fair
choices.text: You agree, at volume, in front of everyone. The eldest puts down the bread and does not pick it up again that evening.

choices.label: Defend the custom of the manor
choices.text: You point out that a divided holding feeds nobody. That is true. You then say it is why the thing has always been done, and that is a different argument wearing the same coat.

choices.label: Change the subject to the pig
choices.text: You raise the matter of pannage in the lord’s wood. It works, for about a year.

beats.title: THE CHRISTENING SPOON
beats.text: A silver christening spoon goes missing after supper. Four siblings remember four separate deathbed promises about it, all made in the same room, apparently on the same afternoon.

choices.label: Search every chest in the house
choices.text: You find no spoon, one hidden purse, and a letter nobody wanted read. The spoon turns up in June behind the salt.

choices.label: Buy a second spoon and say nothing (8g)
choices.text: The silversmith asks no questions for an extra penny. Two spoons now exist and the family peace rests on nobody ever putting them side by side.

memory.note: You forged family peace with a duplicate christening spoon.

choices.label: Let the accusation lie where it fell
choices.text: The blame settles on the sibling least able to argue back, which is why it settled there. Everyone is relieved and nobody says so.

beats.title: A LINE IN A DIFFERENT HAND
beats.text: {{other.name}} produces the parish copy of the will, and a witness who says the priest’s clerk took twopence to change one line of it after the sealing.

choices.label: Sue in the church court (5g)
choices.text: Probate belongs to the church and the church takes its time. Two years later a ruling arrives that pleases nobody and costs more than the land.

choices.label: Have a quiet word with the clerk
choices.text: He is very frightened and very forthcoming. You leave with six shillings of his money and a permanent hold on him.

choices.label: Let the will stand as written
choices.text: One line stays changed. The family stops shouting and starts keeping accounts of who owes whom, which lasts considerably longer.

beats.title: AT THE LAMMAS ALE
beats.text: The quarrel follows the family to the Lammas ale, where the whole village is within earshot and saying nothing looks exactly like admitting it.

choices.label: Say the grievance in the open
choices.text: You lay it out in front of forty people and a barrel. It is true, it is satisfying, and the family will be explaining it at every ale for a decade.

choices.label: Toast the family and lie beautifully
choices.text: You give a short speech about your parents that is almost entirely false and genuinely moving. Three people weep. The quarrel goes back under the table intact.

choices.label: Leave before the second barrel
choices.text: You walk home in the light. Everything said after you go is worse than anything you would have said, and all of it is attributed to you.

beats.title: WHAT THE DEAD ACTUALLY LEFT
beats.text: The last of the elder generation is buried and the heriot is paid: the best beast, gone to the lord before the family sees a penny. What is left is the land, the spoon, and every word said while fighting over both.

choices.label: Divide it evenly, whatever custom says
choices.text: You split a holding that was never meant to be split. Each share feeds one household badly instead of one household well, and nobody has to leave.

memory.note: You split the family land against custom rather than turn kin out.

choices.label: Take what the custom gives you
choices.text: You take the whole of it, lawfully, and two of your siblings are cottars by Michaelmas. The custom is on your side every single day of it.

memory.note: You took the whole inheritance by custom and left your siblings landless.

beats.title: SICKNESS AT THE MILLRACE
beats.text: {{other.name}} takes a fever after a week clearing the wet millrace. Within four days nobody in Swineford will buy flour, and the miller is standing in his own doorway watching the queue not form.

choices.label: Buy a sack in front of everyone
choices.text: You carry it home on your shoulder past the whole market. Three households buy after you and one of them tells you it was foolish.

choices.label: Keep well clear of the mill
choices.text: You grind by hand for a season and stay entirely well. The miller notices which neighbours crossed the lane to avoid his door.

choices.label: Fetch the herb-wife for them (2g)
choices.text: She comes for tuppence and stays two nights. The fever breaks on the second, and she is honest enough to say she may have had nothing to do with it.

beats.title: THE MILL HOUSE FALLS
beats.text: Three more in the mill house take it. Swineford argues over which kills faster, an empty belly or a wet cough, and grinds its corn by hand in the meantime, badly.

choices.label: Organise shared querns and shared labour
choices.text: Six households, four hand-querns, and a rota you have to referee twice a week. Everyone eats and everyone complains about the rota.

choices.label: Grind your own and say nothing
choices.text: Your household eats well and quietly. The smoke from your oven is visible from most of the lane.

choices.label: Argue for burning the mill’s stock
choices.text: You get your way and a great deal of grain goes up in the yard. The sickness stops. So does the flour, three months before harvest.

beats.title: THE CHARGE OF CONCEALMENT
beats.text: {{other.name}} mends. A customer swears at the hallmote that the mill hid the sickness for a fortnight to keep selling, and asks for an amercement and the loss of the mill’s suit.

choices.label: Swear for the mill
choices.text: You stand as an oath-helper and say the fortnight never happened. It probably did. The mill keeps its suit and you keep a debt you cannot name.

choices.label: Swear against it
choices.text: You say what you saw. The mill is amerced two shillings, the customer buys you a drink, and the miller’s family stops speaking to yours entirely.

choices.label: Swear you saw nothing at all
choices.text: The steward looks at you for slightly too long and writes it down anyway. Both sides now consider you unreliable, which is at least even-handed.

beats.title: FORTY DAYS AND THE LAST GOOD GRAIN
beats.text: A physician from the town wants the mill house shut up for forty days. The last sound grain in Swineford is inside it, and there are five weeks until harvest.

choices.label: Shut the door and go hungry
choices.text: The door is nailed and the grain sits behind it. Nobody else takes the fever and everybody else is thinner by Whitsun.

choices.label: Grind it out first, then shut the door
choices.text: Two days of grinding with the sick upstairs. Swineford eats through the summer and two more households take the fever in June.

choices.label: Pay the physician to find them well (5g)
choices.text: He writes what you paid for and rides out before dusk. The mill opens, the grain sells, and in August the parish clerk starts a longer burial list than usual.

memory.note: You paid a physician to certify a plagued house as sound.

beats.title: THE WHEEL TURNS AGAIN
beats.text: The mill runs. Swineford keeps an unusually exact memory of who carried bread up that lane and who carried accusations, and both lists are still current.

choices.label: Buy the first sack of the new grinding (4g)
choices.text: You take it at the old price in front of the market. The miller does not thank you, which is how you know it landed.

choices.label: Take your custom to the next village’s mill
choices.text: It is a four-mile walk each way and a penny more a bushel. You make it every month for a decade and never once explain why.

beats.title: A HAND ON THE WINTER ROAD
beats.text: {{other.name}} has caught half the children born in Swineford. On the ice by the ford she puts her hand through a hurdle, and by the time she reaches the village she cannot close it.

choices.label: Take her in until it mends
choices.text: She stays nine weeks and is a terrible guest. Every woman in the parish comes to your door to ask her things. It ruins your mornings and puts your household at the centre of the lane.

choices.label: Pay the barber-surgeon to set it (6g)
choices.text: He sets it badly and charges well. The hand works, mostly, and neither of you says which two fingers do not.

choices.label: Send to the next parish for a midwife
choices.text: One comes over for the worst of it and charges by the mile. It is sensible, it works, and {{other.name}} understands exactly what it means.

beats.title: THE APPRENTICE ASKS FOR A HEARTH
beats.text: The apprentice has attended four births and watched seven. She asks to use your hearth as the place she learns the rest properly, where there is light and clean water and somebody sober.

choices.label: Give her the hearth
choices.text: Your main room becomes the place Swineford is born for the better part of a decade. It costs you firewood, sleep and privacy, and the parish burial list for infants gets noticeably shorter.

choices.label: Refuse. A birth is not a lesson
choices.text: You say it plainly and she does not argue. She just looks at the fire until you leave. She learns anyway, on kitchen floors, in the dark.

choices.label: Give it, and charge for it
choices.text: A penny a birth, payable by the household concerned. It is entirely reasonable and the entire village finds it repulsive.

beats.title: THE HAND THAT WILL NOT WAIT
beats.text: {{other.name}} goes back to work far too early and hides how the fingers lock in cold weather. You watch her drop a bowl in your own kitchen and blame the frost.

choices.label: Say it aloud in front of the apprentice
choices.text: You name it in the room, once. She does not forgive you for a long time, and she stops going out alone in January.

choices.label: Keep it between the two of you
choices.text: You say nothing to anyone and she knows you saw. It holds until the winter she cannot hide it, and then it does not hold at all.

choices.label: Quietly take the heavy work off her
choices.text: You start turning up at the right moments with the right excuses. It costs you sleep and she pretends not to notice for both your sakes.

beats.title: A HARD BIRTH AT CANDLEMAS
beats.text: A birth turns bad past midnight. Master and apprentice stand on either side of the bed accusing each other of pride, and the woman on it is past caring which of them is right.

choices.label: Back the master
choices.text: Forty years of hands against two. It goes badly for an hour and then it does not, and nobody afterwards can say which of them turned it.

choices.label: Back the apprentice
choices.text: She does the thing the master called proud, and it works. The master leaves before dawn and does not attend another birth in that house.

choices.label: Put both out and send for the physician (8g)
choices.text: He arrives at first light, charges a mark, and does almost exactly what the apprentice had proposed at midnight.

beats.title: WHOSE HANDS SWINEFORD SENDS FOR
beats.text: The next child is coming and the village has already quietly decided which pair of hands it wants at the door. You had rather more to do with that than you meant to.

choices.label: Speak for the old hands
choices.text: They send for the master, as they always have. She is grateful, she is slower than she was, and everyone agrees not to mention the second thing.

choices.label: Speak for the new
choices.text: They send for the apprentice. The master hears about it the same afternoon, from someone who enjoyed telling her.

beats.title: THE MARKS ON THE MOULD
beats.text: {{other.name}} has cast every bell in three parishes and can no longer see the tuning marks scratched on the mould. The workshop opens at dawn exactly as it always has.

choices.label: Read the marks aloud for them
choices.text: You go down before the pour and call the numbers. It becomes a habit neither of you ever names, and it lasts five years.

choices.label: Tell the guild wardens
choices.text: The wardens are correct, thorough and merciless. The workshop keeps its licence and loses its commissions, which amounts to the same thing more slowly.

choices.label: Say nothing to anyone
choices.text: You leave it alone. Somebody else will see it eventually, and you will remember that you saw it first.

beats.title: THE CORRECTIONS MADE AT NIGHT
beats.text: The apprentice has been re-cutting the master’s moulds after dark and receiving neither credit nor thanks. He shows you once, by candle, and asks you to look away.

choices.label: Look away
choices.text: You go home. The bells keep ringing true and the wrong name keeps going on them, and everyone concerned has agreed to this.

choices.label: Make the master see it
choices.text: You put both of them in front of the same mould in daylight. It is a bad hour and the workshop is better run afterwards.

choices.label: Tell the apprentice to sign his own work
choices.text: He starts cutting his mark into the crown of each bell where only the founder would look. Within two years the wardens have noticed.

beats.title: THE BELL THAT CRACKED ON THE THIRD PEAL
beats.text: The new bell splits on its third ringing. The parish blames failing eyes. You have seen the guild’s bill of metal for that pour and the tin in it was cheap and poor.

choices.label: Produce the bill of metal
choices.text: You read the weights out in the churchyard in front of the wardens. The guild pays for the recast and does not forget who made them.

memory.note: You proved a guild sold bad tin and made them pay for the recast.

choices.label: Let the old eyes take the blame
choices.text: The wardens are relieved, the parish is satisfied, and the workshop is finished. You are paid a mark for a silence nobody names as such.

choices.label: Pay for the recast yourself (12g)
choices.text: Twelve shillings and no explanation offered to anyone. The parish gets its bell and spends a decade guessing why.

beats.title: THE DEED ON THE BENCH
beats.text: {{other.name}} pushes a parchment across the bench and asks you to read it out. It keeps the workshop open and puts the name over the door into somebody else’s hand entirely.

choices.label: Read it plainly, clause by clause
choices.text: You read every line including the one about the moulds. They sign anyway, but they sign knowing, which was the only thing you could give them.

choices.label: Buy the foundry yourself (30g)
choices.text: Thirty shillings, the moulds, the debts and the apprentice. The name over the door is now yours and half the parish thinks you circled it for years.

memory.note: You bought a failing bell foundry from the man who built it.

choices.label: Tell them to sign and take the pension
choices.text: They sign. There is a clause about a chair by the fire and the right to watch the pours, and it is honoured until the second winter.

beats.title: WHOSE NAME GOES ROUND THE SHOULDER
beats.text: The next bell rings clean over four fields. The inscription cut round its shoulder will be read by people who have not been born for three hundred years.

choices.label: The old master’s name
choices.text: It goes up with his mark on it and he is helped out to hear the first peal. He says it is a little flat. It is not.

choices.label: The apprentice’s name
choices.text: His mark, on the crown, in daylight, at last. The master does not come to the ringing and everyone notices the empty place.

choices.label: Yours, for paying for it
choices.text: Your name, round the shoulder, in letters a hand high. It is entirely accurate and it sounds worse every time the bell rings.

memory.note: You put your own name on a bell somebody else spent a life learning to cast.

beats.title: THE CHALICE IS GONE FROM THE AUMBRY
beats.text: The parish chalice is missing from the aumbry, and {{other.name}} was seen coming out of the north door before first light with something under a coat.

choices.label: Ask them yourself, first
choices.text: They say it was a lamb they were hiding from the reeve, and produce a lamb. The lamb is real. The timing is not.

choices.label: Raise the hue and cry
choices.text: The whole tithing turns out, as the law requires, and finds nothing. {{other.name}} spends the night in the reeve’s outhouse on the strength of your word.

choices.label: Keep what you saw to yourself
choices.text: You go home. Six people saw them come out of that door and you are the only one who has decided to be no help whatsoever.

beats.title: A SLIVER OF GILT IN THE MARKET
beats.text: A scrap of gilded rim turns up in a pedlar’s tray at market. {{other.name}} says flatly that it was planted by a man who owes them seventeen shillings and would like the debt to die with them.

choices.label: Trace where the pedlar got it
choices.text: Three days of asking ends at a tinker who bought it at Stourbridge fair from a man he cannot describe. It proves nothing and unproves nothing.

choices.label: Buy the scrap and pocket it (3g)
choices.text: Threepence and no questions asked. You now own the only piece of evidence in the parish. It sits in your purse for a month before you understand what you are carrying.

choices.label: Take it straight to the reeve
choices.text: He puts it in the box with the writs and thanks you formally. The pedlar is arrested and is very obviously not the man anyone is looking for.

beats.title: A NEW ROOF AND SEVERAL FAT HENS
beats.text: The one witness who was certain has changed his account. He also has a new roof this month, and considerably more hens than his yard can honestly explain.

choices.label: Count the hens aloud at the hallmote
choices.text: You do the arithmetic in public: a roof, nine hens, and a labourer’s wage. The steward strikes the testimony and the witness leaves the parish before Advent.

choices.label: Offer him more to change it back (10g)
choices.text: He takes it, changes his story a third time, and is now worth precisely nothing as a witness to anybody at all, yourself included.

memory.note: You paid a witness to change his testimony back.

choices.label: Let the new roof stand
choices.text: You say nothing about the hens. The case bends round the bribe the way water bends round a stone, and everyone can see the shape of it.

beats.title: THE REEVE AND THE ARCHDEACON DISAGREE
beats.text: The reeve is preparing a trial at the manor court. The archdeacon holds that a consecrated vessel is the Church’s business, and wants the relic recovered before anybody is judged for taking it.

choices.label: Back the reeve and the manor court
choices.text: Secular justice, and quickly. The archdeacon writes a letter about jurisdiction that is still being quoted in that parish forty years later.

choices.label: Back the archdeacon
choices.text: It goes to the church court, where the penalty is penance and the object comes before the person. The reeve does not speak to you until Lady Day twice over.

choices.label: Tell {{other.name}} to claim sanctuary
choices.text: Forty days in the chancel, then abjure the realm and walk to the coast barefoot carrying a cross. It is not mercy. It is not the gallows either.

beats.title: THE CHALICE COMES BACK IN A MEAL SACK
beats.text: The chalice reappears on the church step in a meal sack, undamaged, with no note. Everybody has now been accused of something and nobody has been cleared of anything.

choices.label: Declare the matter closed
choices.text: You say it loudly and often until it becomes true. Three households never speak again, and the parish is content to call that a resolution.

choices.label: Keep asking who carried the sack
choices.text: You ask for twelve months and get an answer nobody wanted. By then the parish had stopped wanting one and rather resents being given it.

beats.title: THE SILVERSMITH’S CONFESSION
beats.text: A silversmith two towns over confesses he copied that chalice fourteen years ago for a churchwarden who wanted the original sold. Which vessel was actually stolen is now an open question.

choices.label: Have the confession read in church
choices.text: The parish learns it nearly hanged a neighbour over pewter under gilt. The churchwarden’s tomb is in the chancel and cannot be asked about it.

choices.label: Pay him for his silence (8g)
choices.text: Eight shillings for his trouble and his quiet. The parish keeps its relic, its story and its grudges, and every one of them is false.

beats.title: THE ACCOUNT READ BEFORE THE PARISH
beats.text: The whole business is read out at the annual view: every accusation, every retraction, every hen. Silence from the innocent will cost as much today as speech from the guilty.

choices.label: Stand and say your own part in it
choices.text: You give your account including the parts that do you no credit at all. Two others follow you up. It is the closest the parish comes to a reckoning.

memory.note: You gave a full public account of your part in the chalice affair.

choices.label: Stay on the bench
choices.text: You keep your seat. The reading ends, everyone files out, and the whole business settles into the parish like damp into a wall.

beats.title: VENISON IN THE WRONG HOUSES
beats.text: {{other.name}} knows exactly who has been taking deer out of the lord’s wood, and knows which six households have eaten meat this winter because of it.

choices.label: Want no part of it
choices.text: You say so plainly and are not asked twice. You are also not told anything, by anybody, for a very long time afterwards.

choices.label: Take a share of the meat
choices.text: A shoulder, wrapped in sacking, left in your byre before dawn. Your household eats, and you are now inside something with no obvious door out.

choices.label: Warn the forester there is a gang
choices.text: You tell him there is a gang without telling him who. Patrols double, the poaching stops for six weeks, and somebody works out where the warning came from.

beats.title: A SNARE TAKES A FORESTER’S LEG
beats.text: A hidden snare opens a forester’s leg to the bone. Poaching the parish quietly tolerated has become a hunt for blood, and the verderers are riding for the eyre.

choices.label: Carry him in and pay the herb-wife (4g)
choices.text: You get him to the village on a hurdle and he keeps the leg. He remembers who took the front end, which turns out to matter enormously.

choices.label: Go out at night and clear the snares
choices.text: Fourteen snares in one night by moonlight. Nobody thanks you, both sides suspect you, and no forester loses a leg in that wood again.

choices.label: Be somewhere else entirely
choices.text: You are seen at the alehouse from noon to dark by nine reliable witnesses, which is the most suspicious alibi in the history of Swineford.

beats.title: A SHARE OF THE SILVER
beats.text: The gang offers you a cut of what the venison earns at market, if you can pull the village patrol off the coppice road for a single night.

choices.label: Take the silver and move the patrol
choices.text: You send them the long way on a story about a broken hurdle. Six shillings arrive wrapped in cloth two days later.

memory.note: You were paid to divert the village patrol for poachers.

choices.label: Refuse, and tell them why
choices.text: You tell them a leg is already open and the next thing opened will be a neck. They call you soft. Two of them privately agree with you.

choices.label: Take the silver and send the patrol anyway
choices.text: Three of them are taken on the coppice road with your six shillings still in your purse. It is the cleverest thing you have ever done and you sleep badly for a decade.

beats.title: THE APPROVER’S PARDON
beats.text: One of the gang is offered a pardon for turning approver: he names every accomplice from the dock, {{other.name}} among them, and fights in the lists any man who denies it.

choices.label: Stand surety for {{other.name}}
choices.text: You pledge your own goods against their appearance. If they run you are ruined, and every man in that court does the arithmetic while you are still speaking.

choices.label: Petition the lord for a common fine instead
choices.text: You argue that hanging four tenants costs the manor four tenants. The steward finds this persuasive in a way that justice had not been.

choices.label: Let the approver name whoever he names
choices.text: He names sixteen people, two of whom were nowhere near the wood. Three hang. His pardon is honoured in full and he is gone by spring.

beats.title: THE WOOD GOES QUIET
beats.text: After the eyre the wood is silent. Several households still eat because of venison buried in salt two winters ago, and loyalties considerably older than the forest law.

choices.label: Keep the buried stores moving
choices.text: You shift salt meat between four byres for another three winters. It is a small crime conducted with enormous administrative care.

choices.label: Dig it up and end it
choices.text: You burn what has gone over and return the rest. Two households go hungry in March who did not have to, and they know which choice did it.

beats.title: THE NEW FORESTER OFFERS AN AMNESTY
beats.text: A new forester offers to forget every snare in that wood, provided the village names who organised the gang. They have until Michaelmas to settle it among themselves.

choices.label: Give him the one who has already fled
choices.text: You name a man who took ship at Boston two winters back. The forester writes it down, everyone knows exactly what has happened, and the amnesty holds.

choices.label: Let the village name nobody
choices.text: Michaelmas passes in total silence. The amnesty lapses, the patrols double, and Swineford holds together in a way that costs it a great deal.

choices.label: Name who actually did it
choices.text: You say the name in the open. The amnesty holds for everybody else, and you are the man who said it for the rest of your life.

beats.title: WHEN THE DEER COME BACK TO THE COPPICE
beats.text: The deer return in numbers nobody has seen in a generation. The poorest households ask, out loud, whether the law made the wood safer or merely emptier of them.

choices.label: Say the law kept the wood
choices.text: You make the case for forest law to people whose grandparents cleared that coppice. It is a sound argument and it persuades nobody who is hungry.

choices.label: Petition for a common right of pannage
choices.text: Not deer. Pigs, in the wood, in autumn, by right. It is a smaller thing to ask for, it is granted, and it feeds Swineford every October after.

memory.note: You won Swineford a standing right of pannage in the lord’s wood.

beats.title: AN ALIBI THAT IS PARTLY TRUE
beats.text: {{other.name}} asks you to swear they were at your hearth on the night in question. They were. For roughly half of it.

choices.label: Swear to the whole night
choices.text: You give the oath entire and they walk free. The half you invented sits in the court roll in a clerk’s beautiful hand for good.

choices.label: Swear only to the hours you had them
choices.text: You give the court exactly what you know: not enough to clear them, not enough to hang them. Both sides find you useless and entirely honest.

choices.label: Refuse the oath entirely
choices.text: You will not stand up at all. They find two oath-helpers elsewhere inside a day, neither of whom was anywhere near your hearth.

beats.title: THE SECOND WITNESS IS TOO TIDY
beats.text: The accuser’s family produces a second witness whose account is cleaner than any real memory has a right to be. He has the hour, the weather, and the colour of a coat.

choices.label: Ask him what the rain did that night
choices.text: You ask in front of the steward. He answers with total confidence and gets it wrong, and the court goes very quiet indeed.

choices.label: Produce a tidier witness of your own
choices.text: You find somebody willing to be equally certain of the opposite. The court now holds two immaculate lies and no means of choosing between them.

choices.label: Let the clean story stand
choices.text: It stands, and it wins. It was the best-told story in the room, and that is what the room was always going to decide on.

beats.title: THE CLERK STILL HAS THE FIRST DRAFT
beats.text: The steward’s clerk lets slip that the testimony was rewritten after the hearing, that he kept the original, and that he is a poor man with a great fondness for being helped.

choices.label: Buy the original (9g)
choices.text: Nine shillings for one sheet of parchment that says something quite different from the roll. You are now a man who buys evidence.

choices.label: Report the clerk to the steward
choices.text: He is dismissed inside the week and the roll stands uncorrected, because correcting it would mean admitting it was wrong. Justice, administratively.

choices.label: Tell him to hide it and say nothing
choices.text: It goes into the church chest under the tithe books. It will surface in fifteen years at the worst possible moment. Neither of you says so, and both of you are counting on it.

memory.note: A rewritten testimony still exists, hidden in the church chest.

beats.title: THE LIE WAS FOR SOMEBODY ELSE
beats.text: {{other.name}} finally admits the lie was never about them at all. It was covering a third person, and naming that person now would do far more damage than the original charge ever could.

choices.label: Name the third person
choices.text: You say it and the whole shape of the case turns over. The damage is exactly as large as promised, and it lands on people who had done nothing.

choices.label: Carry the name yourself
choices.text: You carry it. It is heavier than you expected and gets no lighter, and the wrong person stays under a shadow for years because you are decent.

choices.label: Make {{other.name}} say it themselves
choices.text: You give them a month, then you stop giving them months. They say it badly, to the wrong people, and it costs them everything it would have cost you.

beats.title: THE WRONGED HOUSEHOLD ASKS FOR THE RECORD
beats.text: Years on, the household that lost the case asks the parish to correct the roll. Everybody who could be embarrassed by it is still alive, and most of them hold some kind of office.

choices.label: Get the roll corrected (6g)
choices.text: Nineteen months, two petitions and a fee. One line struck and one line added, and the family read it aloud to each other every evening for a week.

memory.note: You got a false judgment struck from the manor roll years after the fact.

choices.label: Pay them instead (15g)
choices.text: Fifteen shillings, and the record stands. They take it because they need it, and both parties understand precisely what has been bought.

choices.label: Tell them it is too late
choices.text: It is too late, factually. They knew that when they asked, and the asking was the whole of the point.

beats.title: NO HERO IN THE CORRECTED ROLL
beats.text: The finished record names no hero. It names a great many people who found a small lie easier than a difficult morning, and it names them in a clerk’s immaculate hand.

choices.label: Read it aloud at the view
choices.text: You read every name, including your own. Nobody enjoys it. It is entered in the roll as read, which is the only monument the business ever gets.

choices.label: File it in the chest unread
choices.text: It goes in with the writs and the tithe books, entirely accurate and entirely unread for the rest of the century.

beats.title: THE COPE-CHEST COMMISSION
beats.text: {{other.name}} brings the guild wardens’ commission: a carved cope-chest in seasoned oak, delivered by Michaelmas. No honest craftsman in the shire could promise that date, and the alderman’s own son wants the work.

choices.label: Promise Michaelmas and worry later
choices.text: You give them the date they wanted. The alderman’s son is furious, the wardens are delighted, and you have nine months to become somebody who can do this.

memory.note: You promised a masterpiece by a date no honest craftsman could meet.

choices.label: Give them the honest date
choices.text: You say Candlemas and explain about seasoning oak. They take it to the alderman’s son, who promises Michaelmas within the hour.

choices.label: Ask to share it with another shop
choices.text: Two shops, one mark, half the fee. The wardens dislike the arrangement and cannot fault the reasoning.

beats.title: THE OAK ARRIVES SPLIT
beats.text: The timber comes in with three boards split along the grain. The supplier stands in your yard and explains at length that your shop dried it wrong, which is not possible, because it has been in your yard for six hours.

choices.label: Take him before the guild court
choices.text: You bring the carter, the tally and the six hours. He replaces the boards and adds your shop to a list he keeps of difficult customers.

choices.label: Swallow it and buy more oak (12g)
choices.text: Twelve shillings out of your own purse and no argument in front of the apprentices. The work stays on time and the supplier does it again in spring.

choices.label: Work round the splits and say nothing
choices.text: You hide two splits inside the carcase where nobody will look for thirty years. Somebody will look in thirty years.

memory.note: There are split boards concealed inside your masterpiece.

beats.title: THE APPRENTICE HAS A BETTER JOINT
beats.text: Your apprentice proposes a housed dovetail nobody in the shire cuts. It would save five weeks and put his hand permanently beside yours in the finished work.

choices.label: Cut it his way and say whose it is
choices.text: You use the joint and tell the wardens whose idea it was. Your standing with the guild improves, and {{other.name}} trusts you with the next suggestion.

choices.label: Cut it his way and say nothing
choices.text: You take the payment and the credit. {{other.name}} knows where the joint came from and loses trust in you; no journey is needed to carry that grievance.

memory.note: The joint your masterpiece is famous for was your apprentice’s idea.

choices.label: Cut it the way it has always been cut
choices.text: Five weeks longer, the old joint, no argument with the wardens. It is the safe decision and the apprentice stops offering things.

beats.title: THE PATRON WANTS IT CHEAPER
beats.text: With six weeks left the patron asks for elm instead of oak and paint instead of carving, while still describing the piece to everyone in the county as a masterpiece.

choices.label: Refuse and finish it properly
choices.text: You finish it in oak at your own cost. The patron pays the reduced fee, tells everyone he commissioned it, and you are thirteen shillings poorer and correct.

choices.label: Give him exactly what he is paying for
choices.text: Elm, paint, and a bill that matches. It looks well from six feet and you make certain the wardens know which decisions were his.

choices.label: Take it to the wardens
choices.text: The guild rules a master may not be made to put his mark on elm. The patron pays in full, loudly, and never commissions anything in this town again.

beats.title: THE UNVEILING AT THE GUILD HALL
beats.text: The cope-chest stands in the hall with the wardens, the parish and the alderman’s son around it. Somebody is about to say aloud whose work it actually is.

choices.label: Tell the whole history of it
choices.text: The oak, the splits, the joint, the elm, the apprentice. It is a very strange speech for an unveiling. They are still repeating it in that hall forty years later, and getting the ending wrong.

memory.note: You gave a full public account of how your masterpiece was really made.

choices.label: Accept the praise and go home
choices.text: You bow, you are admired, and you leave early. The chest is beautiful and everything anybody says about it is slightly wrong.

beats.title: FOUR CARTS TO STOURBRIDGE
beats.text: {{other.name}} proposes a shared venture to Stourbridge fair: four carts, four partners, one purse. The profit is real and so are the roads between here and Cambridge.

choices.label: Put in a full share (20g)
choices.text: Twenty shillings into a common purse held by a man you have known nine years. The others put in the same and everyone shakes on it in the alehouse.

choices.label: Put in a quarter share and keep the rest
choices.text: You take a small stake and a small risk, and {{other.name}} notes exactly how small before agreeing very pleasantly.

choices.label: Lend them the money at interest instead
choices.text: You are not a partner, you are a creditor, and the difference will matter enormously in about nine months.

beats.title: ONE CART GONE IN THE NIGHT
beats.text: A cart vanishes overnight outside Huntingdon with goods belonging to every partner except {{other.name}}, whose bales were moved onto another cart the previous evening for reasons that were entirely sensible at the time.

choices.label: Say the obvious thing aloud
choices.text: You put it to them in front of the other partners. They have an answer for the bales and no answer at all for the timing.

choices.label: Insist the loss is shared four ways
choices.text: You argue it through half a night and win. Everyone loses the same amount and the partnership survives, slightly bent.

choices.label: Say nothing and start keeping notes
choices.text: You write down dates, bales and names in a little book. By Candlemas you have a very complete picture and nobody knows you have it.

beats.title: THE DRIVER COMES BACK
beats.text: The missing driver walks into Swineford three weeks later with a story about soldiers, mud, and a bargain struck at knifepoint. Roughly half of it can be checked and roughly half of it checks out.

choices.label: Believe him and pay his wages
choices.text: You pay him for the weeks he was gone. He works for you for eighteen years and never once mentions it, which is either gratitude or discipline.

choices.label: Ride to Huntingdon and check it
choices.text: Four days and a lame horse. Half the story is true. That is the worst answer he could have brought back, and you have to act on it anyway.

choices.label: Hand him to the constable
choices.text: He is held six weeks and released without charge. He does not come back to Swineford and his family stops speaking to yours entirely.

beats.title: SAFE PASSAGE, MINUS ONE
beats.text: A rival merchant offers the partnership armed escort on the Cambridge road for the rest of the season. His condition is that the poorest partner is dropped from the venture first.

choices.label: Refuse and travel unescorted
choices.text: You go without the escort and nobody is dropped. It costs you two more losses that season and the partnership never once discusses breaking up.

choices.label: Take the escort
choices.text: The poorest partner is out by Lady Day. The roads are safe, the season is excellent, and there is now an empty chair at every meeting.

memory.note: You traded a partner for safe passage on the Cambridge road.

choices.label: Buy the poor partner’s share yourself (14g)
choices.text: You buy him out at a fair price, take the escort, and hold his stake in your own name. It is generous, it is profitable, and it is not the same as loyalty.

beats.title: WHAT COMES BACK DOWN THE ROAD
beats.text: The carts come home with less silver than anyone hoped and a reputation that may prove worth more. Every merchant between here and Cambridge now knows how this partnership behaved when it went wrong.

choices.label: Renew the partnership for another season
choices.text: The same four names, or the three that are left. They sign again, which after this year is a considerably more serious thing than it was.

choices.label: Dissolve it and trade alone
choices.text: You divide the purse on the table and shake hands. It is amicable, it is final, and you are considerably richer and slower for the next ten years.

beats.title: HOURS BEYOND THE ORDINANCE
beats.text: {{other.name}} speaks for the apprentices of three shops. The guild ordinance sets the working day from dawn bell to curfew; the masters have been quietly adding two hours at each end since Lady Day.

choices.label: Back the apprentices openly
choices.text: You put your name to their complaint. Two masters stop sending you work the same week and the apprentices remember it for thirty years.

choices.label: Read the ordinance to both sides
choices.text: You find the clause, copy it, and nail it to three shop doors. Nobody can claim not to know now. That was the point, and it costs you three friendly shops by Whitsun.

choices.label: Keep out of it
choices.text: It is not your shop and not your quarrel. It becomes your quarrel by Candlemas, on worse terms.

beats.title: A CONTRACT OFFERED QUIETLY
beats.text: A master dismisses the complaint in public. In private he offers you the good commissions, first refusal, for a year, on the understanding that you have no further opinions.

choices.label: Take the contracts
choices.text: The work is genuinely good and the silence is genuinely purchased. Both facts are true at once and only one of them is discussed.

memory.note: You were paid in commissions to stop speaking for the apprentices.

choices.label: Refuse, and say what was offered
choices.text: You describe the offer word for word at the next guild meeting. The master denies it, everyone believes you, and nothing whatsoever is done about it.

choices.label: Take the contracts and speak anyway
choices.text: You take the work and go on saying exactly what you said before. He cannot withdraw it without admitting what it was for, and you both know it.

beats.title: TOOLS DOWN IN THREE SHOPS
beats.text: The apprentices lay down their tools. Three shops are silent, the unfinished orders are somebody’s wedding chest and somebody’s coffin, and the town starts losing money on the second day.

choices.label: Get both sides in one room
choices.text: Four hours, one barrel, and a written agreement about bells. It holds because everybody had to say their terms out loud in front of the other side.

choices.label: Finish the urgent orders yourself
choices.text: You work nine days straight and deliver the coffin on time. The masters are grateful and the apprentices watch you undercut the only pressure they had.

choices.label: Feed the apprentices out of your own stores
choices.text: Bread and pottage for nine young men for three weeks. It empties your lardarium and it is the reason the strike lasts long enough to win anything.

beats.title: ONE NAME OR ALL OF THEM
beats.text: The guild threatens to strike every apprentice from the register unless one of them accepts the blame in writing and is expelled for it. {{other.name}} is the obvious name and knows it.

choices.label: Put your own name on it instead
choices.text: You sign as the instigator. You are barred from guild work for two years and nine apprentices keep their indentures, and everybody in the trade knows why.

memory.note: You were struck off the guild register to save nine apprentices.

choices.label: Let {{other.name}} take it
choices.text: They sign, they are expelled, and they leave for Bristol in April. The eight who stayed are careful never to say the name out loud again.

choices.label: Tell the guild to strike off all fifteen
choices.text: You point out that nine expelled apprentices is nine shops without hands in July. The threat is quietly withdrawn and never referred to again.

beats.title: THE NEW CHARTER READ ALOUD
beats.text: A revised shop charter is read out in the guild hall: hours, bells, holidays, and the price of a broken indenture. Everybody present can hear exactly whose bad year became a permanent rule.

choices.label: Put your seal to it
choices.text: You seal it with the rest. It is worse than what was asked for and enormously better than what there was, and it outlives everyone in the room.

choices.label: Refuse to seal it
choices.text: You say it gives back less than it took and decline. The charter passes without you, and in eight years somebody quotes your refusal in a very different argument.

beats.title: THE BUSHEL THAT WEIGHS SHORT
beats.text: {{other.name}} says the great tithe was taken this year with a bushel measure that does not match the one chained in the market house. In a lean year, one-tenth measured wrong is a fortnight of somebody’s bread.

choices.label: Carry both measures to the market house
choices.text: You set them side by side in front of thirty people. The rector’s bushel is short by better than a quart and there is nothing anybody can say about it.

choices.label: Have a quiet word with the rector
choices.text: He is embarrassed, blames a servant, and the measure is corrected before Lady Day without one word said in public. Nobody is punished and everybody eats.

choices.label: Pay the tithe as measured
choices.text: You give the tenth as demanded and say nothing. Four households follow your example. The rector had been waiting all morning for exactly that.

beats.title: THE GRANARY OPENS, WITH CONDITIONS
beats.text: The rector opens the church granary and requires each household receiving grain to make its submission in writing first. The clerk has the roll ready and the grain is behind him.

choices.label: Sign first and openly
choices.text: You put your name at the head of the roll so that poorer households do not have to be the first to bend. It costs you nothing but the sight of your own signature.

choices.label: Refuse to sign and go hungry
choices.text: You walk out past the grain. Nine households sign, two do not, and the parish spends the rest of the winter deciding which of you was the fool.

choices.label: Buy grain elsewhere and share it out (12g)
choices.text: Twelve shillings of Cambridge wheat, distributed from your own yard with no roll and no clerk. The rector’s granary stays remarkably full.

beats.title: THE BISHOP’S CLERK COMES TO COUNT
beats.text: A clerk arrives from the bishop to inspect the tithe accounts. Within a day it is plain that he is much more interested in who has been loyal than in whether the arithmetic works.

choices.label: Give him the accounts, all of them
choices.text: You hand over every roll including the ones that embarrass the parish. He reads for two days and writes down four names, none of them about arithmetic.

choices.label: Coach the parish on what to say
choices.text: You spend an evening in the alehouse making sure everybody tells the same true story. He finds nothing and reports the parish sullen. A parish with nothing to hide does not close ranks.

choices.label: Give him the name he came for
choices.text: You name the churchwarden who has been selling tithe hay on the side. It is entirely true, it satisfies the clerk completely, and it ends a family in this parish.

beats.title: THE NEXT COLLECTION REFUSED
beats.text: The parish prepares to refuse the next collection outright. The rector has begun using the word excommunication in sermons, which means no burial ground and no marriages for anyone who holds out.

choices.label: Broker a modus: a fixed sum in place of the tenth
choices.text: A money payment, fixed by agreement, entered in the book. Both sides lose the argument and gain a number, which is what a settlement is.

memory.note: You settled the tithe dispute with a fixed money payment.

choices.label: Hold the refusal
choices.text: The refusal hardens religious tension and lowers public order. Your standing with the Commons rises, while the rector’s authority remains a matter for the church rather than a victory you can announce.

choices.label: Pay in full and break the refusal
choices.text: You pay the whole tenth on the first day. The refusal collapses within a week and the parish is very clear about who collapsed it.

beats.title: THE TITHE AS IT IS NOW TAKEN
beats.text: A new arrangement is proclaimed at the church door and written into the book. Every threat, bargain and short bushel of the last six years is somewhere in the wording of it.

choices.label: Have the terms read out every year
choices.text: You get it entered that the modus is to be read aloud each Lady Day. It is read for a hundred and forty years, long after nobody remembers why.

choices.label: Let it lie in the book
choices.text: It goes into the parish chest. Within a generation both sides are quoting it inaccurately and with total confidence.

beats.title: THE COMMISSION OF ARRAY
beats.text: {{other.name}} brings the writ down the lane: men, carts and grain for the king’s host, assessed at a figure Swineford could meet in a good year. This is not a good year.

choices.label: Draw up an honest assessment
choices.text: You go house by house with the tax roll and set what each can actually bear. It takes nine days and everybody hates the number and pays it.

choices.label: Plead the village down
choices.text: You take the murrain, the flood and the burial list to the commissioners in person. They cut the assessment by a third and mark Swineford as difficult.

choices.label: Offer money instead of men (20g)
choices.text: You raise twenty shillings and buy the village out of the array. No Swineford man marches, and the money is gone in a way the grain would not have been.

beats.title: NAMES OFF THE MUSTER ROLL
beats.text: Five names vanish from the roll between the drafting and the reading. All five households have made private payments to somebody, and everyone can guess to whom.

choices.label: Put the four names back
choices.text: You write them in again in front of the constable. Two of the five never speak to you again and the roll is honest for the first time in nineteen years.

choices.label: Take a payment to leave your own name off (10g)
choices.text: Ten shillings changes hands and your name is not read out. It is precisely what the five households did, and you were a great deal angrier about it in March.

memory.note: You paid to keep your own name off the muster roll.

choices.label: Read the roll as it stands
choices.text: You read out what is written. Five men who should be marching are at home, and the rest of the column noticed exactly which five.

beats.title: LOTS DRAWN IN FRONT OF THE HALL
beats.text: The Commons demand a public drawing of lots for who marches. The lord’s retainers are stood along the hall wall in mail, which is not a coincidence and is not quite a threat.

choices.label: Hold the drawing, and draw first
choices.text: You put your own hand in the bag before anybody else. You draw a short straw and it is the single most useful thing you do all year.

memory.note: You drew a lot for the levy before anyone else and lost.

choices.label: Let the steward choose the men
choices.text: He picks twelve and the retainers stay against the wall. The fourteen are the sixteen you would have expected, and the hall empties in complete silence.

choices.label: Take the place of a man with children
choices.text: You march in place of a father of four. His wife brings your household bread for six years and never explains why to anybody who asks.

beats.title: THE ESCHEATOR ASKS ABOUT THE NUMBERS
beats.text: A royal officer arrives on a rumour that Swineford falsified both its population and its harvest returns. He has the old rolls with him and a great deal of time.

choices.label: Give him the true figures
choices.text: You lay out what the village actually has. The assessment goes up by a fifth, permanently, and no one is ever hanged for it.

choices.label: Stand by the returns as filed
choices.text: Every man in the village tells him the same figure. He does not believe a word of it and cannot prove otherwise, and he says so in writing.

choices.label: Blame the dead reeve
choices.text: You put it all on a man buried three years ago who cannot argue. The officer accepts it because it is convenient, and his widow hears about it by Friday.

beats.title: THE LEVY MARCHES OUT
beats.text: They go up the Cambridge road with the carts behind them. Swineford now has to decide, out loud and for the record, whether the burden was shared or merely hidden well.

choices.label: Say plainly how it was shared
choices.text: You give the full account at the view: who paid, who marched, who bought their way clear. It is entered in the roll and read at every array afterwards.

choices.label: Let the village forget it
choices.text: Nobody says anything. By the next array the story has quietly rearranged itself so that everyone behaved rather better than they did.

beats.title: TWO SEALS, ONE MATRIX
beats.text: {{other.name}} discovers that two guild officers are issuing orders under impressions of the same seal. One matrix, two men, and a fortnight of contradictory instructions already out on the roads.

choices.label: Seize the matrix and lock it in the chest
choices.text: You take it, put it under three keys held by three men, and no order goes out for twenty days. The town is furious and the forgery stops dead.

choices.label: Recognise one officer and ignore the other
choices.text: You pick the one who is more likely to win and start honouring his orders. Half the guild does the same and the other half does the opposite.

choices.label: Take orders from whichever suits you
choices.text: For a season you have written authority for absolutely anything you care to do. It is extremely profitable and it cannot possibly last.

beats.title: THE MERCHANTS STOP TAKING SWINEFORD PAPER
beats.text: Merchants at Lynn and Stourbridge refuse anything sealed out of Swineford until somebody proves which council is lawful. Three carts of wool are sitting on a wharf accruing nothing but charges.

choices.label: Ride to Lynn and vouch for the wool yourself
choices.text: You stand surety in person for three carts on nothing but your own name. It works, it takes nine days, and your name is worth more at Lynn afterwards than it is at home.

choices.label: Sell the wool at whatever it fetches
choices.text: It goes for two-thirds and the charges eat a third of that. Everybody is paid something and nobody is paid enough.

choices.label: Leave it on the wharf and wait them out
choices.text: Eight weeks of charges and the wool is worth less than the storage. The dispute is settled the following spring, far too late for that wool.

beats.title: A CHARTER FRAGMENT IN A FAMILY CHEST
beats.text: Half a charter turns up in a dead man’s chest, granting the guild rights that neither faction had thought to claim and that the borough would very much prefer stayed lost.

choices.label: Produce it before both councils
choices.text: It is read out and it changes the argument completely. Both factions immediately begin claiming they always knew about it.

choices.label: Sell it to the borough (25g)
choices.text: The borough pays well for a document that ceases to exist the moment it is paid for. You are twenty-five shillings richer and the guild is smaller forever.

memory.note: You sold a guild charter to the borough and it was never seen again.

choices.label: Go looking for the other half
choices.text: Two years of chests, priories and one very unhelpful archdeacon. You never find it, and everybody now knows there is half a charter somewhere.

beats.title: THE CROWN OFFERS RECOGNITION
beats.text: The Crown will recognise one council and settle the whole business tomorrow. The fee is an annual payment that will bind the guild for a generation and be described in the writ as a free gift.

choices.label: Take the recognition and the debt
choices.text: Sealed by Whitsun. The guild is lawful, undisputed, and paying the Crown eight marks a year in 1390 for a quarrel settled in 1352.

choices.label: Refuse and settle it yourselves
choices.text: Four more years of argument, two ruined merchants, and a settlement written by the guild for the guild that costs it nothing annually forever.

choices.label: Go to the borough instead
choices.text: The borough will recognise the guild for less money and considerably more interference. It is a smaller collar and it is a collar.

beats.title: ONE SEAL RETURNS TO THE HALL
beats.text: A single matrix goes back into the guild chest under three keys. Its authority now rests entirely on a history that every man in the hall remembers differently and none of them wrongly.

choices.label: Have the whole history written into the book
choices.text: Four pages, both factions, the wool on the wharf, the charter. It is read to every new warden at their swearing-in for two hundred years.

choices.label: Turn the key and get back to trade
choices.text: Nobody writes it down. Inside a generation the guild is confidently telling a version in which nothing much went wrong at all.

beats.title: THE THATCH WILL NOT SEE ANOTHER WINTER
beats.text: {{other.name}} pushes a thumb through the thatch above the hearth end and it goes in to the knuckle. There are seven weeks to Martinmas and a thatcher wants nine shillings.

choices.label: Pay the thatcher properly (9g)
choices.text: Nine shillings, three days, and new reed over the whole hearth end. It is the correct decision and it empties the purse before winter.

choices.label: Patch it yourself with what you have
choices.text: Two days on the roof with old reed and borrowed spars. It will hold. It will hold in the way that things hold when you are the one who fixed them.

choices.label: Move the bed and leave it
choices.text: You shift the beds to the dry end and put a pot under the wet one. Everybody sleeps in one room until March and nobody says a word about it.

beats.title: ROT UNDER A RECENT REPAIR
beats.text: The carpenter strips back the hearth end and finds the main tie-beam soft as bread. Somebody patched over this within living memory and charged for a sound repair.

choices.label: Find out who did it and make him pay
choices.text: It was the man who is now the churchwarden. He pays for the beam rather than have it discussed, and he is never civil to you again.

choices.label: Buy the beam and say nothing (16g)
choices.text: Sixteen shillings for oak and two men to raise it. The house will stand for two hundred years and nobody will ever know why it needed to.

choices.label: Prop it and hope
choices.text: A post under the beam and a prayer. It holds for thirteen years. Nobody who signed it expected five.

memory.note: The main beam of your house is rotten and propped.

beats.title: RAIN IN THE BEDDING
beats.text: A week of rain comes through before the work is done and ruins the stored bedding. Two households are now sharing one dry room and both have opinions about who sleeps nearest the fire.

choices.label: Give up your own place by the fire
choices.text: You sleep by the door for six weeks and take a cough that lasts into April. The other household never forgets which side of the room you chose.

choices.label: Draw lots for it each week
choices.text: A rota, drawn publicly, changed every Sunday. It is fair, everybody grumbles about it, and there is not one serious quarrel all winter.

choices.label: Keep your place; it is your roof
choices.text: It is your roof, factually. You are warm all winter and the arrangement is discussed in the lane for considerably longer than the winter lasts.

beats.title: THE TIMBER GOES TO THE LORD’S GRANARY
beats.text: The oak promised to your roof is diverted to repair the lord’s granary. The steward is apologetic and entirely immovable, and the carpenter is stood in your yard with nothing to raise.

choices.label: Petition the steward at the hallmote
choices.text: You cite the custom of the manor on timber-right for repairs. It is real, and he had plainly assumed nobody in Swineford could quote it. Half the oak comes back.

memory.note: You quoted manorial custom at the steward and got your timber back.

choices.label: Buy timber from the next parish (18g)
choices.text: Eighteen shillings and a two-day haul. The roof is finished a fortnight before Martinmas and the purse is emptier than it has been in years.

choices.label: Take what you need off the granary pile at night
choices.text: Three spars, moved after dark, from a pile of forty. Nobody counts them and you spend the next five years expecting somebody to.

beats.title: THE SACKS COME UP LIGHT
beats.text: {{other.name}} finds three sacks gnawed open at the seam. The loss is larger than any rat could account for, and the granary door has a good lock on it.

choices.label: Set traps and count every sack weekly
choices.text: You catch nine rats and establish, by arithmetic, that the rats account for about a third of it. The other two-thirds have a key.

choices.label: Blame the rats and get a better cat
choices.text: A good mouser from the mill, fed on scraps, worth every one of them. The loss halves and the half that remains keeps quietly happening.

choices.label: Sit in the granary all night
choices.text: Four nights in the cold before you see who has the key. You know, now, and knowing turns out to be considerably harder than not knowing was.

beats.title: A CHILD CARRYING FLOUR AT DUSK
beats.text: A child is stopped in the lane with flour under a coat, going to a household that has had nothing since Tuesday. The child is nine and does not attempt to lie about it.

choices.label: Fill the coat properly and send them on
choices.text: You put a full measure in and walk them to the door yourself. Four households know by morning and two of them start doing the same.

choices.label: Take the child to the reeve
choices.text: The reeve is obliged to record it and does so with visible reluctance. The child is amerced twopence their family cannot pay, and everyone involved feels precisely as bad as they should.

choices.label: Take the flour back and say nothing
choices.text: The child goes home with an empty coat. Nothing is recorded, nothing is said, and nothing is eaten in that house until Friday.

beats.title: DAMP GRAIN BEHIND A NEW WALL
beats.text: Somebody has walled up a section of the granary with grain still damp behind it. By the time the smell reaches the yard, a quarter of the winter store has gone to mould.

choices.label: Break the wall out and salvage what is sound
choices.text: Two days of shovelling and sorting in a stench that gets into your clothes. You save rather more than anyone expected and lose the rest.

choices.label: Sell the doubtful sacks at market
choices.text: It goes at a good price to a buyer three villages off who does not open the sacks in your presence. You are paid and you are not proud of it.

memory.note: You sold spoiled grain at market to a buyer three villages away.

choices.label: Burn the lot in the yard
choices.text: A quarter of the winter store, on a fire, in front of the household. Nobody in Swineford is poisoned that year and nobody in your house forgives you until March.

beats.title: THE RECKONING AT WINTER’S END
beats.text: The household counts what is left in March: what was eaten, what was stolen, what was shared out and what was quietly saved. All four numbers are known and only two of them are ever said aloud.

choices.label: Say all four numbers out loud
choices.text: You read the whole account to the household including the sharing and the theft. It is a difficult evening and the granary is never short again.

choices.label: Say the two that are easy
choices.text: Eaten and spoiled. The other two numbers stay in your head, where they go on being true and go on being expensive.

beats.title: SPARKS ON YOUR OWN THATCH
beats.text: {{other.name}} is in the lane shouting that the roof next door is gone. The wind is coming your way and there are already sparks landing on your thatch.

choices.label: Wet your own roof first
choices.text: Every bucket in the house onto your own thatch. Your roof survives, theirs does not, and both of those facts are noted in the lane.

choices.label: Pull the burning roof down with hooks
choices.text: You get the fire-hooks off the church wall and drag the whole roof into the lane. It is the right answer, it saves the row, and it takes the skin off your hands.

choices.label: Get the people out and let it burn
choices.text: Three children and an old man out through the smoke, and the row goes up behind you. Everyone lives. Nothing else does.

beats.title: THREE HOUSEHOLDS, TWO ROOMS
beats.text: The fire is out. Three households now have between them two rooms with roofs on, and the frost is a fortnight off.

choices.label: Take a household into your own room
choices.text: Six people where six lived. The food goes twice as fast, nobody sleeps well, and not one of them is out of doors when the frost comes.

choices.label: Let out your byre at a fair rent
choices.text: A penny a week for the byre, which is honest, sheltered and cold. They take it and they pay it and something between you never quite comes back.

choices.label: Get the church house opened for them
