choices.text: You badger the churchwardens until they open the church house, which has stood empty for six years for no reason anybody can defend.

beats.title: A STRONGBOX IN THE ASHES
beats.text: Raking the burnt row turns up a small iron box with fifteen shillings and a ring in it. Nobody living in that row will admit to owning it, which is the most interesting thing about the box.

choices.label: Have it cried in church three Sundays
choices.text: Three Sundays and no claimant. It goes to the parish chest for the rebuilding, lawfully, and everybody knows you could have kept it.

choices.label: Keep it
choices.text: Nine shillings and a ring you never wear. Whoever it belonged to knows it was in that row, and one day may work out who did the raking.

choices.label: Split it between the three households
choices.text: Three shillings and eightpence each and the ring drawn for. It is not lawful and nobody in that lane ever raises the point.

beats.title: WHO GETS A ROOF FIRST
beats.text: The rebuilding begins and there is timber for one house before the frost. The poorest of the three families has the most children and the least claim on anybody.

choices.label: The poorest family first
choices.text: They are under a roof by Martinmas. The other two wait until spring and say, mostly, that it was right, and mean it, mostly.

memory.note: You had the poorest burnt-out family roofed before the others.

choices.label: Whoever can pay toward the timber
choices.text: The family that can find twelve shillings is roofed first, which is how it is normally done and is the reason the poorest family is the poorest family.

choices.label: Split the timber three ways and rough-roof all three
choices.text: Three bad roofs instead of one good one. All three leak, all three stand, and nobody spends the winter in somebody else’s byre.

beats.title: A RAIN-SOAKED MAP FOR FOURPENCE
beats.text: {{other.name}} buys a ruined sheet of vellum off a pedlar for fourpence. Under the water damage is a line running beneath Swineford’s oldest boundary stones, and a cross where no cross should be.

choices.label: Dry it out and read it properly
choices.text: Three days over a low fire and most of it comes back. It is a genuine survey, badly copied, of something under the mere field.

choices.label: Buy it off {{other.name}} for a shilling
choices.text: A shilling for fourpence of vellum. They take it happily and tell nine people about the profit. By Sunday the whole village knows there is a map.

choices.label: Tell them to burn it
choices.text: Maps of things under boundary stones have a way of becoming inquests. They do not burn it. They put it somewhere you cannot find it.

beats.title: BONES, TOOLS, AND A NEWER FOOTPRINT
beats.text: A night in the mere field with a spade opens a sealed chamber under the third boundary stone. There are bones in it, iron tools of a shape nobody uses, and one bootprint considerably fresher than the rest.

choices.label: Seal it up again and tell the priest
choices.text: The priest has it consecrated and blessed and firmly closed. He also asks, twice, who else had been down there, and you do not have an answer.

choices.label: Take the tools
choices.text: Five iron pieces of a make no smith in the shire recognises. They are worth money to the right person and questions to everybody else.

choices.label: Go looking for whose boot it was
choices.text: You measure it against every man in Swineford over the next month, entirely without explaining why. You find the match and you very much wish you had not.

beats.title: THE MISSING CORNER IN THE REEVE’S ARCHIVE
beats.text: The torn-off corner of the map turns up in the reeve’s own chest, filed among records of land confiscated from a family that stopped existing in this parish some ninety years ago.

choices.label: Ask the reeve about it directly
choices.text: He goes grey, says it was there when he came, and is entirely honest about that. He is much less honest about why he never mentioned it.

choices.label: Take the corner out of the chest
choices.text: You now have the whole map and a theft from the manor archive on your conscience and, potentially, on the record.

choices.label: Trace the family that stopped existing
choices.text: Ninety years of rolls and one very reluctant priory. They did not die out. They were dispossessed, and there are descendants, and they are three miles away.

memory.note: You found living descendants of a family dispossessed ninety years ago.

beats.title: THE PATH ENDS UNDER A LIVING HOUSE
beats.text: The line on the map runs out beneath a house with a family asleep in it. Whatever is down there and whoever owns the ground are now precisely the same argument.

choices.label: Tell the family what is under their floor
choices.text: You tell them everything and let them decide. They decide to do nothing at all, and they sleep on it for another forty years, and they are grateful you asked.

choices.label: Dig at night from the byre side
choices.text: Ten nights of quiet digging under somebody else’s floor. You find it. Whatever it is worth, you can never once explain how you came by it.

memory.note: You dug treasure out from under a sleeping family’s house.

choices.label: Declare it as treasure trove
choices.text: You report it to the coroner as the law requires. The Crown takes the whole of it, you are thanked in writing, and the family gets the hole in their floor filled in.

beats.title: A RELIQUARY AND A LARGE CLAIM
beats.text: {{other.name}} arrives with a small enamelled reliquary and the assertion that the finger-bone inside belonged to a saint that nobody in this diocese has heard of.

choices.label: Look at the reliquary rather than the bone
choices.text: The enamel is Limoges work and eighty years old at least. Whatever is inside it, the box is real and the box is worth more than the parish makes in a year.

choices.label: Take it to the rector at once
choices.text: He is cautious, delighted, and writing to the bishop before you are out of the door. It is out of your hands inside a week.

choices.label: Tell them to keep it in a box and say nothing
choices.text: It goes under a floorboard. It stays there for nine years and then somebody’s child finds it, at the worst possible moment, in front of a visiting archdeacon.

beats.title: PILGRIMS ON THE SWINEFORD ROAD
beats.text: Word gets out. Pilgrims come, and bring with them coin, sickness, and five competing accounts of miracles performed within sight of the reliquary.

choices.label: Sell them beds, bread and badges
choices.text: Swineford makes more in one summer than in the four years before it. It also buries nine people in August who came in already coughing.

choices.label: Limit them to the churchyard and the well
choices.text: You organise where they sleep, where they wash and where they do not go. It makes half the money and buries nobody, and the alehouse never forgives you.

choices.label: Ask the miracle-witnesses some questions
choices.text: Of six miracles, eight are weather, two are recovery from things people recover from, and one is genuinely unaccountable. You write all seven down anyway.

beats.title: THE SCHOLAR WILL NOT SPEAK OF THE BONE
beats.text: A scholar from Cambridge examines the reliquary and certifies the enamel as genuine and old. Asked directly about the bone inside it, he changes the subject three times and then leaves.

choices.label: Follow him to the gate and press him
choices.text: He tells you, quietly, that it is a sheep’s. He also tells you he will deny having said so, and that he is not the first man to have found this out.

memory.note: A scholar told you privately that the parish relic is a sheep bone.

choices.label: Let him go and publish the certificate
choices.text: The certificate says the reliquary is genuine. That is true, and it is not what anybody who reads it will think it says.

choices.label: Ask him the question in front of the parish
choices.text: He gives a beautiful eight-minute answer about the limits of scholarly method that says nothing whatsoever, and the parish is entirely satisfied by it.

beats.title: TWO CHURCHES AND AN ARMED GUARD
beats.text: A priory and a cathedral both claim the relic. There are now armed men sleeping in the church porch, and the poor of Swineford are asking loudly why holiness needs a guard.

choices.label: Give it to whichever house will take it furthest away
choices.text: It goes to the cathedral with an escort. The pilgrims follow it inside a twelvemonth and Swineford goes back to being a village with a wet field.

choices.label: Fight to keep it in the parish
choices.text: Two years of proctors and letters and one shoving match in the nave. Swineford keeps it, keeps the trade, and keeps the armed men in the porch indefinitely.

choices.label: Put the offerings to the poor and say so loudly
choices.text: Every penny in the box goes to the burnt-out and the widowed, published at the church door each quarter. Both claimant houses lose interest remarkably quickly.

memory.note: You put every penny of the relic offerings to Swineford’s poor, publicly.

beats.title: THE CHILD WHO DESCRIBED THE FLOOD
beats.text: {{other.name}} reports that a child in the lane described the mere coming over the causeway four days before a cloud was seen. It came over the causeway.

choices.label: Write down exactly what was said and when
choices.text: You take it in the child’s own words with the date and two witnesses. It is either the most valuable page in the parish or a piece of paper.

choices.label: Tell the priest at once
choices.text: He is far more worried than impressed and says three things about discernment of spirits that the family does not understand and does not like.

choices.label: Call it a coincidence, loudly
choices.text: You say the obvious thing about a wet spring and a low causeway. Half the lane agrees with you and the other half remembers, in detail, that you said it.

beats.title: A SECOND DREAM NAMES SOMETHING PRIVATE
beats.text: The child describes a thing about a household that they could not possibly have known and that two adults have spent five years making sure nobody knew.

choices.label: Get the child out of the lane for a while
choices.text: You send them to kin at Barton for the summer. The household concerned calms down, and the two who are protecting the secret work out exactly who moved the child.

choices.label: Ask the child how they knew
choices.text: They say a woman told them, and describe somebody who has been dead since before they were born, accurately, including the limp.

choices.label: Use what the child said
choices.text: You go to the household concerned and let them understand that you know. They are extremely accommodating from that day and they hate you for the rest of their lives.

memory.note: You used a child’s vision to blackmail a household.

beats.title: CROWDS AT THE DOOR ASKING ABOUT HARVESTS
beats.text: People come from three parishes to ask about weather, marriages and the price of wool. The child is eight, is frightened of them, and the family is asking for it to stop.

choices.label: Shut the door and stand in front of it
choices.text: You turn away sixty people in a month, some of them angry and more of them desperate. The child sleeps properly for the first time since Lady Day.

choices.label: Let them come, but on your terms
choices.text: You limit the questioning to one morning a week and refuse payment. Religious tension still rises a little; the smaller gathering is a boundary, not proof that the child is no longer frightened.

choices.label: Charge a penny a question
choices.text: You collect twenty gold and increase household wealth. Existing debts are not erased by the takings, and {{other.name}} trusts you less for pricing the frightened child’s answers.

beats.title: A DREAM THAT SUITS NOBODY
beats.text: The final dream contradicts what the priest has been preaching and what the lord has been planning, in the same sentence. Everybody in the parish now has to say out loud what they actually believe.

choices.label: Say you believe the child
choices.text: You say it in the nave with both of them present. It costs you the rector’s goodwill, the steward’s goodwill, and absolutely nothing that you needed.

choices.label: Say the child is ill and needs quiet
choices.text: It is the answer that ends the matter without anybody being burned or believed. The child is left alone and grows up ordinary, which was possibly the point.

choices.label: Side with the rector
choices.text: You say what the rector needs said. The dream is condemned from the pulpit, the family leaves the parish by spring, and you are on very good terms with the church.

beats.title: THE DREAMER COMES BACK GROWN
beats.text: Years on, the grown dreamer walks back into Swineford to find out which parts of the story the parish decided to keep. They are entirely ordinary now, and they want to know.

choices.label: Tell them what actually happened
choices.text: The flood, the secret, the crowds, the penny a question, what you did about each. They listen the whole way through and thank you, and they do not stay.

choices.label: Tell them the version the parish tells
choices.text: It is a better story than the truth and considerably kinder to everybody in it, including you. They know it is not right and do not press.

professional.title: THE DYER’S BLUE DEBT
professional.text: {{client}} offers a winter’s cloth on credit. The blue dye washes out in rain. {{rival}} has already promised to sell it as royal indigo.
choices: Test the dye before signing
Sell it before the weather turns
Pay a dyer to fix the cloth
professional.followup: The first rain has arrived. Your buyers bring their sleeves to the counting house as evidence.
ending: Your assay protects the buyers. The guild grants you its merchant seal.
You settle the complaints cheaply and retain a profitable, widely distrusted concern.
The corrected cloth holds its colour. Your dyer becomes the first worker in your trading concern.

professional.title: THE RIVAL’S LAST BALE
professional.text: {{rival}} claims that {{client}}’s wool bears a stolen mark. The guild may seize the entire consignment, including your stake.
choices: Call the shepherd as witness
Buy the rival’s silence
Hire a clerk to trace the sales
professional.followup: The guild opens the bales before both households. Inside one lies a very indignant living lamb.
ending: The shepherd proves your title. Your rival loses the commercial claim in open guild court.
You acquire the disputed stock and a profitable understanding with your rival.
Your clerk reconstructs the chain of sale. The household’s title is recorded for your heirs.

professional.title: THE FUNERAL BELL WARRANTY
professional.text: {{client}} orders a bell guaranteed to outlive the abbot. The mould is cracked. {{rival}} offers a coat of paint and a quiet blessing.
choices: Recast the faulty bell
Conceal the crack beneath the inscription
Hire an apprentice for a second casting
professional.followup: The bell is raised above the churchyard. Your maker’s mark sits where the whole parish can read it.
ending: Your sound casting rings through the valley. The guild accepts your masterpiece.
The bell rings badly. You keep the fee, lose the parish’s trust and acquire an enduring warranty dispute.
Your apprentice’s casting passes inspection. The workshop gains another trained pair of hands.

professional.title: THE WIDOW’S WORKSHOP
professional.text: {{client}} keeps a workshop after the master’s burial. {{rival}} petitions the guild to confiscate the tools before the candles burn down.
choices: Defend the household’s charter
Take the disputed commissions yourself
Pay a clerk to establish the succession
professional.followup: The guild court hears whether a dead master’s tools must become a living rival’s property.
ending: The charter stands. Your workshop is recognised for defending guild custom rather than abusing it.
You take the contracts and leave the widow a powerful reason to oppose you.
The succession is recorded and an apprentice is retained. Two households now stand behind your guild petition.

professional.title: THE PHYSICIAN’S GREAT SUCCESS
professional.text: {{client}} asks you to organise care for a household. {{rival}} advertises expensive bloodletting without first asking who is ill. Your own record must distinguish actual symptoms from preventive advice.
choices: Select the difficult cases
Accept every patient and every fee
Hire a medical apprentice
professional.followup: Three new patients arrive with identical complaints and contradictory instructions from the same cousin.
ending: You establish a respected practice by recording recoveries and refusing needless bleeding.
You collect substantial fees, but exhaustion and a failed treatment bring a medical scandal.
Your apprentice takes the routine dressings. Your patient recovers under continuous care.

professional.title: THE WELL OF SAINT ITCH
professional.text: Fever follows the water sold by {{client}} as a saint’s blessing. {{rival}} proposes charging double for blessed leeches.
choices: Inspect the well and separate the sick
Sell the fashionable treatment
Pay an assistant to boil cloth and water
professional.followup: The parish asks why the blessed well stands downhill from the privy. The well keeper invokes mystery.
ending: Your records persuade the parish to close the well. Fever pressure falls and your practice earns public recognition.
Your treatment harms a patient. The fees survive longer than your reputation.
Your assistant organises clean dressings and safe water. The epidemic is contained and the household keeps the records.

professional.title: THE TITHE OF THE DEAD
professional.text: {{client}} discovers that the abbey charges burial tithe on bones washed out of last year’s graves. {{rival}} calls this recurring revenue.
choices: Seek restitution for the households
Defend the abbey’s profitable custom
Pay a clerk to reconcile the burial roll
professional.followup: The archdeacon summons you to explain why one parish has buried the same tanner five times.
ending: Restitution settles the dispute. You receive formal parish responsibility.
The abbey keeps the silver. Parish hostility rises, along with your influence among its collectors.
Your clerk corrects the roll. The archdeacon recognises your administration and retains the clerk.

professional.title: THE SAINT’S HORSE TOOTH
professional.text: {{client}} seeks a ruling on the priory’s newest relic. {{rival}} has already sold indulgences for venerating what looks remarkably like a horse’s tooth.
choices: Submit the relic to an honest inquiry
Protect the priory’s profitable reputation
Hire a scholar to examine its provenance
professional.followup: The bishop requests the relic, its history and an explanation for the stable boy’s recognition of it.
ending: Your inquiry removes the false relic and wins ecclesiastical confidence.
The relic remains on display. Your influence grows, but religious tension follows the exposed lie.
The scholar identifies the tooth. The priory’s records are corrected and your learning is formally recognised.

professional.title: THE COMPANY AT THE BROKEN BRIDGE
professional.text: {{client}} brings orders to cross a broken bridge before dawn. {{rival}} proposes sending the levy first to test its strength.
choices: Find a ford and protect the levy
Force the crossing before the enemy arrives
Pay engineers to shore the bridge
professional.followup: The supply train arrives as enemy scouts appear on the far bank. The company waits for your command.
ending: Your company reaches the ford intact. You are entrusted with command on the road.
You win the crossing and lose men. The survivors fear your orders more than the enemy.
The reinforced bridge carries the convoy. A trained engineer joins your company.

professional.title: THE CAPTIVES’ EMPTY PURSES
professional.text: {{client}} brings three captured scouts. {{rival}} insists they are noblemen in unusually convincing poverty.
choices: Exchange them for your missing soldiers
Extort a ransom from their families
Hire a clerk to verify their names
professional.followup: A messenger offers peace on the road if the prisoners return alive. Your soldiers recognise one missing man’s belt.
ending: The exchange returns a living soldier and wins an honour for protecting your company.
The ransom fills your purse and turns the road into a feud.
Your clerk verifies the prisoners. A documented exchange wins Crown support and a place for the clerk.

professional.title: THE CHANCELLOR’S SALTED CAMEL
professional.text: {{client}} sends a draft levy taxing every salt camel. The realm has no camels. {{rival}} recommends retaining the revenue estimate.
choices: Rewrite the levy around actual trade
Sell exemptions before anyone notices
Hire a clerk to survey the ports
professional.followup: The council demands the promised revenue. The treasurer presents a drawing of a camel in place of payment.
ending: Your correction prevents a ruinous levy. A noble patron endorses you as a trusted adviser.
The exemptions enrich you and leave evidence of corruption in the port accounts.
Your clerk’s survey produces a workable decree and a lasting administrative office for the clerk.

professional.title: THE DEAD FALCONER’S WAGES
professional.text: {{client}} pays a falconer dead these nine years. {{rival}} claims the hawks remain loyal enough to justify his wages.
choices: Expose the accounts to the council
Sell your silence to the beneficiary
Hire an auditor to follow the payments
professional.followup: The council calls for the falconer. Someone sends a glove on a cushion. The accounts are rather more talkative.
ending: The false wages return to the treasury. Your counsel earns an official record of service.
You retain the hush money and gain a rival who holds the evidence.
Your auditor traces the payments. The treasury recovers funds and the court gains a trained clerk.
